Find all polynomials  $f$  with integer coefficients such that for all positive integers  $n$ ,
\[ n\text{ divides } \underbrace{f(f(\dots(f(0))\dots )}_{n+1\ f\text{'s}} - 1. \]

*Pitchayut Saengrungkongka*
solution_md:
Incredible problem! Congrats @MarkBcc16 for it.
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $f^a(b)$  denote  $\underbrace{f(f(\dots(f(b))\dots)}_{a \ f'\text{s}}$ .
Call  $P(n)$  the statement " $n \mid f^{n+1}(0)-1$ ".

<details><summary>General NT Polynomial Lemma (which I just realized to not have used it...)</summary>If  $f^k(c)=c$  for some integers  $c,k$  with  $k>0$ , then  $f^2(c)=c$ .

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Take  $m$  to be the minimum positive integer such that  $f^m(c)=c$ . We claim that none of  $c, f(c), f^2(c), \dots, f^{m-1}(c)$  are equal. Because if  $f^i(c)=f^j(c)$  for some  $0 \leq j < i \leq m-1 \implies c=f^m(c)=f^{m-i}(f^i(c))=f^{m-i}(f^j(c))=f^{m-(i-j)}(c)$  and thus  $m-(i-j)<m$  would be a smaller orbit for  $c$  with respect to  $f$  (contradicting minimality).

Since  $a-b \mid f(a)-f(b)$  for any distinct integers  $a$  and  $b$ , we have that  $f(c)-c \mid f^2(c)-f(c) \mid f^3(c)-f^2(c) \mid \dots \mid f^m(c)-f^{m-1}(c) \mid f^{m+1}(c)-f^m(c) = f(c)-c$  (since  $f^m(c)=c$  and all those  $c, f(c), \dots, f^{m-1}(c)$  are distinct)  $\implies |f(c)-c|=|f^2(c)-f(c)|=\dots=|f^m(c)-f^{m-1}(c)|$ . So, either  $f^i(c)-f^{i-1}(c)=f^{i+1}(c)-f^i(c)$  or  $f^i(c)-f^{i-1}(c)=-(f^{i+1}(c)-f^i(c))$ , but the second one would imply that  $f^{i-1}(c)=f^{i+1}(c) \implies m \leq 2 \implies f(f(c))=c$ , so we must have that all signs are equal. And thus, calling  $f(c)-c=f^2(c)-f(c)=\dots=f^m(c)-f^{m-1}(c)=S$  and summing up all equalities of the form  $f^{i+1}(c)-f^i(c)=S$  we get that  $0=f^m(c)-c=m \cdot S \implies S=0 \implies f(c)=c \implies m=1 \implies f(f(c))=c\ \blacksquare$</details></details>

Now, if two terms of the sequence  $0, f(0), f^2(0), \dots$  are equal, we'd have  $f^a(0)=f^b(0)$  for some  $a>b \implies f^{b+t(a-b)}(0)=f^b(0) \implies f^{b+t(a-b)+i}(0)=f^{b+i}(0)$ . But by  $P(b+t(a-b)+i-1)$  we'd get that  $b+t(a-b)+i-1 \mid f^{b+t(a-b)+i}(0)-1=f^{b+i}(0)-1$  for all  $t \geq 0 \implies f^{b+i}(0)=1$  for all  $i \geq 0 \implies f^b(0)=1$  and  $f(f^b(0))=1 \implies f(1)=1$ . But, since  $f(0) \mid f^k(0)$  (because  $f(0) \equiv 0 \pmod{f(0)}$ ) we'd have that  $f(0) \mid 1 \implies f(0) = \pm 1$  (since  $f(0) \neq 0$ ). But the same reasoning applies to  $f(f(0)) \mid f^{2k}(0) = 1$  (for  $2k \geq b$ )  $\implies f(f(0))=1$ . And thus,  $f(0)=1$  and since  $f(1)=1 \implies f^k(0)=1$ , or  $f(0)=-1$  and  $f(f(0))=1$  (if it is  $-1$ , then  $f(-1)=-1 \implies -1=f^k(0)=1$ , which is a contradiction), thus  $f(-1)=1$  and  $f(1)=1$ . And this second one implies that  $f^k(0)=1$  for all  $k \geq 2$  which both satisfies the problem statement. And so, if we have two equal terms in  $0, f(0), f^2(0), \dots$ , this gives us the families of solutions of the form  $\boxed{f(x) \equiv x(x-1)g(x)+1}$  and  $\boxed{f(x) \equiv x(x-1)(x+1)g(x)+2x^2-1}$  (which is the same as setting those values for  $f(-1)$ ,  $f(0)$  and  $f(1)$ ).

So, now we can assume that  $\boxed{\text{no two terms of }0, f(0), f^2(0), \dots\text{ are equal}\ (\clubsuit)}$ . With that, take  $N$  large enough such that  $|f^{i+1}(0)|>|f^i(0)|$  for all  $i \geq N$  (this exists by the fact that if  $f$  is non-constant, we're assuming so, otherwise  $f \equiv 1$ , then  $|f(x)| \rightarrow \infty$  when  $|x| \rightarrow \infty$ ) and, by PHP with  $(\clubsuit)$  we know it has to explode. Thus, by taking  $P(f^k(0))$  for  $k \geq N$  we have that  $f^k(0) \mid f^{f^k(0)+1}(0)-1$  and, since  $f^a(0) = f^{a-k}(f^k(0)) \equiv f^{a-k}(0) \pmod{f^k(0)}$  for  $a>k$ , we have that  $f^k(0) \mid f^{f^k(0)+1-kq}(0)-1$ , where  $0 \leq f^k(0)-kq<k$ . And, if  $f(x) \equiv x+c$ , we know that  $c=1$  and it indeed works. So, supposing  $f(x) \not\equiv x+c \implies |f^{f^k(0)+1-kq}(0)-1| \leq |f^{k-1}(0)|+1 < |f^k(0)| \implies f^{f^k(0)+1-kq}(0)-1=0 \implies f^{f^k(0)+1-kq}(0)=1$  and, as we saw, this means that  $f(0) \mid 1$  and  $f(f(0)) \mid 1 \implies$  either  $f(0)=1$  or  $f(f(0))=1$  (since we can't have both  $f(0)=f(f(0))=-1$ , otherwise we wouldn't have  $f^m(0)=1$  for some positive integer  $m$ ).

By  $(\clubsuit)$ , we know that we can't have both  $f(0)=1$  and  $f(f(0))=1$ , thus only one of those happens. Suppose  $f^2(0)=1$ , thus by  $(\clubsuit)$  we know that  $f^{f^k(0)+1-kq}(0)=1=f^2(0) \implies f^k(0)+1-kq=2 \implies k \mid f^k(0)-1$ , but since  $k \mid f^{k+1}(0)-1$  by  $P(k)$ , we get that  $f(1) \equiv f(f^k(0)) \equiv f^{k+1}(0) \equiv 1 \pmod{k} \implies k \mid f(1)-1$  for all  $k \geq N \implies f(1)=1 \implies f(f(f(0)))=f(1)=1=f(f(0))$ , leading to a contradiction by  $(\clubsuit)$ .

So, the only remaining case to check is if  $f(0)=1$  which, by  $(\clubsuit)$  would imply that  $f^k(0)+1-kq=1 \implies k \mid f^k(0)$ . But, by setting  $k=p \in \mathbb{P}$  we have that  $f^p(0) \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ . And so, by considering the orbit of  $0$  under  $f$   $\pmod{p}$  (smallest positive integer  $m$  such that  $f^m(0) \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ ) we get that  $m \mid p \implies m \in \{1, p\}$ . But if  $m=1 \implies p \mid f(0)=1$ , which is clearly a contradiction. Thus  $m=p$ , and so  $\{0, f(0), f^2(0), \dots, f^{p-1}(0)\}$  must be a complete residue system  $\pmod{p}$ . And, by the same idea used on [this problem](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h1565499p9588797), we know that if  $f(x) \not\equiv x+c$ , we can guarantee infinitely many prime numbers  $p$  dividing  $f(x)-x \implies f^{i+1}(0) \equiv f^i(0) \pmod{p}$  for some  $i \implies$  the orbit would be one, contradicting our previous observation! So, we must have  $f(x) \equiv x+c$ , and as we saw, this implies  $\boxed{f(x) \equiv x+1}$  which is indeed a solution.

And with that, we get that our solutions are either  $\boxed{f(x) \equiv x+1}$ ,  $\boxed{f(x) \equiv x(x-1)g(x)+1}$  for some  $g \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ , or  $\boxed{f(x) \equiv x(x-1)(x+1)g(x)+2x^2-1}$  for some  $g \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$  as well  $\blacksquare$</details>

Key 1: We will repeatedly use the fact that  $a - b \mid f(a) - f(b)$  for all  $a,b$  in that if  $a \equiv b \pmod n$ , then  $f(a) \equiv f(b) \pmod n$ , and so iteratively we have  $f^k(a) \equiv f^k(b) \pmod n$  for any positive integer  $k$ .
Key 2: Additionally, define  $f$  to be bijective modulo  $p$  for a prime  $p$  if  $p \mid f(a) - f(b) \iff p \mid a - b$ . So\[ p \mid a - b \iff p \mid f(a) - f(b) \iff p \mid f^2(a) - f^2(b) \iff \cdots \iff p \mid f^k(a) - f^k(b) \forall k \in \mathbb N \]In particular if  $f$  is bijective modulo  $p$ , then  $f^k(a) \equiv f^k(b)$  modulo  $p$  implies  $a \equiv b \pmod p$ .

Key 3: If  $p \mid f(0)$ , then  $f(0) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ , so using key  $1$ ,  $f^{k + 1} (0) \equiv f^k(0) \pmod p$ . Since  $f(0) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ , we can inductively get that  $f^k(0) \equiv 0 \pmod p$  for all  $k$ . We can also similarly, get that if  $p \mid f^c(0)$ ,  $p \mid f^{kc}(0)$  for any integer  $k$ .

Key 4: If  $f$  is surjective modulo  $p$  (it takes on all residues) then it is bijective modulo  $p$  as well. The proof of this is simple; note that  $f(n)$  for each  $n$  must be the same modulo  $p$  as  $f(t)$  for some  $t \in [0,p-1]$  ( $t$  is the remainder when  $n$  is divided by  $p$ ). Thus,  $\{f(0), f(1), \ldots, f(p-1)\}$  must take on all residues modulo  $p$ . But since it has  $p$  elements, every two elements must be different modulo  $p$ . So if  $f(a) \equiv f(b) \pmod p$ , but  $p \nmid b - a$ , then let  $r,s$  be the remainders when  $a,b$  are divided by  $p$ , respectively. Clearly  $f(r) \equiv f(a) \equiv f(b) \equiv f(s) \pmod p$ , a contradiction.

Key 5: If  $f^a(t) \equiv f^{a+d}(t)  \pmod n$  for some positive integers  $a,d,t,n$ , note that by taking  $f^{kd}$  of both sides gives that\[ f^{a + kd} (t) \equiv f^{a + (k + 1) d} (t) \pmod n,\]so inductively we have that  $f^a(t) \equiv f^{a + md}(t) \pmod n$ .

Now, if $f(1) \neq 1$ , then $f^3(0) = 1$ can be the only occurrence of $1$ in the sequence, or else we get a cycle that can be exploited by taking $N$ large. As a result, if this case occurs infinitely many times, then $f^{\ell}(0) \equiv 3 \pmod{\ell}$ for infinitely many $\ell$ . However, $f^{\ell+1}(0) \equiv 1 \pmod{\ell}$ , so we have $f(3) \equiv 1 \pmod{\ell}$ for infinitely many $\ell$ . Therefore, $f(3) = 1$ , but this is a contradiction since $4 \nmid f(3) - f(-1)$ . As a result, there exists an integer $\ell$ such that for all peaks $\ell > N$ , $f^k(0) = f^{\ell}(0)+1$ . Therefore, the function \begin{align*} g(n) \coloneq \operatorname{max}(|f(0)|, |f(f(0))|, \dots, |f^n(0)|)\end{align*} increases by at most $1$ at each step. In other words, $g(n+1) - g(n) \le 1$ . If there are infinite $n$ such that $g(n+1) = g(n)$ , then $g(n) < n$ for large enough $n$ , which is a contradiction. Therefore, there exists some $N'$ such that for all $n > N'$ , we have $s_n = f^{n+1}(0) - f^n(0) = -1$ , contradicting $|s_n|$ being unbounded. $\square$ Now, clearly this implies $|s_n|$ achieves a constant value for sufficiently large $n$ . If there exists some $i$ such that $s_i + s_{i+1} = 0$ , then $f^{i}(0) = f^{i+2}(0)$ , which gives us a contradiction by taking large $N$ with $2 \nmid N-i$ . As a result $s_n$ achieves a constant value, which we denote as $\ell$ , for large $n \ge m$ . First, assume $\ell$ is non-zero. We also let $f^m(0) = z$ for brevity. Now, \begin{align*} m+k \mid f^{m+k+1}(0) - 1 = z - 1 + \ell (k+1) \equiv z-1 - \ell (m-1) \end{align*} which implies $\ell = \tfrac{z-1}{m-1}$ , from taking large $k$ . This means that $\ell = \tfrac{s_1 + s_2 + \cdots + s_{m-1}}{m-1}$ is precisely the average of the first $s_i$ entries, and since $|s_i|$ is non-decreasing, this implies all $s_i = \ell$ , for $i > 1.$ Now, this implies that $f^{n+1}(0) = n\ell \pm 1$ for all $n$ , but from the divisibility assertion, we find that only the $f(0) = 1$ case is possible. Now, notice that this implies $f(k) - k = \ell$ has infinitely many solutions, so $f \equiv x + \ell$ , but since $f(0) = 1$ , this corresponds to $f \equiv x+1$ . Finally, if $\ell = 0$ , then there must be a fixed point along the sequence of $f^k(0)$ . From the divisibility condition, it is clear that this fixed point must be $1$ , implying that $f(1) = 1$ . Now, $f(0) = 1$ simply corresponds to the second family, so we assume $f(0) = -1$ . For the final push, let $m$ be the smallest integer such that $f^{m}(0)=1$ , then $f^{m-1}(0) \in \{-2, -1, 2\}$ . If $f^{m-1}(0) = 2$ , we may take $f^{m-2}(0) \in \{0, 2\}$ , which gives us that $f(2)=2$ , or $f(0) = 2$ , bad. If $f^{m-1}(0) = -2$ , we may take $f^{m-2}(0) \in \{1, -1\}$ , implying $f(-1) = -2$ . However this means that $2 \nmid f(1) - f(-1)$ , which is a contradiction. This means that we need $f(-1) = 1$ , which gives the third and final solution set. All cases are exhausted so we are finally done.

$f$  must be periodic mod  $p$ . We obtain that  $f^{2p+1} \equiv f^{p+1} \equiv 1$ , so  $f^p(1)\equiv 1 \pmod p$ . We also have that if  $f(0) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ , then  $0 \equiv -1 \pmod p$ , contradiction. Therefore,  $f(0) = \pm 1$ . First suppose that  $f(0)=1$ . If the period is  $1$ , then  $f(x) \equiv 1$  works. Otherwise, we know that  $p \mid f(p)-f(0)$ . Next, we consider the set  $\{1, f(1), f^2(1), \ldots\}$ . If this set is bounded, then there exists distinct  $a$  and  $b$  satisfying  $f^a(1) = f^b(1)$ . Let  $b$  be minimal, and let  $d=b-a$  be the period. But there exists infinitely many primes in the sequence  $a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots$ . Therefore,  $f^a(1) \equiv 1$ , so  $f(x)=1$  is a solution. Otherwise, the set is unbounded, and all its elements are distinct. The consider  $f^{n+1}(1)-f^n(1) \mid f^{n+2}-f{n+1} \mid \ldots \mid f(1)-1$ . Therefore, either  $f(1)=1$  or  $f^{n+1}(1)-f^{n}(1)$  is a fixed point, giving a linear solution. The only linear solution that works is  $f(x)=x+1$ . Otherwise, if  $f(1)=1$ , we can let  $f(x) = x(x-1)g(x)+1$ . Otherwise,  $f(0)=-1$ . Then plugging  $n = f(-1) \equiv 1 \pmod 2$  gives  $f(-1) \mid f^{f(-1)+1}-1$  so  $f^{f(-1)+1}(0) \equiv 1 \pmod{f(-1)}$ . However, this means that  $0 \equiv 1 \pmod{f(-1)}$ , so  $f(1)=\pm 1$ . If  $f(-1)=-1$ , then  $f^{n}(0)=-1$ , contradiction. Then  $f(-1)=1$ , and we obtain  $f(x)=(x^3-x)g(x)+2x^2-1$

Let $p$ denote an arbitary prime throughout. See that if some $p \mid f(0) \implies 1 \equiv f^{p+1}(0) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ , contradiction. Hence $|f(0)|=1$ .**Case A: $f(0)=1$ ** Note that we have \[n \mid f^n(1)-1 \implies p \mid f^p(1)-1\] Say $f(1) \ne 1$ (as otherwise it is a solution) then for large $p$ we have that when we draw the digraph of $f$ on $\mathbb Z/p \mathbb Z$ then it forms a $p$ -cycle. This basically implies there is no $x$ such that $p \mid f(x)-x$ hence by converse of Schur's theorem we have that for some $c$ we have $f(x)=x+c$ for some constant $c$ and as $f(0)=1 \implies f(x)=x+1$ which works. **Case B: $f(0)=-1$ ** Note that we have \[n \mid f^n(-1)-1 \implies n \mid 2n \mid f^{2n}(-1)-1 \implies n \mid f^n(1)-1\] Again if $f(1) \ne 1$ then for large $p$ , there is a $p$ -cycle so $1 \equiv f^p(-1) \equiv -1 \pmod p$ , contradiction. Hence $f(1)=1$ and also $f(-1)$ is odd. Now see that $f^n(0) \equiv -1,0 \pmod {|f(-1)|}$ for any $n \ge 0$ but this means \[|f(-1)| \mid f^{|f(-1)|+1}(0)-1 \implies |f(-1)| \mid -1,-2 \implies |f(-1)|=1\] If $f(-1)=-1$ then $n \mid f^n(-1)-1=-2$ , contradiction. So $f(-1)=1$ must be true and it can be checked to work. Hence all in all the only solutions are \[\boxed{f(x)=x+1} \text{ AND } \boxed{f(x)=x(x-1)P(x)+1} \text{ AND } \boxed{f(x)=(xQ(x)+2)(x-1)(x+1)+1}\] where $P$ , $Q \in \mathbb Z [X]$ .

Answers are $f(x)=(x^2-x)g(x)+1$ and $f(x)=(x^3-x)g(x)+2x^2-1$ and $f(x)=x+1$ which indeed fit. Assume that $f$ is a polynomial other than these, holding $n|f^{n+1}(0)-1$ . **If $0'$ s orbit is bounded:** Since $k|f^{km+1}(0)-1$ , zero cannot be in the orbit. Notice that $|f^r(0)|>1$ would yield $|f^{kr}(0)|>1$ by $f^{r}(0)|f^{kr}(0)$ however, $kr-1|f^{kr}(0)-1$ is impossible. Thus, $|f^k(0)|=1$ . If $f(0)=-1$ , then $f(-1)\neq -1$ hence $f(-1)=1$ and $f(1)\neq -1$ so $f(1)=1$ , too. We get a desired solution, now assume that $f(0)=1$ . Then, $f(1)=-1$ would give $f(-1)=1$ which is impossible so $f(1)=1$ and we get a solution we have given again. $\square$ **If $0'$ s orbit is unbounded: **Pick a sufficiently large prime $p$ . Since $p|f^x(0)-f^y(0)$ implies $p|f^{x+1}(0)-f^{y+1}(0)$ by $f^x(0)-f^y(0)|f^{x+1}(0)-f^{y+1}(0)$ , we observe that $f^k(0)$ is periodic $\pmod p$ . Let this period be $T$ . We have $pm|f^{pm+1}(0)-1$ hence $f^{pm+1}(0)\equiv 1\pmod p$ which gives $T|p$ . Since $T=1$ contradicts with our initial assumption, we obtain $T=p$ . This requires $p|f^{p+1}(0)-f(0)$ and also $f^{p+1}(0)\equiv 1\pmod p$ thus, $p|f(0)-1$ or $f(0)=1$ . Let $d=|f^{k+1}(0)-f^k(0)|$ . We see that $f^k(0)$ has period $1$ $\pmod d$ . We have $dm|f^{dm+1}(0)-1$ so $f^\ell(0)\equiv 1 \pmod d$ for sufficiently large $\ell$ . Since $d|f^{k}(0)-f(0)$ we get $d|f^{k+1}(0)-f^2(0)$ hence $d|f^2(0)-1$ which implies that $d$ is bounded. Consider $f(x)-x=g(x)$ . If $g$ is nonconstant, then $g$ is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing for sufficiently large $x$ however, $g(f^k(0))$ is bounded where $f^k(0)$ is unbounded so $f(x)-x$ is constant. Plugging $f(x)=x+c$ gives $n|(n+1)c-1$ thus, $c=1$ as desired. $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Let acute triangle  $ABC$  have orthocenter  $H$ . Let  $B_1$ ,  $C_1$ ,  $B_2$ , and  $C_2$  be collinear points which lie on lines  $AB$ ,  $AC$ ,  $BH$ , and  $CH$ , respectively. Let  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$  be the circumcircles of triangles  $BB_1B_2$  and  $CC_1C_2$ , respectively. Prove that the radical axis of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$  intersects the line through their centers on the nine-point circle of triangle  $ABC$ .

*Ruben Carpenter*
solution_md:
We use  $\angle\ell$  to denote the argument of line  $\ell$ . Let  $O_B$  and  $O_C$  be the circumcenters of  $\triangle{}BB_1B_2$  and  $\triangle{}CC_1C_2$ .

We will use the method of moving points. Vary  $\overline{B_1B_2C_1C_2}$  linearly with respect to  $t$  with a fixed argument. Then  $B_1$  and  $C_1$  vary linearly. Note that  $$ \angle\overline{BO_B}=\angle\overline{BB_1}+\angle\overline{BB_2}-\angle\overline{B_1B_2}-90^\circ=\angle\overline{AB}+\angle\overline{AC}-\angle\overline{B_1B_2C_1C_2}. $$  Similarly  $\angle\overline{CO_C}$  is also equal to this fixed value, so  $\overline{BO_B}$  and  $\overline{CO_C}$  are fixed, parallel lines. Then  $O_B$  is the intersection of fixed line  $\overline{BO_B}$  and the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{BB_1}$ , which moves linearly, so  $O_B$  moves linearly. Similarly  $O_C$  moves linearly.

Claim. Circles  $\left(BB_1B_2\right)$  and  $\left(CC_1C_2\right)$  vary linearly in the sense that they have equations  $$ x^2+y^2+a(t)x+b(t)y+c(t) $$  for linear  $a,b,c$ , in Cartesian coordinates.

Proof. Let  $B$  be the origin and  $\overline{BO_B}$  be the  $x$  axis. Then  $O_B=(f(t),0)$  for some linear  $f$ , so the equation of  $\left(BB_1B_2\right)$  is  $$ \left(x-f(t)\right)^2+y^2=(f(t))^2, $$  or  $$ x^2+y^2-2f(t)x=0. $$  This satisfies the claim, and similarly for  $\left(CC_1C_2\right)$ .

Now, the radical axis of  $\left(BB_1B_2\right)$  and  $\left(CC_1C_2\right)$  is the difference of the equations of the  $2$  circles, so it has degree  $1$ . Also  $\overline{O_BO_C}$  ahs degree  $1$  since  $O_B$  and  $O_C$  vary linearly on parallel lines.

Now as  $\overline{O_BO_C}$  and the radical axis of  $\left(BB_1B_2\right)$  and  $\left(CC_1C_2\right)$  vary with degree  $1$ , they pass through some fixed points  $X$  and  $Y$ . Since these  $2$  lines are perpendicular, it suffices to show that  $X$  and  $Y$  are antipodes on the nine point circle.

Consider specifically the cases when  $\overline{B_1B_2C_1C_2}$  pass through  $A$  and when they pass through  $H$ . Then let  $O_B$  and  $O_C$  be labeled  $O_B$  and  $O_C$  and let  $\ell_1$  be the radical axis for when  $\overline{B_1B_2C_1C_2}$  passes through  $H$  and let  $O_B$  and  $O_C$  be labeled  $O'_B$  and  $O'_C$  and let  $\ell_2$  be the radical axis for when  $\overline{B_1B_2C_1C_2}$  passes through  $A$ .

Now we will move more points. Forget about the previous moving points, and instead move  $\overline{BO_BO'_B}$  and  $\overline{CO_CO'_C}$  with degree  $1$ . Then  $O_B,O'_B,O_C,$  and  $O'_C$  lie on the fixed perpendicular bisectors of  $\overline{BH},\overline{AB},\overline{CH},$  and  $\overline{AC}$ , so they move with degree  $1$ . Now  $\overline{O_BO_C}$  and  $\overline{O'_BO'_C}$  vary with degree  $2$ . Then  $\ell_1$  is the perpendicular from  $H$  to  $\overline{O_BO_C}$ , so it also varies with degree  $2$ , and similarly for  $\ell_2$ . Then when  $\overline{BO_B}=\overline{CO_C}=\overline{BC}$  we see that  $\overline{O_BO_C}=\overline{O'_BO'_C}=\overline{BC}$  and  $\ell_1=\ell_2=\overline{AH}$ . Also, when  $O_B$  and  $O_C$  are the reflections of the circumcenter of  $\triangle{}ABC$  over  $\overline{AB}$  and  $\overline{AC}$ , so that  $BCO_CO_B$  is a parallelogram, we see that  $O_B=O'_B$  and  $O_C=O'_C$ , so  $\overline{O_BO_C}=\overline{O'_BO'_C}$  and then  $\ell_1=\ell_2=\overline{AH}$ . Therefore by Zack's lemma  $X=\overline{O_BO_C}\cap\overline{O'_BO'_C}$  has degree  $2+2-2=2$  and  $Y=\ell_1\cap\ell_2$  has degree  $2+2-2=2$ . Now to show that  $X$  lies on the nine point circle and  $Y$  is the reflection of  $X$  over  $N$ , it suffices to check  $5$  cases, as both conditions are degree  $4$ .

If  $\overline{BO_B}=\overline{BH}$  then we have that  $O_B$  is the midpoint of  $\overline{BH}$ , that  $O'_B$  lies on  $\overline{BH}$ , that  $O_C$  is the center of the circle  $\omega$  through  $H$  tangent to  $\overline{AC}$  at  $C$ , and that  $O'_C$  is the point at infinity on  $\overline{BH}$ . Then  $\overline{O'_BO'_C}=\overline{BH}$ , so  $X=O_B$  lies on the nine point circle. Now the antipode of  $X$  on the nine point circle is the midpoint  $M$  of  $\overline{AC}$ , so it suffices that  $Y$  is the midpoint of  $\overline{AC}$ . Note that  $\ell_2=\overline{AC}$ , so it suffices that  $\ell_1=\overline{HM}$ . For this it suffices that  $M$  has equal powers with respect to both the circle with diameter  $\overline{BH}$  and  $\omega$ . Note that the circle  $\gamma$  with diameter  $\overline{AC}$ , which is centered at  $M$ , is orthogonal to both circles. This is because  $B$  lies on the polar of  $H$  with respect to  $\gamma$  by Brokard's theorem on  $ACFD$  where  $F$  and  $D$  are the feet of the altitudes from  $C$  to  $\overline{AB}$  and from  $A$  to  $\overline{BC}$ , respectively, and furthermore  $\gamma$  and  $\omega$  have perpendicular tangents at  $C$ . Therefore  $M$  has power  $MB^2=MC^2$  with respect to both the circle with diameter  $\overline{BH}$  and  $\omega$ , proving this case. Note that the problem is symmetric about  $A$  and  $H$  and also symmetric about  $B$  and  $C$ , so we can also take the cases  $\overline{BO_B}=\overline{BA},\overline{CO_C}=\overline{CH},$  and  $\overline{CO_C}=\overline{CA}$ . This gives  $4$  cases for both conditions.

Now, we consider the limiting case as  $\overline{BO_B}$  and  $\overline{CO_C}$  both approach  $\overline{BC}$ . Then note that we always have the ratio  $$ \frac{XO_B}{XO_C}=\frac{XO'_B}{XO'_C}. $$  In the limiting case  $O_B,O_C,O'_B,$  and  $O'_C$  approach points on line  $\overline{BC}$ , so  $X$  approaches the center of the involution swapping  $O_B$  and  $O'_C$  and swapping  $O_C$  and  $O'_B$ . We want that  $X$  lies on the nine point circle, for which it suffices that  $X$  is the midpoint of  $\overline{BC}$ . For this we prove the following lemma.

Lemma. Let  $A,B,C,$  and  $D$  be four points and let  $\ell$  be a line. Then there exists an involution swapping the intersection of  $\ell$  and the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{AB}$  and the intersection of  $\ell$  and the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{CD}$ , swapping the intersection of  $\ell$  and the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{AC}$  and the intersection of  $\ell$  and the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{BD}$ , and swapping the intersection of  $\ell$  and the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{AD}$  and the intersection of  $\ell$  and the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{BC}$ .

Proof. Let  $O_A,O_B,O_C,$  and  $O_D$  be the circumcenters of  $\triangle{}BCD,\triangle{}CDA,\triangle{}DAB,$  and  $\triangle{}ABC$ . The lemma is then proved by using Desargues's Involution Theorem on  $O_AO_BO_CO_D$  with line  $\ell$ .

Using the lemma with  $\left(A,B,C,D,\ell\right)\rightarrow\left(A,B,C,H,\overline{BC}\right)$  proves one case for the condition that  $X$  lies on the nine point circle of  $\triangle{}ABC$ . Therefore we have  $5$  cases where  $X$  lies on the nine point circle, so  $X$  must always lie on the nine point circle.

Now, since the locus of  $X$  is the nine point circle, we can consider any case where  $X$  is a circle point  $\mathcal{I}$  or  $\mathcal{J}$ . Then  $\overline{O_BO_C}$  and  $\overline{O'_BO'_C}$  go through  $X$ . Therefore any line perpendicular to  $\overline{O_BO_C}$  or  $\overline{O'_BO'_C}$  must also go through  $X$ , so  $Y=\ell_1\cap\ell_2=X$ . If  $N$  is the nine point center then  $\overline{NX}$  is tangent to the nine point circle, so  $X$  is the antipode of itself on the nine point circle. Therefore  $Y$  is the antipode of  $X$ , giving a case where  $Y$  is the antipode of  $X$  on the nine point circle. This gives  $5$  cases where  $Y$  is the antipode of  $X$  on the nine point circle, so  $Y$  must always be the antipode of  $X$  on the nine point circle.

We have proved that  $X$  and  $Y$  are always antipodes on the nine point circle, so we are done.

&=\frac{2b(b+c)+v(2b^2c-2b(b+c)r)}{2b}
&=b+c+bcv-(b+c)vr=bc(s_2+r(b+c)(a+h)).
\end{align*}
Now,  $T=(r,t)$  lies on the radical axis of  $(BB_1B_2)$  and  $(CC_1C_2)$ . We conclude that  $(t-\alpha)(t-\beta)=(t-\gamma)(t-\delta)$ . This gives us
\begin{align*}
t&=\frac{\alpha\beta-\gamma\delta}{(\alpha+\beta)-(\gamma+\delta)}
&=\frac{\frac{(a+b-r)(h+b-r)}{ahb^2}-\frac{(a+c-r)(h+c-r)}{ahc^2}}{\frac{a-r}{ab}+\frac{h-r}{hb}-\frac{a-r}{ac}-\frac{h-r}{hc}}
&=\frac{-\frac{c(a+b-r)(h+b-r)}{b}+\frac{b(a+c-r)(h+c-r)}c}{\frac{(a-r)(c-b)}{abc}+\frac{(h-r)(c-b)}{hbc}}
&=ah\frac{b^2(a+c-r)(h+c-r)-c^2(a+b-r)(h+b-r)}{(c-b)(h(a-r)+a(h-r))}
&=\frac{r^2(b^2-c^2)-r(b^2(a+h+2c)-c^2(a+h+2b))+(b^2(a+c)(h+c)-c^2(a+b)(h+b))}{-(b-c)k}
&=-\frac{(b+c)r^2-r((a+h)(b+c)+2bc)+(b+c)ah+bc(a+h)}{k}.
\end{align*}
We conclude that
\[T\cdot(\ell,-k)=r(2bc-(b+c)r)+(b+c)r^2-r((a+h)(b+c)+2bc)-s_2=-r(a+h)(b+c)-s_2.\]
Letting  $\Delta=r(a+h)(b+c)+s_2$ , we conclude that
\[O_B\cdot(k,\ell)=bc\Delta,\ T\cdot(\ell,-k)=-\Delta.\]**Solving the problem.** Recall that we must show
\[\lvert(N-O_B)\cdot(k,\ell)\rvert^2+\lvert(N-T)\cdot(\ell,-k)\rvert^2=\lvert N\cdot(k,\ell)\rvert^2+\lvert N\cdot(\ell,-k)\rvert^2.\]
This rearranges to
\[\lvert O_B\cdot(k,\ell)\rvert^2+\lvert T\cdot(\ell,-k)\rvert^2=2(N\cdot(k,\ell))(O_B\cdot(k,\ell))+2(N\cdot(\ell,-k))(T\cdot(\ell,-k)).\]
Using the results of the previous section and dividing by  $\Delta$  (if  $\Delta=0$ , we are done), we must show
\[2\Delta(1+b^2c^2)=4bc(N\cdot(k,\ell))-4(N\cdot(\ell,-k)).\]
Calling the right side of the above  $M$ , we may compute
\begin{align*}
M&=4bc(N\cdot(k,\ell))-4(N\cdot(\ell,-k))
&=bc(s_1k+s_2\ell)-(s_1\ell-s_2k)
&=k(bcs_1+s_2)+\ell(bcs_2-s_1)
&=2(bcs_1+s_2)+2bc(bcs_2-s_1)-r\left(\left(\frac1a+\frac1h\right)(bcs_1+s_2)+(b+c)(bcs_2-s_1)\right)
&=2(1+b^2c^2)s_2-r\left(\left(bc\left(\frac1a+\frac1h\right)-(b+c)\right)s_1+s_2\left(\frac1a+\frac1h+bc(b+c)\right)\right)
&=2(1+b^2c^2)s_2-rbc\left(s_1\left(\frac1a+\frac1h-\frac1b-\frac1c\right)+s_2(b+c-a-h)\right)
&=2(1+b^2c^2)s_2-2rbc\left((b+c)\left(\frac1a+\frac1h\right)-(a+h)\left(\frac1b+\frac1c\right)\right)
&=2(1+b^2c^2)s_2-2rbc(a+h)(b+c)\left(\frac1{ah}-\frac1{bc}\right)
&=2(1+b^2c^2)(s_2+r(a+h)(b+c))=2(1+b^2c^2)\Delta,
\end{align*}
as desired.

Let  $O_B$  and  $O_C$  be the centers of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ , respectively. Let  $(ABC)$  be the unit circle, and let the line  $\ell$  containing  $B_1$ ,  $C_1$ ,  $B_2$ , and  $C_2$  have equation  $t\bar z + \bar tz + 1 = 0$ . Let  $E$  be the reflection of  $H$  across  $AC$ . Let 

The lines  $BB_1$ ,  $BB_2$ , and  $B_1B_2$  coincide with lines  $AB$ ,  $BE$ , and  $\ell$ , respectively. They have equations
\begin{align*}
z + ab\bar z - a - b &= 0 
z - ac\bar z + \frac{ac}b - b &= 0 
\bar tz + t\bar z + 1 &= 0.
\end{align*}
The conics  $BB_1 \cup BB_2$ ,  $BB_2 \cup B_1B_2$ ,  $BB_2 \cup B_1B_2$  then have equations
\begin{align*}
(z + ab\bar z - a - b)\left(z - ac\bar z + \frac{ac}b - b\right) &= 0 
\left( z - ac\bar z + \frac{ac}b - b \right)(\bar tz + t\bar z + 1) &= 0 
(\bar tz + t\bar z + 1)\left( z + ab\bar z - a - b \right) &= 0.
\end{align*}
We will compute the equation of the circle  $\omega_B$  by taking a suitable linear combination of these three conics to make the  $z^2$  and  $\bar z^2$  terms vanish. First, expanding gives the full forms of the conics as
\begin{align*}
z^2 - a^2bc\bar z^2 + a(b - c)z\bar z + \left( \frac{ac}b - a - 2b \right)z + a(2ac + bc - b^2)\bar z + \frac{a^2c}b + ac - ab - b^2 &= 0 
\bar tz^2 - act\bar z^2 + (t - ac\bar t)z\bar z + \left(1 + \left(\frac{ac}b - b\right)\bar t\right)z + \left(t\left( \frac{ac}b - b \right) - ac\right)\bar z + \frac{ac}b - b &= 0 
\bar tz^2 + abt\bar z^2 + (ab\bar t + t)z\bar z + (1 - \bar t(a + b))z + (ab - t(a + b))\bar z - a - b &= 0.
\end{align*}
Let  $u = \frac 1t$ . We sum these conics with weights  $1$ ,  $q$ , and  $r$ , where  $q + r = -\bar u$  and  $rb - qc = abcu$ .

We will compute each coefficient individually.
\begin{align*}
[z\bar z] &= a(b - c) + t(q + r) + a\bar t(rb - qc) 
&= a(b - c) - t\bar u + a^2bc\bar tu 
[z] &= \frac{ac}b - a - 2b + q + r + \bar t\left( \frac{ac}bq - bq - ar - br \right) 
&= \frac{ac}b - a - 2b - \bar u + \bar t(-a^2cu + b\bar u) 
&= \frac{ac}b - a - b - \bar u - a^2c\bar tu 
[\bar z] &= a(2ac + bc - b^2) + a(rb - qc) - \frac{at}b(rb - cq) - bt(q + r) 
&= a(ac + bc - b^2) + a^2bcu + bt\bar u 
[1] &= \frac{a^2c}b + ac - ab - b^2 - \frac ab(rb - qc) - b(q + r) 
&= \frac{a^2c}b + ac - ab - b^2 - a^2cu + b\bar u
\end{align*}
The circle  $\omega_C$  is the same, but  $b$  and  $c$  are swapped.

By power of a point formula, any linear combination of two circle equations yields a coaxial circle, hence the circle obtained by subtracting the equations for  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$  and dividing by  $(b - c)$  is coaxial with them. This circle has equation
\[2az\bar z + \left( -\frac{a(b + c)}{bc} - 1 + a^2\bar tu \right)z + (-a(a + b + c) + t\bar u)\bar z - \frac{(a^2 + bc)(b + c)}{bc} - 2a + a^2u + \bar u = 0.\]
Let the center of this circle be  $P$ , we have
\[p = \frac{a + b + c}2 - \frac t{2a\bar t}.\]
This lies on the nine-point circle and on the line passing through  $O_B$  and  $O_C$ . However, this is not the desired intersection, since it is invariant with respect to scaling  $t$  by reals, which is equivalent to translating  $\ell$ , impossible. Hence the desired point must be the other intersection of line  $O_BO_C$  and the nine-point circle. We need to show this point lies on the radical axis of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ .

It's enough to show the antipode of  $P$  with respect to the nine-point circle,  $Q$ , lies on the radical axis of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ , since the radical axis of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$  and the line  $O_BO_C$  are orthogonal. We have
\[q = \frac{a + b + c}2 + \frac t{2a\bar t}.\]
We need to show
\[(q - O_B)\overline{(q - O_B)} - (b - O_B)\overline{(b - O_B)} = (q - O_C)\overline{(q - O_C)} - (c - O_C)\overline{(c - O_C)},\]
or
\[\bar qO_B + q\overline{O_B} - \bar bO_B - b\overline{O_B} - \bar qO_C - q\overline{O_C} + \bar cO_C + c\overline{O_C} = 0.\]

Fix  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ , and the argument of  $t$ . We will vary  $\lambda$ , the magnitude of  $t$ . Observe that since  $t\bar u$  and  $\bar tu$  are constant,
\[O_B = -\frac{a(ac + bc - b^2) + a^2bcu + bt\bar u}{a(b - c) - t\bar u + a^2bc\bar tu}\]
is a degree-one polynomial in  $\lambda$ . Similarly,  $O_C$  is a degree-one polynomial in  $\lambda$ , and  $q$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$  are constant in  $\lambda$ . Therefore,
\[\bar qO_B + q\overline{O_B} - \bar bO_B - b\overline{O_B} - \bar qO_C - q\overline{O_C} + \bar cO_C + c\overline{O_C}\]
is a degree-one polynomial in  $\lambda$ . To show this is in fact the zero polynomial, we need to check two special cases of  $\lambda$ . But  $\lambda$  varying is equivalent to translating  $\ell$ , so we may make  $\ell$  pass through arbitrary points. It's enough to check the special cases  $\ell$  passes through  $A$ , and the special case where  $\ell$  passes through  $H$ . However, they are equivalent, since the problem statement is symmetric in  $A$  and  $H$ , so it suffices to check the case where  $\ell$  passes through  $H$ .

Let  $R \neq H$  be the second intersection point of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ . Since
\[\measuredangle BIC = \measuredangle BIH + \measuredangle HIC = \measuredangle BFH + \measuredangle HGC = \measuredangle ABC + \measuredangle BCA,\] $R$  lies on  $(ABC)$ . Let  $Q$  be the intersection of  $\overline{O_BO_C}$  and the radical axis of  $\omega_B$  and  $\omega_C$ . A half homothety at  $H$  sends  $R$  to  $Q$  and  $(ABC)$  to the nine-point circle of  $(ABC)$ , hence  $Q$  lies on the nine-point circle of  $(ABC)$ , as desired.

stem_md:
Let  $\mathbb Z$  be the set of integers, and let  $f\colon \mathbb Z \to \mathbb Z$  be a function. Prove that there are infinitely many integers  $c$  such that the function  $g\colon \mathbb Z \to \mathbb Z$  defined by  $g(x) = f(x) + cx$  is not bijective. 
*Note:* A function  $g\colon \mathbb Z \to \mathbb Z$  is bijective if for every integer  $b$ , there exists exactly one integer  $a$  such that  $g(a) = b$ .
solution_md:
Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists a function  $f:\mathbb{Z}\to \mathbb{Z}$  such that  $g(x) = f(x)+cx$  is not bijective for only finitely many integers  $c$ . We prove a key fact about  $f$ .**Claim:** The value of  $f(x+1)-f(x)$  can only take on a finite number of integer values.

*Proof:* Suppose otherwise; we show that  $g(x)$  fails to be injective, and hence bijective, for infinitely many integer values of  $c$ , which is the desired contradiction. Suppose that  $f(a+1)-f(a) = d$  for integers  $a$  and  $d$ . Let  $c = -d$ ; this implies that  $g(a+1)=f(a+1)+c(a+1) = f(a)+ca = g(a)$ . Hence  $g(x)=f(x)+cx$  fails to be injective for this particular value of  $c$ . Since  $d$  can take on infinitely many integer values, there are infinitely many integers  $c$  such that  $g(x) = f(x)+cx$  is not injective.  $\blacksquare$ Thus, let  $S$  be the set of all possible values of  $f(x+1)-f(x)$ , and let  $k$  denote the largest absolute value of an element of  $S$ . To finish. we now claim that for all integers  $c \ge k+2$ ,  $g(x)=f(x)+cx$  fails to be surjective, and hence bijective. Recall that we have  $|f(x+1)-f(x)| \le k$  for all integers  $x$ . When  $c \ge k+2$ , we have  $g(x+1)-g(x) = f(x+1)-f(x) + c\ge 2$ . This clearly implies that  $g(x)=f(x)+cx$  fails to be surjective for all  $c\ge k+2$ , which finishes the problem.  $\blacksquare$

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $d(x)$  be defined as  
\[
d(x) = f(x+1) - f(x).
\]

If we set  $c = -d(x)$  for some integer  $x$ , we have  
\[
\begin{aligned}
    g(x+1) &= f(x+1) - (x+1)(f(x+1) - f(x)) 
           &= f(x+1) - (f(x+1) - f(x)) - x(f(x+1) - f(x)) 
           &= f(x) - x(f(x+1) - f(x)) 
           &= g(x),
\end{aligned}
\]
which implies that  $g(x)$  is not bijective.  

If  $d(x)$  takes on infinitely many distinct values over the integers, we are done. Otherwise, let  $m$  be the minimum of  $d(x)$  over the integers and consider all  $c \geq |m| + 2$ .  

We have  
\[
\begin{aligned}
    g(x+1) &= g(x) + d(x) + c 
           &\geq g(x) + m + c 
           &\geq g(x) + 2,
\end{aligned}
\]
which implies that  $g(x)$  is not bijective.</details>

\[ g(x)\le h(x)\le h(0), \]
so  $g$  when  $k=1$  never attains the value of  $h(0)+1$ , contradicting bijectivity. Thus, the values of  $c$  for which  $g$  is not bijective is not bounded above and therefore infinite.  $\square$

Assume for contradiction that there exists a finite ``bad'' set $S$ such that $f(x)+cx$ is bijective for all $c \notin S$ . The first observation is basically that given just $f(0)$ and $f(1)$ , or any two consecutive $f$ -values, we can already find bad values of $c$ .**Claim:** The numbers $f(0)-f(1)$ , $f(1)-f(2)$ , $f(2)-f(3)$ , \dots\ are all in $S$ . That is, consecutive differences of $f$ only take finitely many values. *Proof.* To see that $f(0) - f(1) \in S$ , just note that \[ x \mapsto f(x) + \left( f(0) - f(1) \right) \cdot x \] is obviously not a bijective function, since it takes the same values at $x=0$ and $x=1$ , namely $f(0)$ . The same is true for other elements. $\blacksquare$ In particular, suppose $M > \max_{s \in S} |s|$ . Then the function \[ g(x) = f(x) + (M+100) x \] is supposed to be a bijection (because $M+100 \notin S$ ), and yet $g(x+1) - g(x) > 100$ for all $x$ , which is a contradiction.

Motivation on how I personally solved it:

We can start by breaking down bijective as injective+surjective. If we look at these components, we see that finding non-injectivity for many  $c$  seems easier, since we have more concrete tools to attack with. Indeed, trying to make two values the same is simpler than finding a non-attained value:

With this in the back of our mind, we look for  $g(a)=g(b)$  with  $a\ne b$ . By the definition of  $g$ , this the case if and only if  $f(a)+ca=f(b)+cb$ . Rearranging, we want to find many different  $c$  such that:  $$ -c=\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b} $$  So what we really want is for  $\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}$  to take on many integer values, so that we can negate those integers and find many choices for  $c$ . At this point we are quite happy, since this fraction seems rather powerful, having two variables to vary ( $a$  and  $b$ ).

However, messing around a bit, it is tricky to pin down  $f(a)-f(b)$  to be a multiple of a specific quantity, so instead we try to force this fraction to be an integer automatically. Therefore, let's make the denominator disappear with  $a=b+1$ . Doing this, we simply want  $f(b+1)-f(b)$  to take on many different values, since we already know it is an integer. Clearly, if  $f(b+1)-f(b)$  takes on infinitely many values we can simply backtrack these steps to find infinitely many  $c$  relatively smoothly, as shown in the above solutions.

We hence examine the case where  $f(x+1)-f(x)$  takes only finitely many values, say  $V_1, V_2, \dots, V_m$ . Writing  $f(x+1)-f(x)$  in terms of  $g$ , we get  $g(x+1)-c(x+1)-g(x)+c(x)=g(x+1)-g(x)-c$ . Thus, we can deduce that for all  $x\in \mathbb{Z}$ :  $$ g(x+1)-g(x)\in \{V_1+c, V_2+c, \dots, V_m+c\} $$  At this point we pause and ponder... How we can try to get this to oppose surjectivity? Well we can try to limit possible jump sizes to make specific values impossible (we would like to be able to point at exactly which values). We see that if we make jump sizes positive and big, then clearly we will skip some intermediate values, that are easy to get a grip on!

Luckily we control the size of the possible jumps that  $g$  can make extremely well, since we can control a variable ( $c$ ) that we can shift. By taking  $c$  to be very large, we can make all the  $V_i+c$  greater than  $2$ , which means that for instance the value  $g(0)+1$  will never be attained by  $g(x)$ . We can easily fill in the gaps for our choice of  $c$  and write the steps in a more sequential order, as the solutions above have done!

stem_md: Let  $k$  and  $d$  be positive integers. Prove that there exists a positive integer  $N$  such that for every odd integer  $n>N$ , the digits in the base- $2n$  representation of  $n^k$  are all greater than  $d$ .
solution_md:
We claim that  $\boxed{N=d2^k}$  works.

Let  $n>N$  be an odd integer and let  $m$  be the number of digits of  $n^k$  when written in base  $2n$ . Clearly we have  $m\leq k$ . For  $1\leq i\leq m$ , let integer  $0\leq r_i<(2n)^i$  be such that  $n^k\equiv r_i\pmod{(2n)^i}$ . Let  $s_i:=\frac{r_{i+1}-r_i}{(2n)^i}$  for  $1\leq i<m$  and let  $s_0:=r_1$ . Note that  $s_i$  is an integer because  $r_{i+1}\equiv r_i\pmod{(2n)^i}$ . Also,  $s_i$  is the  $(i+1)$ th digit (counting from the right) of  $n^k$  when written in base  $2n$ , because  $0\leq s_i<\frac{(2n)^{i+1}}{(2n)^i}=2n$  and
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}s_i(2n)^i=r_1+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(r_{i+1}-r_i)=r_m=n^k.
\]
It suffices to prove that  $s_i>d$  for all  $i$ .

Note that  $s_0=r_1=n$  since  $n$  is odd. Hence  $r_i>0$  for all  $i$ . Fix  $1\leq i\leq m-1$ . Since  $\frac{n^k-r_{i+1}}{(2n)^i}\equiv 0\pmod{2n}$  it follows that
\[
s_i\equiv\frac{r_{i+1}-r_i}{(2n)^i}+\frac{n^k-r_{i+1}}{(2n)^i}\equiv\frac{n^k-r_i}{(2n)^i}\pmod{2n}.
\]
Then  $n^{i+1}\mid n^k-r_i-s_i(2n)^i$  so  $n^{i+1}\leq r_i+s_i(2n)^i<(2n)^i+s_i(2n)^i$  since  $r_i+s_i(2n)^i\geq r_i$  is positive. Thus  $s_i>\frac{n}{2^i}-1\geq 2d-1\geq d$ , as desired.  $\square$

$N > (d+1)\cdot2^{k - 1}$ works **Claim:** For all sufficiently large $n,$ $n^k$ has exactly $k$ digits. **Proof:** Note that $N > 2^{k - 1}.$ Furthermore, \begin{align*} \text{\# of digits} & = 1+\lfloor\log_{2n}(n^k)\rfloor & = 1 + \lfloor k \log_{2n}(n)\rfloor & = 1 + \lfloor k(1 - \log_{2n}(2))\rfloor \end{align*} Also note that $0 < \log_{2n}(2) < \frac 1k$ from the bound $N > 2^{k - 1}.$ This finishes. Let $n^k = \overline{a_{k - 1}\dots a_1a_0}.$ Let $0 \leq \ell < k.$ **Claim:** $a_{\ell} = \left\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell}}\right\rfloor - 2n\cdot\left\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell + 1}}\right\rfloor $ **Proof:** Note that: \begin{align*} \left\lfloor\frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell}}\right\rfloor & = \left\lfloor\frac{\sum_{j = 0}^{k - 1} a_j (2n)^{j}}{(2n)^\ell}\right\rfloor & = \left\lfloor\sum_{j = \ell}^{k - 1}a_j(2n)^{j - \ell} + \sum_{j = 0}^{\ell - 1}a_j(2n)^{j - \ell}\right\rfloor & = \sum_{j = \ell}^{k - 1}a_j(2n)^{j - \ell} \end{align*} where the last equality is since that sum is obviously an integer and the other sum is obviously less than 1. Hence, \begin{align*} a_j & = \sum_{j = \ell}^{k - 1}a_j(2n)^{j - \ell} - 2n\cdot\sum_{j = \ell + 1}^{k - 1}a_j(2n)^{j - \ell - 1} & = \left\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell}}\right\rfloor - 2n\cdot\left\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell -1}}\right\rfloor \end{align*} Now, we can finish. Next, note that $\left\{\frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell + 1}}\right\} = \left\{\frac{n^{k- \ell + 1}}{2^{\ell + 1}}\right\} \geq \frac1{2^{\ell+1}} \geq \frac1{2^{k}}$ where the first inequality follows from $n$ being odd, and the second follows from $\ell < k.$ Now, pick some $N > (d + 1)\cdot 2^{k - 1}.$ From the first claim, we have: \begin{align*} a_\ell & = \left\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell}}\right\rfloor - 2n\cdot\left\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell+1}}\right\rfloor & = \left\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell}}-2n\cdot \left\lfloor\frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell+1}}\right\rfloor\right\rfloor & = \left\lfloor2n\cdot\left\{\frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\ell+1}}\right\}\right\rfloor & \geq\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{2^k}\right\rfloor & \geq d + 1 \end{align*}

Claim 1: The base  $2n$  representation of  $n^k$  has at most  $k$  digits.
Proof: Suppose  $n^k$  had at least  $k + 1$  digits. Then the least value of  $n^k$  would be  $100000\cdots$  ( $k$   $0$ s)  $= (2n)^k$ , which would imply  $n^k \geq (2n)^k \to 1 \geq 2^k$  which is absurd since  $k$  is positive.
Claim 2: The  $m$ th digit of  $n^k$  from the right in base  $2n$  is greater than  $\frac{n}{(2)^{m-1}} - 1$ .
Proof: By claim 1,  $k \geq m$ . Since we are working in base  $2n$ , the  $m$ th digit from the right will be equal to  $\frac{p_{m} - p_{m-1}}{(2n)^{m-1}}$ , where  $p_m$  is the unique positive integer  $0 \leq p_m < (2n)^m$  for which  $p_m \equiv n^k \pmod{(2n)^m}$ .  $p_{m-1}$  is defined analogously. Since  $m \leq k$ , we have  $n^m | n^k$  so by Chinese Remainder Theorem (note that CRT is applicable since  $n$  is odd so  $\gcd{(2^m, n^m)} = 1$ ),  $p_m = q_mn^m$  for some  $q_m \geq 1$  ( $q_m = 0$  is impossible since then  $n^k$  would be even). We are given by definition that  $q_{m-1} < (2n)^{m - 1}$  so:   $$ \frac{p_m - p_{m-1}}{(2n)^{(m-1)}} > \frac{p_m}{(2n)^{(m-1)}} - 1 = \frac{q_mn^m}{2^{m-1}n^{m-1}} - 1 \geq \frac{n^m}{2^{m-1}n^{m-1}} - 1 = \frac{n}{2^{m-1}} - 1 $$   as desired.
Claim 3:  $N = (d+1)2^{k-1}$  is sufficient \newline
Proof: Let  $b_m$  be the nth digit from the right. Since we have  $b_m > \frac{n}{2^{m - 1}} - 1$  and  $m \leq k$ , it follows that  $b_m > \frac{n}{2^{k-1}} - 1$   $\forall m \in \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ , so letting  $n > N = (d + 1)2^{k - 1}$ , we get that  $b_m > \frac{n}{2^{k-1}} - 1 > \frac{(d+1)2^{k-1}}{2^{k-1}} - 1 = d$ , as desired.

The problem actually doesn't have much to do with digits: the idea is to pick any length $\ell \le k$ , and look at the rightmost $\ell$ digits of $n^k$ ; that is, the remainder upon division by $(2n)^\ell$ . We compute it exactly:**Claim:** Let $n \ge 1$ be an odd integer, and $k \ge \ell \ge 1$ integers. Then \[ n^k \bmod{(2n)^i} = c(k,\ell) \cdot n^i \] for some odd integer $1 \le c(k,\ell) \le 2^\ell-1$ . *Proof.* This follows directly by the Chinese remainder theorem, with $c(k,\ell)$ being the residue class of $n^{-k} \pmod{2^\ell}$ (which makes sense because $n$ was odd). $\blacksquare$ In particular, for the $\ell$ th digit from the right to be greater than $d$ , it would be enough that \[ c(k,\ell) \cdot n^\ell \ge (d+1) \cdot (2n)^{\ell-1}. \] But this inequality holds whenever $n \ge (d+1) \cdot 2^{\ell-1}$ . Putting this together by varying $\ell$ , we find that for all odd \[ n \ge (d+1) \cdot 2^{k-1} \] we have that - $n^k$ has $k$ digits in base- $2n$ ; and - for each $\ell = 1, \dots, k$ , the $\ell$ \textsuperscript{th} digit from the right is at least $d+1$ so the problem is solved.**Remark:** Note it doesn't really mater that $c(k,i)$ is odd *per se*; we only need that $c(k,i) \ge 1$ .

When we halve  $x$ , the digit  $d$  is replaced by either  $d \to \lfloor \tfrac{d}{2} \rfloor$  or  $d \to \lfloor \tfrac{d}{2} \rfloor + n$ .**Proof:** This is apparent from interpreting half of  $x$  as  $x \cdot 0.b_{\text{base } 2b}$ , and carrying out the column multiplication. Any digit is at least (the floor of) half of its previous value in one iteration, as established in the claim, so after all the iterations, the value of the digit is at least
\[\left \lfloor \frac{n}{2^{k-1}} \right \rfloor \geq \left \lfloor \frac{N}{2^{k-1}} \right \rfloor > d.\]

Let  $m$  and  $n$  be positive integers, and let  $\mathcal R$  be a  $2m\times{2n}$  grid of unit squares. 

A *domino* is a  $1\times2{}$  or  $2\times{1}$  rectangle. A subset  $S$  of grid squares in  $\mathcal R$  is *domino-tileable* if dominoes can be placed to cover every square of  $S$  exactly once with no domino extending outside of  $S$ . *Note*: The empty set is domino tileable. 

An *up-right path* is a path from the lower-left corner of  $\mathcal R$  to the upper-right corner of  $\mathcal R$  formed by exactly  $2m+2n$  edges of the grid squares. 

Determine, with proof, in terms of  $m$  and  $n$ , the number of up-right paths that divide  $\mathcal R$  into two domino-tileable subsets.

We claim the answer is
spoiler$\boxed{\binom{m+n}{m}^2}$
. Color $\mathcal R$ in a black-and-white checkerboard pattern such that the lower left square is black. Suppose an up-right path $P$ splits $\mathcal R$ into two subsets $S$ and $S'$ such that $S$ is below $P$ . Call a subset *balanced* if there are an equal number of black and white squares. **Claim 1**: $S$ and $S'$ are tileable iff $S$ is balanced. *Proof*: Since $\mathcal R$ itself is balanced and rotating it by $180^\circ$ swaps $S$ and $S'$ , it suffices to only consider $S$ . Note that dominoes each cover exactly one black and one white square, so $S$ being tileable implies $S$ is balanced. We will proceed with the converse by attempting to remove a domino from $S$ such that $S$ can still be traced by a new up-right path. Indeed, so long as $P$ contains a sequence of $\uparrow\rightarrow\rightarrow$ or $\uparrow\uparrow\rightarrow$ , we can replace these with $\rightarrow\rightarrow\uparrow$ and $\rightarrow\uparrow\uparrow$ , respectively, and effectively remove a domino (this also preserves balanced-ness). Repeating this until we reach the empty set suffices, as we can reconstruct using the sequence of domino removal. The only cases where this fails is when $P$ forms a staircase and remains on the upper or left edges of $\mathcal R$ for at most one edge each. However, we can trivially observe that $S$ is then unbalanced, since if the largest diagonal in $S$ has $k$ squares (which must be of the same color), $k+(k-2)+\cdots>(k-1)+(k-3)+\cdots$ . $\square$ Assign coordinates to the gridline intersections such that the lower left corner is $(0,0)$ and the upper right is $(2m,2n)$ . Assign each $\rightarrow$ move with starting point $(x,y)$ a two-letter designation, where the first letter is $o$ or $e$ depending on the parity of $x+y$ and the second letter depends on the parity of $x$ . (I blame this naming system on leo; he was making some *really* weird sounds :**P)**Claim 2**: $S$ is balanced iff there are an equal number of $\rightarrow$ 's with starting letter $o$ and $e$ . *Proof*: Consider $S$ as a union of multiple columns of squares, each topped with a $\rightarrow$ . Upon inspection, $oe$ 's give one more black square than white square, while $eo$ 's give one more white square. There are an even number of squares, and therefore equal number of black and white squares, under an $oo$ or $ee$ . Thus, for $S$ to be balanced, there must be an equal number of $oe$ 's and $eo$ 's; but since there are also an equal number of odd-numbered and even-numbered columns, we must have $oe+ee=eo+oo$ , so $ee=oo$ and $oe+oo=eo+ee$ , as desired. Reversing the logic gives the converse. $\square$ We finish by splitting moves into two sets based on the parity of $x+y$ and then ordering $m~\rightarrow$ 's amongst the $m+n$ moves in each set, giving the desired $\tbinom{m+n}{m}^2$ paths. $\square$ unfortunately, I got everything except the proof for the second claim and instead attempted a different, much more complicated parity argument :( (how many points would that be? hopefully graders aren't too harsh) EDIT: somehow i got a 7 on this. :-D

outline: We color the board in a checkerboard, and we prove that the two subsets are domino-tileable iff the number of tiles of the two colors in each subset is equal (we refer to such a subset as balanced). Consider one set, the bottom one. FTSOC let this set have the smallest possible size while still being balanced and non-domino-tileable. Then the only way this can be minimal is if it is a "staircase", as anything else (difference of 0 or 2) results in a domino being able to be placed horizontally or vertically to result in a smaller subset achievable by an up-right path. As it is non-domino-tileable the staircase has nonzero size, but all such staircases have an imbalance between tiles, contradiction.
For the final counting, let  $S(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{2m})$  denote the set  $S_1$  on the bottom from the up-right path, where  $a_k$  denotes the number of cells in  $S_1$  in column  $k$  (they are the bottommost  $a_k$  cells). Then the only conditions on the sequence  $a$  are that it is nonstrictly increasing, every term is an integer in  $[0,2n]$ , and there are the same number of odd numbers in even positions as odd numbers in odd positions (this is to account for the imbalance between colors in individual columns; they must cancel). Let  $b_k=a_k+k$ . Then the only conditions on  $b$  are that it is strictly increasing, every term is an integer in  $[1,2m+2n]$ , and there are the same number of odd numbers in even positions as even numbers in odd positions, or equivalently, there are  $m$  odd numbers and  $m$  even numbers. There are  $\binom{m+n}{m}^2$  ways to choose the sequence  $b$ , so that is our answer.

Easy problem.
Color at chessboard with white and black.
If the subset under the path is tileable it must have the same number of white and black cells.
We claim that this condition is also sufficent and we can prove that by induction on the number of white and black cells.
If the subset is the empty set this is true.
Look at the path as a sequence of up and right moves. Remove (if there are) the first block of right moves and the finale block of up moves so that the sequence start from the first up and end with the last right.
If there are two consecutive moves of the same tipe in this sequence than we can find a sequence of up-up-right or up-right-right and so a domino on the "boarder" of the path so of we remove it we have a new set that is under a path with a smaller number of cells.
If there are no  $2$  consecutive moves of the same tipe the set under the path will be a triangle and so cannot have the same number of white and black.
We can do similarly for the set over the path and notice that if a path have the same number of white and black that also the other will have.
So we need to find the number of paths such that the set under the path has the same number of white and black cells.
Suppose we start at  $(0,0)$  and end at  $(2n,2m)$  and color all the cells in the quadrant  $x>0$  and  $y>0$ .
At any step consider the set above line  $y=0$  under the path and under the line from the point where we are parallel to  $x+y=0$  (so if we have done  $k$  moves the line  $x+y=k$ ).
Consider the difference  $D$  of white area and black area in this region in every moment. After a right moves this quantity don't change. Now suppose that at  $k$ th move we go up. If  $k$  is odd  $D$  increases of  $1/2$  otherwise it decreases by  $-1/2$ .
So  $D$  at the end depends only by the number  $A$  of up moves in even position and odd position. And a value of  $D$  can be reached by at most one value of  $A$ .
The difference  $d$  of white cells and black cells under the path differ by  $D$  by a constant (difference of white area and black area in triangle  $(2n,0),(2n,2m),(2n+2m,0)$ ).
We want  $d=0$  and this is possible when  $A$  egual  $0$  because we can consider the path of all up and then all right.
So the path we are looking for are the path where the number of up moves in even position and odd position are the same and egual to  $m$ .
So also the number of right moves in even and odd position must be egual to  $n$ .
Notice that we proved that this condition is both necessary and sufficent.
So the number of possible choices is  $\binom{m+n}{n}$  for order the  $n$  right moves and the  $m$  up moves in the even position times  $\binom{m+n}{n}$  for the odd positions.
So the answer is  $\binom{m+n}{n}^2$ .

Assume the number of black and white cells is equal. The proof is by induction with empty staircases being vacuous. We consider the following four cases (which could overlap, pick one arbitrarily if so). Note that the latter two cases are just mirrors of the first two. - **Case 1** If the rightmost two columns of the staircase have the same height, tile those two columns. - **Case 2** If some two consecutive columns of the staircase differ by more than two cells in height, say the $(i-1)$ \textsuperscript{st} and the $i$ \textsuperscript{th}, then tile the top two cells in the $i$ \textsuperscript{th} column and rightwards. - **Case 3** If the bottom two rows of the staircase have the same length, tile those two rows. - **Case 4** If some two consecutive rows of the staircase differ by more than two cells in length, say the $(j-1)$ \textsuperscript{st} and the $j$ \textsuperscript{th}, then tile the leftmost two cells in the $j$ \textsuperscript{th} column and below. The point is that we need to find the number of up-right paths for which the two resulting regions have equal numbers of black and white squares; call such paths [i]balanced*. Since the overall $2m \times 2n$ grid has $2mn$ black and $2mn$ white squares, it's sufficient for just the bottom-right staircase to have equal black and white cells. Then in general, an up-right path is characterized by integer sequences \[ 0 \le h_1 \le h_2 \le \dots \le h_{2n} \le 2m \] corresponding to the heights of the staircase.**Claim:** The $(h_i)$ correspond to a balanced up-right path if and only if $\{ i : h_i \equiv 1 \pmod 2\}$ has an equal number of even and odd indices. *Proof.* WLOG let's fix our coloring so that the bottom-left square is black. Then in the $i$ \textsuperscript{th} column, for $i = 1, \dots, 2n$ , has (i) one more black square than white if $h_i$ is odd and $i \equiv 1 \pmod 2$ ; (ii) one more white square than black if $h_i$ is odd and $i \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ ; (iii) equal black and white squares if $h_i$ is even. The conclusion follows immediately. $\blacksquare$ The trick is to instead define \[ t_i \coloneq h_i + i. \] That is, we will instead describe the up-right paths by integer sequences $t_i$ with \[ 1 \le t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{2n} \le 2n+2m. \]**Claim:** The $(t_i)$ correspond to a balanced up-right path if and only if the set $\{t_1, \dots, t_{2n}\}$ has an equal number of even and odd elements. *Proof.* Translating the four cases between the two notations gives the following table: \[ \begin{array}{c|cc} & i \text{ even} & i \text{ odd} \hline h_i \equiv 1 \pmod 2 & a & b h_i \equiv 0 \pmod 2 & 2n-a & 2n-b \end{array} \iff \begin{array}{c|cc} & i \text{ even} & i \text{ odd} \hline t_i \equiv 1 \pmod 2 & a & 2n-b t_i \equiv 0 \pmod 2 & 2n-a & b. \end{array}. \] Then we have \[ \text{balanced} \iff a=b \iff a+(2n-b) = (2n-a)+b \iff \#\{\text{odd } t_i\} = \#\{\text{even } t_i\} \] as desired. $\blacksquare$ Hence we must count the number of $2m$ -element subsets of $\{1, 2, \dots, 2n+2m\}$ with $m$ even and $m$ odd terms. Since the even and odd terms can be chosen separately, this gives an answer of $\binom{n+m}{m}^2$ .

Color the board like a chessboard. We claim that the subsets are domino-tileable if and only if there are an equal number of black squares as white squares in each region. The only if part is clear because each domino cover one black square and one white square.

For the if part, there is an inductive algorithm: shift the path downwards and to the right by one unit each, and keep doing this. The regions between the shifted paths should be clearly domino-tileable.

Now, let  $a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{2m}$  be the  $y$ -coordinates the horizontal edges are on. This should uniquely determine the path. We require  $0 \leq a_1 \leq a_2 \leq a_3 \leq \cdots \leq a_{2m} \leq 2n.$  It suffices to have  $\#_{i odd, a_i odd}=\#_{i even, a_i odd}.$  Now, shifting by using  $b_i=i+a_i,$  we have   $$ 1 \leq b_1 < b_2 < b_3 < \cdots < b_{2m} \leq 2m+2n. $$   So, we must have  $\#_{i odd, b_i even} = \#_{i even, b_i odd}.$  Since there is an equal number of both parity-indices, we must also have  $\#_{i odd, b_i odd}=\#_{i even, b_i even}.$  Swapping the order of this and adding to the other equation yields that we have an even number of even  $b_i$  and odd  $b_i.$ For the other direction, if we have an even number of even  $b_i$  and odd  $b_i,$  letting  $a, b, c, d$  be  $\#_{i odd, b_i even}, \#_{i even, b_i odd}, \#_{i odd, b_i odd}, \#_{i even, b_i even}$  respectively, we have  $a+c=m=b+d,$  and  $a+d=\#_{b_i even} = \#_{b_i odd} =b+c.$  Solving yields  $a=b, c=d.$ Hence the answer is clearly  $\binom{m+n}{m}^2.$

We use barycentric coordinates with  $A=(1,\,0,\,0),\,B=(0,\,1,\,0),\,C=(0,\,0,\,1)$ . Then  $F=(S_B:S_A:0)$ . Let  $E$  be the foot from  $A$  to  $\overline{BC}$  so  $E=(0,\,S_C,\,S_B)$ . Then  $P$  is the intersection of  $\overrightarrow{AE}$  with  $(ABC)$  so let  $P=:(p:S_C:S_B)$ . Then
\[
-a^2S_CS_B-b^2S_Bp-c^2pS_C=0.\tag{1}
\]
Note that  $(AFP)$  is given by  $-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(x+y+z)(vy+wz)=0$ . Plugging in  $F$  gives  $-c^2S_AS_B+c^2S_Av=0$  so  $v=S_B$ . Plugging in  $P$  and using  $(1)$  gives  $v=-S_C$ . Thus  $(AFP)$  is given by  $-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+S_By-S_Cz=0$ . Setting  $x=0$  to intersect with  $\overline{BC}$ , we have  $y+z=0$  and
\[
-a^2yz+S_By-S_Cz=0
\]
so
\[
-a^2y(1-y)+S_By-S_C(1-y)=0.
\]
Solving yields  $y=\pm\frac{\sqrt{S_C}}{a}$  so  $X=\left(0,\,\frac{\sqrt{S_C}}{a},\,1-\frac{\sqrt{S_C}}{a}\right)$  and  $Y=\left(0,\,-\frac{\sqrt{S_C}}{a},\,1+\frac{\sqrt{S_C}}{a}\right)$ . Since  $\frac{X+Y}{2}=C$ ,  $C$  is the midpoint of  $\overline{XY}$ .  $\square$

By PoP, we have: \begin{align} BX \cdot BY = BF \cdot BA = BD \cdot BC XD \cdot DY = AD \cdot DP = BD \cdot DC \end{align}Let $a = BX, b=XD, c=DC, d=CY$ . We want to show that $d = b+c$ . Rewriting $(1)$ and $(2)$ in terms of $a,b,c,d$ gives: \begin{align} a(a+b+c+d) &= (a+b)(a+b+c) b(c+d) &= (a+b)c \end{align} Simplifying $(3)$ gives \[a(d-b) = b^2+bc.\] Solving $(4)$ for $a$ gives $a=\frac{bd}{c}$ . Plugging this into the previous equation, multiplying both sides by $\frac cb$ ,and rearranging gives \[d^2 - bd - bc-c^2=(d-b-c)(d+c) = 0.\] Since $c,d > 0$ , we must have $d=b + c$ as desired.

Let  $S$  be a set of integers with the following properties:


- $\{ 1, 2, \dots, 2025 \} \subseteq S$ .
- If  $a, b \in S$  and  $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ , then  $ab \in S$ .
- If for some  $s \in S$ ,  $s + 1$  is composite, then all positive divisors of  $s + 1$  are in  $S$ .

Prove that  $S$  contains all positive integers.
solution_md: Does this work **Claim:** $2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}-1$ , $2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}, 2^{3\cdot 2^{k}}+1$ are all in $S.$ **Proof:** By Induction. The base case, $k=0,$ follows by the condition $\{1, 2, \dots, 2025\} \subset S,$ as it simply states that $7,8,9 \in S.$ For the inductive step, assume that $2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}-1$ , $2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}, 2^{3\cdot 2^{k}}+1$ are in $S.$ By the second condition, since $$ 2^{3 \cdot 2^{k+1}}-1 = (2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}-1)(2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}+1), $$ we have that $2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}} \in S,$ as $2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}$ is composite. Also, $$ 2^{2^{k}}+1 \mid 2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}+1, $$ so $2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}+1$ is composite, and thus is in $S.$ Thus, we have finished the induction. $\square$ **Claim:** $2^{a}$ and $2^{a}+1$ are both in $S$ .**Proof:** By the previous claim, and the third condition, we get $2^{a} \mid 2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}},$ so $a \in S,$ as long as $k$ is sufficiently large. Then, if $a$ is not a power of $2,$ then since $$ 2^{\nu_{2}(a)}+1 \mid 2^{a}+1, $$ We know that $2^{a}+1$ is composite, so by the third condition, we have $2^{a}+1 \in S.$ If $a$ is a power of $2,$ then we are done by condition $3$ , as $$ 2^{2^{k}}+1 \mid 2^{3 \cdot 2^{k}}+1. $$ So, we have that $2^{a}, 2^{a}+1$ are in $S,$ as desired. $\square$ So, now, we have covered the first two claims. We will prove that $[k] \subset S,$ by induction on $k.$ The base case is $k=2025,$ which is true by assumption. For the inductive step, assume that $[k-1] \subset S.$ We will prove that $k \in S,$ using the first two claims. We have a few cases: **Case 1:** $k$ is even: If $k$ is a power of $2,$ then we are done by the second claim. Otherwise, take $a = \frac{k}{2^{\nu_{2}(k)}}$ and $b = 2^{\nu_{2}(k)}.$ Notice that $a,b < k$ , and $\gcd(a,b)=1.$ So, by the inductive step, $a,b \in S.$ Now, $ab = k,$ so $k \in S$ in this case. **Case 2:** $k=2^{a}+1$ for some $a$ : We have already proven this is in $S$ in the second claim. **Case 3:** $k$ is odd, but is not of the form $2^{a}+1,$ for some $a$ : Let $\ell = \lfloor \log_{2}(k)\rfloor,$ and define $m$ to be the multiplicative inverse of $k$ mod $2^{\ell}$ (i.e. $2^{\ell} \mid mk-1,$ and $m < 2^{\ell}$ ). Notice first that $m > 1,$ as if $m = 1,$ then $k \equiv 1 \pmod 2^{\ell},$ so $k = 2^{\ell}+1,$ which we assumed was not the case. Now, let $$ a = \frac{mk-1}{2^{\nu_{2}(mk-1)}}, b = 2^{\nu_{2}(mk-1)}. $$ Obviously $\gcd(a,b) = 1.$ By the second claim, $b \in S,$ and $$ a = \frac{mk-1}{2^{\nu_{2}(mk-1)}} \le \frac{mk-1}{2^{\ell}} < \frac{mk}{2^{\ell}} < k, $$ So we get that $a \in S$ by the inductive hypothesis. So, by the second condition, $k \in S.$ It is easy to see that these are the only cases. Thus, we have shown $k \in S.$ So, $[k] \subset S,$ as wanted. $\square$

We will prove that $\{1, 2, \dots, 2^k\} \in S \implies \{ 2^k, 2^k + 1, \dots, 2^{k + 1} \} \in S$ via induction with base case $k = 4$ , which is enough. The key claim is that:**Claim:** Let $k \ge 4$ be an integer. if $\{ 1, 2, \dots, 2^k \} \in S$ , then $2^{k + 2} \in S$ . *Proof.* Consider the integers $a = 2^{k - 1} - 1$ and $b = 2^{k - 1} + 1$ . Then $ab = 2^{2k - 2} - 1$ is in $S$ by condition (ii), so by condition (iii) $2^{2k - 2}$ and all its divisors are in $S$ . For $k \ge 4$ , $k + 2 \le 2k - 2$ , so $2^{k + 2} \mid 2^{2k - 2}$ implies that $2^{k + 2}$ is in $S$ as desired. (This also implies that $2^{k + 1}$ is in $S$ .) $\square$ We can now use an algorithm to "fill in" all the integers between $2^k$ and $2^{k + 1}$ , then induct upwards. Note that all integers $n \mid \operatorname{lcm}(1, 2, \dots, 2^k)$ are in $S$ by condition (ii), so all even integers $2^k \le n \le 2^{k - 1}$ are in $S$ . Henceforth assume $n$ is odd, so that $n - 1$ and $n + 1$ are even and satisfy $\gcd(n - 1, n + 1) = 2$ . Consider $(n - 1)(n + 1) = n^2 - 1$ . It can be expressed as $2^{\nu_2(n - 1) + \nu_2(n + 1)} \cdot \frac{n - 1}{2^{\nu_2(n - 1)}} \cdot \frac{n + 1}{2^{\nu_2(n + 1)}}$ . This is a product of three relatively prime integers, the latter two being positive integers less than $2^k$ (so they are in $S$ by inductive step) and the first being a power of $2$ at most $2^{k + 2}$ (so it is in $S$ by the claim). Thus, by two applications of condition (ii), $n^2 - 1$ is in $S$ . Finally, by condition (iii), $n \mid (n^2 - 1) + 1$ implies that $n$ is in $S$ , as desired.

Suppose by way of contradiction  $p$  is the smallest positive integer not in  $S$ . Clearly  $p$  is prime. We claim that either  $p - 1$  or  $p + 1$  is a power of  $2$ . If not, then write
\[p^2 - 1 = 2^{\nu_2(p^2 - 1)} \cdot \frac{p - 1}{2^{\nu_2(p - 1)}} \cdot \frac{p + 1}{2^{\nu_2(p - 1)}}.\]
Clearly these three are pairwise relatively prime. Since  $p$  is odd, the second and third terms are less than  $p$ . And since  $p - 1$  and  $p + 1$  are both not powers of  $2$ ,
\begin{align*}
	2^{\nu_2(p^2 - 1)} &= 2^{\nu_2(p - 1)}2^{\nu_2(p + 1)} 
	&= 2\operatorname{max}(2^{\nu_2(p - 1)},2^{\nu_2(p + 1)}) 
	&\le 2\max\left( \frac13(p - 1),\frac13(p + 1) \right) 
	&< p.
\end{align*}
So all three of these numbers are in  $S$ , so  $p^2 - 1 \in S$ , so  $p \in S$  (since  $p \mid p^2 - 1 + 1 = p^2$ ).

So either  $p - 1$  or  $p + 1$  is a power of  $2$ . We proceed by cases:


- Suppose  $p - 1$  is a power of  $2$ , then write  $p = 2^m + 1$ . If  $m$  has any odd divisors, this factors, but  $p$  is prime. So let  $p = 2^{2^n} + 1$ . Since  $p \ge 2025$ ,  $n \ge 4$ , so  $4 \mid 2^n$ , so  $p \equiv 2 \pmod 5$ . Then  $\tfrac{3p - 1}5 \in S$ . Observe that  $3p - 1$  cannot be a power of  $5$  (by taking modulo  $4$ ), so
\[3p - 1 = 5^{\nu_p(3p - 1)} \cdot \frac{3p - 1}{5^{\nu_p(3p - 1)}}\]
are two relatively prime integers less than  $p$ , so they are both in  $S$ . So  $3p - 1 \in S$ , so  $p \mid 3p - 1 + 1$  implies  $p \in S$ .

- Suppose  $p + 1$  is a power of  $2$ , then write  $p = 2^m - 1$ . Since  $p$  is prime,  $m$  is odd, so  $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ . So  $3 \mid 4p - 1$ .
	
Observe that  $4p - 1$  cannot be a power of  $3$ , since the Diophantine equation  $4 \cdot 2^m - 3^n = 5$  has no solutions for  $m \ge 11$ .
	
Now suppose  $\nu_3(4p - 1) = 1$ . Observe that
\[\left(\frac{4p - 1}3\right)^2 - 1 = 16 \cdot \frac{p - 1}6 \cdot \frac{2p + 1}3\]
is a decomposition of  $(\tfrac{4p - 1}3)^2 - 1$  into three numbers less than  $p$ , all relatively prime. So  $(\tfrac{4p - 1}3)^2 - 1 \in S$ , so  $\tfrac{4p - 1}3 \mid (\tfrac{4p - 1}3)^2 - 1 + 1$  implies  $\tfrac{4p - 1}3 \in S$ . If  $\nu_3(4p - 1) = 1$ , then
\[4p - 1 = \frac{4p - 1}3 \cdot 3\]
implies  $4p - 1 \in S$ , so  $p \mid 4p - 1 + 1$  implies  $p \in S$ .
	
Otherwise,
\[4p - 1 = \frac{4p - 1}{3^{\nu_3(4p - 1)}} \cdot 3^{\nu_3(4p - 1)}\]
is a decomposition of  $4p - 1$  into two relatively prime integers less than  $p$ , so  $4p - 1 \in S$ , so  $p \mid 4p - 1 + 1$  implies  $p \in S$ .

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there exists $n$ such that $n$ is not in $S$ . By the 2nd and 3rd condition, all numbers of the form $an-1, a \geq 2$ , are not in S. Let $m$ be the smallest value of $n$ . Lemma $1$ : $m$ is [a] prime [power] Suppose not. Then, since it has at least 2 relatively prime factors less than $m$ , by the 2nd condition, $m$ is in $S$ , contradiction. Lemma $2$ : All $2^k$ are in $S$ Consider the numbers $2^{3k} - 1$ , $2^{3k}$ , $2^{3k} + 1$ , all composite. Base: $k=1$ — By the 1st condition, $7, 8, 9$ are in $S$ . Induction: $(2^{3k}-1)(2^{3k}+1) = 2^{6k}-1$ , then by the 3rd condition, $2^{6k}$ and $2^{6k}+1$ By induction, $k$ in $2^{3*2^k}-1$ is unbounded, by the 3rd condition, all $2^n$ are in $S$ . Lemma 3: $m \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ Suppose not, and instead $m \equiv 3$ . Then, $\frac{3m-1}{4} < m$ is an integer, $4*2^k\left(\frac{3m-1}{2^k}\right)$ creates $3m-1$ , contradicting the 3rd condition. Lemma 4: $m \equiv 1 \pmod {2^k}$ for all positive integers $k$ Base: $k=2$ Proven in Lemma 3. Induction: If $m \equiv 1 \pmod {2^k}$ , then $m \equiv 1, 2^k+1 \pmod {2^{k+1}}$ . However, if $m \equiv 2^k + 1$ , then $\frac{(2^k + 1)m - 1}{2^{k+1}} < m$ is an integer (this works because of Lemma 2), contradicting the 3rd condition. Thus, $m \equiv 1 \pmod {2^k}$ . Then, since $k$ is unbounded, the only possible value of $m$ is $1$ . However, by the 1st condition, $m$ is in $S$ . Therefore, there is no $m$ and thus no $n$ .

We will show that if  $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\}\in S$ , then  $n+1\in S$ . Note that if  $n+1$  is composite, we are done, so we assume that  $n+1$  is an odd prime.

Case 1:  $n+1\ne 2^k\pm 1$  for some integer  $k>2$ .
Since  $n+2\ne 2^k$ , we have that  $2^{v_2 (n+2)}, \frac{n+2}{2^{v_2 (n+2)}}\le n\implies 2^{v_2 (n+2)}, \frac{n+2}{2^{v_2 (n+2)}}\in S\implies n+2\in S$ . Either  $v_2(n)=1$  or  $v_2(n+2)=1$ , so  $2^{v_2(n)+v_2(n+2)}=2^{1+\max(v_2(n), v_2(n+2))}=2\cdot 2^{\max(v_2(n), v_2(n+2))}\le 2\cdot \frac{n+2}{3}\le n\implies 2^{v_2(n)+v_2(n+2)}\in S$ . Since  $\gcd(n, n+2)=2$ , we have that  $\gcd\left(\frac{n}{2^{v_2(n)}}, \frac{n+2}{2^{v_2(n+2)}}\right)=1$ , so   $$ 2^{v_2(n)+v_2(n+2)}\cdot \frac{n}{2^{v_2(n)}}\cdot \frac{n+2}{2^{v_2(n+2)}}=n(n+2)\in S\implies n(n+2)+1=(n+1)^2\in S\implies n+1\in S. $$  Case 2:  $n+1=2^k+1$  for some integer  $k>2$ .
Note that  $k$  must be even, otherwise  $2^k+1\equiv 0\pmod 3$ . Then we have the following:  $$ \left(2^{\frac{k}{2}}+1\right)^2-1=2^{\frac{k}{2}}\left(2^{\frac{k}{2}}+2\right)=2^{\frac{k}{2}+1}\left(2^{\frac{k}{2}-1}+1\right)\in S \implies\left(2^{\frac{k}{2}}+1\right)^2\in S $$    $$ \implies 2^{\frac{k}{2}-1}\left(2^{\frac{k}{2}}+1\right)^2 = \left(2^{\frac{k}{2}-1}+1\right)\left(2^k+1\right)-1\in S\implies \left(2^{\frac{k}{2}-1}+1\right)\left(2^k+1\right)\in S\implies 2^k+1\in S, $$  as desired.

Case 3:  $n+1=2^k-1$  for some integer  $k>2$ .
Let  $x<k$  be a positive integer. Then   $$ (2^x-1)(2^k-1)-1=2^x\left(2^k-2^{k-x}-1\right)\in S\implies 2^k-1\in S, $$   as desired.

Hence, since  $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\}\in S\implies n+1\in S$ , the set  $S$  spans all positive integers.

Solution from *Twitch Solves ISL*: We prove by induction on $N$ that $S$ contains $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with the base cases being $N = 1, \dots, 2025$ already given. For the inductive step, to show $N+1 \in S$ : - If $N+1$ is composite we're already done from the third bullet. - Otherwise, assume $N+1 = p \ge 2025$ is an (odd) prime number. We say a number is *good* if the prime powers in its prime factorization are all less than $p$ . Hence by the second bullet (repeatedly), good numbers are in $S$ . Now our proof is split into three cases: [list=1] - Suppose neither $p-1$ nor $p+1$ is a power of $2$ (but both are still even). We claim that the number \[ s \coloneq p^2-1 = (p-1)(p+1) \] is good. Indeed, one of the numbers has only a single factor of $2$ , and the other by hypothesis is not a power of $2$ (but still even). So the largest power of $2$ dividing $p^2-2$ is certainly less than $p$ . And every other prime power divides at most one of $p-1$ and $p+1$ . Hence $s \coloneq p^2-1$ is good. As $s+1 = p^2$ , Case 1 is done. - Suppose $p+1$ is a power of $2$ ; that is $p = 2^q-1$ . Since $p > 2025$ , we assume $q \ge 11$ is odd. First we contend that the number \[ s' \coloneq 2^{q+1} - 1 = \left( 2^{(q+1)/2}-1 \right) \left( 2^{(q+1)/2}+1 \right) \] is good. Indeed, this follows from the two factors being coprime and both less than $p$ . Hence $s'+1 = 2^{q+1}$ is in $S$ . Thus, we again have \[ s \coloneq p^2-1 = (p-1)(p+1) \in S \] as we did in the previous case, because the largest power of $2$ dividing $p^2-1$ will be exactly $2^{q+1}$ which is known to be in $S$ . And since $s+1=p^2$ , Case 2 is done. - Finally suppose $p-1$ is a power of $2$ ; that is $p = 2^{2^e}+1$ is a Fermat prime. Then in particular, $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ . Now observe that \[ s \coloneq 2p-1 \equiv 0 \pmod 3 \] and moreover $2p-1$ is not a power of $3$ (it would imply $2^{2^e+1} + 1 = 3^k$ , which is impossible for $k \ge 3$ by Zsigmondy/Mihailescu/etc.). So $s$ is good, and since $s+1 = 2p$ , Case 3 is done. [/list] Having finished all the cases, we conclude $p \in S$ and the induction is done. [/list]**Remark:** In fact just $2025 \in S$ is sufficient as a base case; however this requires a bit more work to check. Here is how: [list] - From $2025 \in S$ we get $2026 = 2 \cdot 1013$ , so $2,1013 \in S$ . - From $1013+1 = 1014 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 13^2$ we get $3,13 \in S$ . - From $3+1 = 4$ we get $4 \in S$ . - $3 \cdot 13 + 1 = 40 = 2^3 \cdot 5$ we get $5 \in S$ . - Once $\{1,2,\dots,5\} \subseteq S$ , the induction above actually works fine; that is, $N \le 6$ are sufficient as base cases for the earlier cases to finish the rest of the problem. (Case 2 works once $q \ge 3$ , and Case 3 works once $e \ge 2$ .) However, $\{1,2,3,4\} \subseteq S$ is not sufficient; for example $S = \{1,2,3,4,6,12\}$ satisfies all the problem conditions.

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer, and let  $a_0,\,a_1,\dots,\,a_n$  be nonnegative integers such that  $a_0\ge a_1\ge \dots\ge a_n.$  Prove that
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n i\binom{a_i}{2}\le\frac{1}{2}\binom{a_0+a_1+\dots+a_n}{2}.
\]
*Note:*  $\binom{k}{2}=\frac{k(k-1)}{2}$  for all nonnegative integers  $k$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We prove the desired result for all nonnegative integers  $n.$  We proceed with induction on  $n.$ The base case is trivial because it is obvious that   $$ 0 \le \frac{1}{2}\binom{a_0}{2} $$   for all nonnegative integers  $a_0.$ Now, let us assume that the desired result holds for all  $n$ -tuples  $(a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1})$  of nonnegative integers satisfying  $a_0 \ge a_1 \ge \ldots, \ge a_{n-1}$  for some  $n=k$  where  $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{+}.$  Then, it follows that if we have some  $k$ -tuple  $(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k)$  of non-negative integers satisfying  $b_1 \ge b_2 \ge \ldots, b_k,$  then we will have   $$ \sum_{i=1}^k (i-1) \binom{b_i}{2} \le \frac{1}{2}\binom{b_1+b_2+\ldots+b_k}{2}. $$   It suffices to show that the desired inequality will then hold for the  $(k+1)$ -tuple  $(b_0, b_1, \ldots, b_nk)$  for any nonnegative integer  $b_0$  satisfying  $b_0 \ge b_1.$ It suffices to prove the inequality
\begin{align*}
&\qquad \sum_{i=0}^k i\binom{b_i}{2} - \sum_{i=1}^k (i-1)\binom{b_i}{2} \le \frac{1}{2}\binom{b_0+b_1+\ldots+b_k}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\binom{b_1+b_2+\ldots+b_k}{2} 
&\iff \sum_{i=1}^k \binom{b_i}{2} \le \frac{1}{4}\left(\left(\sum_{i=0}^k b_i\right)\left(\left(\sum_{i=0}^kb_i\right)-1\right)-\left(\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\right)\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^k b_i \right)-1\right)\right) 
&\iff 2\sum_{i=1}^k b_i(b_i-1) \le \left(\sum_{i=0}^k b_i\right)^2-\sum_{i=0}^k b_i-\left(\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\right)^2+\sum_{i=1}^k b_i 
&\iff 2\sum_{i=1}^k b_i^2 - 2\sum_{i=1}^k b_i \le b_0^2+2b_0\sum_{i=1}^k b_i + \left(\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\right)^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\right)^2 - b_0 
&\iff 2\sum_{i=1}^k b_i^2 \le 2\sum_{i=1}^kb_0b_i + b_0^2-b_0 + 2\sum_{i=1}^k b_i.
\end{align*}
It is easy to show that  $b_0^2-b_0$  is nonnegative for all nonnegative integers  $b_0,$  and we also know that   $$ 2\sum_{i=1}^k b_i \ge 0 $$   because all of  $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k$  are nonnegative. Therefore, it suffices to prove that   $$ 2\sum_{i=1}^k b_i^2 \le 2\sum_{i=1}^k b_0b_i. $$   This easily follows from the fact that  $b_0 \ge b_i$  for all  $i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\},$  concluding the inductive step.

Hence, by the Principle of Mathematical Induction, we have proven the desired statement for all nonnegative integers  $n$  and thus all positive integers  $n.$   $\square$</details>

solConsider a group of \(a_0\) people, no two of which have the same age. There exist clubs \(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_n.\) Everyone is in club \(c_0,\) and \(|c_i| = a_i.\) Additionally, \(c_j \subseteq c_i\) when \(i < j.\) Clubs with higher indices are considered more prestigious because they are more exclusive. Each person possesses one card for each club they are in. The left-hand side counts the number of "wild pairs," where a wild pair is an unordered pairs of cards such that: - they are from different people - they are from different clubs - the older person has the less prestigious card - the older person is in the club of the younger person's card To show this, note that if we focus on the case where the younger person's card is for club \(c_i,\) then there are \(\binom{a_i}2\) ways to choose \(2\) people from the younger person's card's club (which both people are in), and the older person can choose any of \(i\) less prestigious clubs to show a card from. Let \[B=\binom{a_0+a_1+\cdots+a_n}2.\] Note that \(B\) is the total number of unordered card pairs. If \(M\) is the number of card pairs that come from the same person OR the same club, the number of unordered pairs of cards such that an older person has a less prestigious card is \(\frac{B-M}2\) by symmetry. This is at least the number of wild pairs, since to be a wild pair entails an additional condition that the older person is in the younger person's card's club. So, \[\sum_{i=0}^n i\binom{a_i}2 \le \frac{B-M}2 \le \frac12 B = \frac12 \binom{a_0+a_1+\cdots+a_n}2 \] as desired.

stem_md: Let  $n$  and  $k$  be positive integers with  $k<n$ . Let  $P(x)$  be a polynomial of degree  $n$  with real coefficients, nonzero constant term, and no repeated roots. Suppose that for any real numbers  $a_0,\,a_1,\,\ldots,\,a_k$  such that the polynomial  $a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$  divides  $P(x)$ , the product  $a_0a_1\cdots a_k$  is zero. Prove that  $P(x)$  has a nonreal root.
solution_md:
Assume FTSOC  $P$  has  $n$  real roots. WLOG  $P$  has leading coefficient  $1$  so let  $P(x)=:(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_n)$ . WLOG  $k=n-1$ , as otherwise we can take  $Q:=(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_{k+1})$  and deal with  $Q$  instead of  $P$ .

By the assertion, each  $\frac{P(x)}{x-r_i}$  for  $1\leq i\leq n$  has a coefficient equal to  $0$ . Since  $r_i\neq 0$  for all  $i$ , this coefficient is not the leading or constant coefficient, so it has  $k-1=n-2$  choices. By pigeonhole, there exists  $1\leq i<j\leq n$  such that  $Q(x):=\frac{P(x)}{x-r_i}$  and  $R(x):=\frac{P(x)}{x-r_j}$  have no  $x^\alpha$  term, for some  $\alpha\geq 1$ . WLOG  $i=n-1$  and  $j=n$ . Hence
\begin{align*}
P(x)&=(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_{n-2})(x-r_n)
Q(x)&=(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_{n-2})(x-r_{n-1}).
\end{align*}
Then  $P(x)-Q(x)=(r_{n-1}-r_n)(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_{n-2})$  has no  $x^\alpha$  term, so  $A(x):=(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_{n-2})$  has no  $x^\alpha$  term since  $r_{n-1}\neq r_n$ . Also,  $r_{n-1}P(x)-r_nQ(x)=x(r_{n-1}-r_n)(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_{n-2})$  has no  $x^\alpha$  term so  $A(x)$  has no  $x^{\alpha-1}$  term.**Claim.**  $A(x)$  cannot have  $n-2$  distinct real roots.
*Proof.* Suppose FTSOC  $A(x)$  has  $n-2$  distinct real roots. We claim that  $A^{(m)}(x)$ , the  $m$ th derivative of  $A(x)$ , has  $n-2-m$  distinct real roots for all  $m\leq n-2$ . We proceed by induction on  $m$  with the base case  $m=0$  trivial.

Assume  $A^{(m)}(x)$  has  $n-2-m$  distinct real roots. Between every  $2$  consecutive real roots there exists a local extremum, where  $A^{(m+1)}(x)$  is  $0$ .  $A^{(m)}(x)$  has  $n-2-m-1$  pairs of consecutive real roots so  $A^{(m+1)}(x)$  has  $n-2-(m+1)$  distinct real roots, completing the induction step. $A^{(\alpha-1)}$  has no  $x^{(\alpha-1)-(\alpha-1)}=x^0$  or  $x^{\alpha-(\alpha-1)}=x$  term, so  $0$  is a double root of  $A^{(\alpha-1)}$ . However, all the roots of  $A^{(\alpha-1)}$  are distinct and real, a contradiction.  $\square$ This is a contradiction since  $r_1,\,\ldots,\,r_{n-2}$  are distinct real numbers. Thus  $P$  has a nonreal root.  $\square$
