stem_md: Let  $ \left(a_n \right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$  defined by  $ a_1 \equal{} 1,$  and  $ a_{n \plus{} 1} \equal{} a^4_n \minus{} a^3_n \plus{} 2a^2_n \plus{} 1$  for  $ n \geq 1.$  Show that there is an infinite number of primes  $ p$  such that none of the  $ a_n$  is divisible by  $ p.$
solution_md: [mod. edit] Let $ n$ be a prime number and take (a prime number) $ p$ such that $ p|a_n^2 \minus{} a_n \plus{} 2$ . Clearly $ a_{n \plus{} 1} \equiv 1 \text{ mod } p$ . Since $ a_1 \equiv 1 \text{ mod } p$ , the sequence has a period $ \text{ mod } p$ , which is a divisor of $ n$ . Such a divisor must be $ n$ or $ 1$ . If the sequence has period $ 1$ , then $ p \mid a_2 \minus{} a_1 \Rightarrow p \equal{} 2$ , contradiction if we choose an odd $ p$ . Now, to prove $ p \nmid a_k$ for any $ k$ , we may suppose $ k \le n$ . If $ p \mid a_k$ , then $ a_{k \plus{} 1} \equiv 1 \text{ mod } p$ , so $ k$ is a period of the sequence $ \Rightarrow n \mid k$ . Thus, $ k \equal{} n \Rightarrow p \mid a_n \Rightarrow a_n^2 \minus{} a_n \plus{} 2 \equiv 2 \text{ mod } p$ , which gives $ p \equal{} 2$ , contradiction. It remains to prove $ a_n^2 \minus{} a_n \plus{} 2$ may have infinitely many distinct prime divisors, $ n$ prime. Notice that, if $ p > 2$ , $ p|a_n^2 \minus{} a_n \plus{} 2$ and $ p|a_m^2 \minus{} a_m \plus{} 2 \Rightarrow$ both $ m$ and $ n$ are periods of the sequence, contradiction. Hence, we just need to prove $ a_n^2 \minus{} a_n \plus{} 2$ is not a power of $ 2$ when $ n$ for infinitely many primes $ n$ . Now I am going to do a very uggly thing. I am sorry. Suppose $ n$ is a very large prime number. Very large. We may assume the next prime number is $ n \plus{} k \plus{} 1$ , where $ k < \text{log}_2 n$ , since the primes' density is $ 1/\text{ln } n$ . We have, for a big $ m$ , $ a_{m \plus{} 1} < a_m^4 \Rightarrow a_{n \plus{} k \plus{} 1} < a_{n \plus{} 1}^{4^k}$ $ a_{m \plus{} 1} \minus{} 1 > (a_m \minus{} 1)^4 \Rightarrow a_{n \plus{} k \plus{} 1} > (a_{n \plus{} 1} \minus{} 1)^{4^k}$ Now, observe that $ a_n^2 \minus{} a_n \plus{} 2 \equal{} 2^t \Rightarrow a_{n \plus{} 1} \equal{} 2^ta_n^2 \plus{} 1$ . We have $ (2^ta_n^2)^{4^k} < a_{n \plus{} k \plus{} 1} < (2^ta_n^2 \plus{} 1)^{4^k}$ Also, $ a_n^2 \equal{} 2^t(1 \plus{} \alpha) \Rightarrow (2^ta_n^2)^{4^k} \equal{} 2^{2t.4^k}(1 \plus{} \alpha)^{4^k} \approx 2^{2t.4^k}(1 \plus{} \alpha.4^k)$ , since $ \alpha \approx 1/a_n$ is very small if compared to $ 4^k < n^2$ . Similarly, $ (a_{n \plus{} 1} \minus{} 1)^{4^k} \approx 2^{2t.4^k}(1 \plus{} \alpha.4^k)$ . From the fact that $ 1 \plus{} \alpha.4^k$ is not an integer, we conclude $ a_{n \plus{} k \plus{} 1}$ is not a power of $ 2$ . Can somebody prove this result to any sequence of the form $ a_1 \equal{} 1, a_{n \plus{} 1} \equal{} a_nP(a_n) \plus{} 1$ ?

solution_md:
Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ such that $ \forall x,y,z \in \mathbb{R}$ we have: If \[ x^3 \plus{} f(y) \cdot x \plus{} f(z) \equal{} 0,\] then \[ f(x)^3 \plus{} y \cdot f(x) \plus{} z \equal{} 0.\]
Nice problem :)
solutionAnswer: The only function which works is the identity. It is clear to check that it works. I prove that no other function does, so for the sake of argument, let $f$ be a function which satisfies the given condition. Henceforth, we will refer to a triple $(x,y,z)$ satisfying $x^3+f(y)x+f(z)=0$ as *valid.* We will use subtly, the fact that any cubic real polynomial has at least one real root.**Claim 1:** There exists a real number $x_0$ such that $f(x_0)=0$ . (Proof) Let $x_0$ be a real solution of $x^3+xf(0)+f(0)=0$ . Evidently, $(x_0,0,0)$ is valid so $f(x_0)^3=0$ so our claim holds. $\square$ **Claim 2:** $f(0)=0$ . (Proof) Note that $(0, y, x_0)$ is valid where $x_0$ satisfies $f(x_0)=0$ so $f(0)^3+yf(0)+x_0=0$ for all reals $y$ which yields $f(0)=0$ . $\square$ **Claim 3:** $f$ is injective. (Proof) Let $f(a)=f(b)$ and take $x, y$ as real numbers for which $(x, y, a)$ is valid. Consequently, $(x,y,b)$ is also valid, so $$ f(x)^3+yf(x)+a=f(x)^3+yf(x)+b=0 \Longrightarrow a=b $$ so injectivity follows. $\square$ Now that we have proved the easy claims, it's time to make bolder ones.**Claim 4:** $f$ is surjective. (Proof) Fix an arbitrary $t \in \mathbb{R}$ . Consider the polynomial $$ P(X)=(X-t)\cdot \left(X^2+tX+(1+t^2)\right). $$ Set $z_0=-t(1+t^2)$ and $y_0=1$ . Take $x_0$ to be a real number for which $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is valid and observe that $$ P(x_0)=f(x_0)^3+y_0f(x_0)+z_0=0. $$ Since $P$ has exactly one real root $t$ we conclude $f(x_0)=t,$ establishing the claim. $\square$ **Claim 5:** For all $y \ge 0$ we have $f(y) \ge 0$ as well. (Proof) For the sake of contradiction, let $y_0>0$ be a real number for which $f(y_0)<0$ . Let $x_0$ be a solution to $x^2=-f(y)$ and see that $(x_0, y_0, 0)$ is a valid triple so $f(x_0)^3+yf(x_0)=0$ which fails to occur since $x_0 \ne 0 \Longrightarrow f(x_0) \ne 0$ by injectivity and $f(x_0)^2+y_0>0$ . Our initial assertion fails so we get a contradiction! $\square$ **Claim 6:** $f$ is additive. (Proof) Fix any three distinct real numbers $a, b, c$ such that $a+b+c=0$ . Note that $f$ is surjective so we can choose real numbers $y_0, z_0$ such that $a, b, c$ are the roots of the polynomial $f(X)=X^3+Xf(y)+f(z)=0$ . Evidently, $f(a), f(b), f(c)$ are distinct real numbers (since $a, b, c$ are distinct), which happen to be the roots of the equation $X^3+yX+z=0$ . It follows that $f(a)+f(b)+f(c)=0$ so for all real numbers $a, b$ we get $$ f(-(a+b))=-(f(a)+f(b)). $$ Put $b=0$ to get $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$ , yielding $f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)$ for all distinct reals $a, b$ . For $a=b$ simply consider $$ f(2a)=f(a+m)+f(a-m)=(f(a)+f(m))+(f(a)-f(m))=2f(a) $$ where $m$ is a sufficiently large number. Thus, $f$ is completely additive. $\square$ **Claim 7:** $f$ is the identity function. stem_md: For which  $ n \geq 2, n \in \mathbb{N}$  are there positive integers  $ A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$  which are not the same pairwise and have the property that the product  $ \prod^n_{i \equal{} 1} (A_i \plus{} k)$  is a power for each natural number  $ k.$
solution_md:
There cannot exist a natural number  $ n$  satisfying the condition.

Assume that there exist integers  $ A_1$ ,  $ A_2$ , ..,  $ A_n$  such that  $ \prod^{n}_{i \equal{} 1} (A_i \plus{} k)$  is a power for all natural  $ k$ .

We may assume without loss of generality that  $ A_n$  is the maximum among  $ A_i$ .

Due to the infinitude of prime numbers, there exists a prime  $ p > A_n$ .
Let  $ k \equal{} p \minus{} A_n$ , and observe that since  $ A_i$  are pairwise distinct, we obtain that  $ p| \prod^{n}_{i \equal{} 1} (A_i \plus{} k)$ 
but  $ p^2$  cannot divide  $ \prod^{n}_{i \equal{} 1} (A_i \plus{} k)$ . This is a contradiction to the fact that  $ \prod^{n}_{i \equal{} 1} (A_i \plus{} k)$  is a power.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Germany Team Selection Test/289411.json

stem_md: Let  $p > 7$  be a prime which leaves residue 1 when divided by 6. Let  $m=2^p-1,$  then prove  $2^{m-1}-1$  can be divided by  $127m$  without residue.
solution_md: Straightforward proof with p-adic valuation: Pick a prime $q$ , that divides $127 \cdot m$ First rewrite the statement as $v_q(127m) \le v_q(2^{m-1}-1)$ Then we can apply the LTE lemma. Hence we can write the expression as $v_q(127) + v_q(m) \le v_q(m-1)$ In order to apply LTE for $v_q(m)$ once again we must assume that $q \not= 127$ . Thus we can reduce the term as $v_q(2^p-1) \le v_q(m-1)$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_q(p) \le v_q(2^p-2)$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_q(p) \le v_q(2) + v_q(p-1)$ , but since $q \not= 2$ , it is equivalent to $v_q(p) \le v_q(p-1)$ . Now we just have to proof that $p$ does not divide $2^p-1$ . Subproof: Assume for a contradiction, that $2^p \equiv 1 mod(p)$ . Then $ord_p(2) \mid p$ $\Rightarrow$ $ord_p(2) = 1,p$ Case 1: $ord_p(2) =1$ $\Rightarrow$ $2^1 \equiv 1 mod(p)$ $\Rightarrow$ $p=1$ contradiction Case 2: $ord_p(2)=p$ But according to Fermat‘s little theorem $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 mod(p)$ , because $p-1 < p$ . We get a contradiction.

stem_md: Initially, on a board there a positive integer. If board contains the number  $x,$  then we may additionally write the numbers  $2x+1$  and  $\frac{x}{x+2}.$  At some point 2008 is written on the board. Prove, that this number was there from the beginning.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Construct an infinite binary tree, with  $2x+1$  the left child of  $x$  and  $\frac{x}{x+2}$  the right child of  $x$  for every node  $x$ . Let  $N$  be the root of this tree.

For any rational number  $x=p/q$  with  $\gcd(p,q)=1$ , define the parity  $o(x)=(p\mod 2,q\mod 2)$ .

If  $o(x)=(1,1)$ , then every number in its subtree has parity  $(1,1)$ , so 2008 is not found in this subtree. From this it follows that  $N$  must be even.

If  $o(x)=(0,1)$ , then  $o(2x+1)=(1,1)$ , so its left subtree does not have a 2008. That means 2008 must be in its right subtree. Similarly, if  $o(x)=(1,0)$ , then  $o\left(\frac{x}{x+2}\right)=(1,1)$ , so 2008 must be in  $x$ 's left subtree.

We now prove an invariant: For every node  $x=p/q$  with  $\gcd(p,q)=1$  on the path from  $N$  to 2008,  $p+q=N+1$ .

We prove this by induction. Certainly this is true for  $N$  itself. Now let  $x$  be a node for which this is true. If  $o(x)=(1,0)$ , then
\[2x+1=\frac{2p+q}{q}=\frac{p+q/2}{q/2}.\]
This fraction is irreducible and the sum of its numerator and denominator is  $p+q=N+1$ . On the other hand, if  $o(x)=(0,1)$ , then
\[\frac{x}{x+2}=\frac{p}{p+2q}=\frac{p/2}{p/2+q}.\]
The same thing applies to this.

At the end of this path is 2008, so it must be that  $N=2008$ .

<details><summary>Note</summary>that 2008 could have been replaced with any even positive integer and the problem would still be true.</details></details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Germany Team Selection Test/418596.json

Both numbers  $\frac{x}{x+2}=\frac{a}{a+2b}$  and  $2x+1=\frac{2a+b}{b}$  have the sum of their denominator and numerator  $2(a+b)$ , an even number. So all the new numbers will have an even sum of their denominator and numerator.
Since  $2008=\frac{2008}{1}$  has an odd sum of its denominator and numerator, it must be the first number on the board.</details>

stem_md: Find positive real numbers  $x,y,z$  that are solutions of the system  $x+y+z=xy+yz+zx$  and  $xyz=1$  , and have the smallest possible sum.
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim that the answer is  $\boxed{(1, 1, 1)}$ . By AM-GM,   $$ x + y + z \ge 3\sqrt[3]{xyz} = 3, $$   which is achieved when  $x = y = z = 1$ . The solution also satisfies the given equality  $x + y + z = xy + yz + zx$ , so this is our answer.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Greece JBMO TST/1830519.json

candidates: AM-GM gives x+y+z is at least 3, x=y=z=1. This also satisfies the given equation.

**<u>Claim</u>**: \( x = y = z = 1 \) is the only solution.**<u>Proof</u>**: We know that,
\[
\frac{(x+y+z)^2}{3} \geq (xy + yz + zx) \quad \text{----(lemma-1)}
\]
The above can easily be verified, as we get:
\[
x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \geq xy + yz + zx \quad \text{(or)} \quad (x-y)^2 + (y-z)^2 + (z-x)^2 \geq 0
\]
Given:
\[
x + y + z = xy + yz + zx \quad \text{----(1)}
\]
\[
xyz = 1 \quad \text{----(2)}
\]
So we get:
\[
x + y + z \geq 3 \quad \text{(using lemma-1)}
\]
As we wanted the minimum value of \( x + y + z \), we will put \( x + y + z = xy + yz + zx = 3 \).

Equality would occur if and only if \( x = y = z = 1 \) and it also satisfies \( xyz = 1 \).

Hence our claimed answer was true.
metadata.original_path: Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Greece JBMO TST/1830519.json

stem_md:
Given are the non zero natural numbers  $a,b,c$  such that the number  $\frac{a\sqrt2+b\sqrt3}{b\sqrt2+c\sqrt3}$  is rational. 
Prove that the number  $\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{a+b+c}$  is an integer .
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Rationalizing the denominator, we have   $$ \dfrac{a\sqrt{2} + b\sqrt{3}}{b\sqrt{2} + c\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{(a\sqrt{2} + b\sqrt{3})(b\sqrt{2} - c\sqrt{3})}{(b\sqrt{2} + c\sqrt{3})(b\sqrt{2} - c\sqrt{3})} = \dfrac{(2ab - 3bc) + (b^2 \sqrt{6} - ac\sqrt{6})}{2b^2 - 3c^2}. $$   Since the number is rational and  $a, b, c$  are non-zero natural numbers, we have   $$ (b^2 - ac)\sqrt{6} = 0 \Rightarrow b^2 = ac. $$   Recall the expansion   $$ (a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - 2(ab + bc + ca), $$   we plug in  $ac = b^2$  and get   $$ (a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - 2b(a + b + c) \Rightarrow (a + 3b + c)(a + b + c) = a^2 + b^2 + c^2, $$   so   $$ \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{a + b + c} = a + 3b + c, $$   which is an integer, as desired.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Greece JBMO TST/1830521.json

candidates:
Rationalizing the denominator, we have  $\frac{a\sqrt{2}+b\sqrt{3}}{b\sqrt{2}+c\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2ab-3bc+(b^2-ac)\sqrt{6}}{4b-9c}$ Since the denominator is rational, we need the numerator to be rational as well. Since  $2ab-3bc$  is rational,  $(b^2-ac)\sqrt{6}$  must be rational. Thus  $b^2=ac$ . 
Next, we have  $GCD(a+b+c, a^2+b^2+c^2)=GCD(a+b+c, a^2+b^2+c^2-(a+b+c)^2)$  by the Euclidean Algorithm.
This is  $GCD(a+b+c, 2ab+2bc+2ac)=GCD(a+b+c,2ab+2bc+2b^2)=GCD(a+b+c, 2b(a+b+c))=a+b+c$  as desired.

stem_md: Given convex quadrilateral  $ABCD$  inscribed in circle  $(O,R)$  (with center  $O$  and radius  $R$ ). With centers the vertices of the quadrilateral and radii  $R$ , we consider the circles  $C_A(A,R), C_B(B,R), C_C(C,R), C_D(D,R)$ . Circles  $C_A$  and  $C_B$  intersect at point  $K$ , circles  $C_B$  and  $C_C$  intersect at point  $L$ , circles  $C_C$  and  $C_D$  intersect at point  $M$  and circles  $C_D$  and  $C_A$  intersect at point  $N$  (points  $K,L,M,N$  are the second common points of the circles given they all pass through point  $O$ ). Prove that  quadrilateral  $KLMN$  is a parallelogram.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $AB$ . Then  $K$  is simply the reflection of  $O$  across  $M$ , so that  $AOBK$  is a parallelogram. If we set  $O$  to be the origin, we have  $\vec{K}=\vec{A}+\vec{B}$ .

Similarly,  $\vec L=\vec B+\vec C,\vec  M=\vec C+\vec D,N=\vec D+\vec A$ , Hence,  $\vec K+\vec M=\vec A+\vec B+\vec C+\vec D=\vec L+\vec N$ , so  $KLMN$  is a parallelogram.</details>

stem_md: Let  $ x,y,z$  be nonnegative real numbers such that  $ x \plus{} y \plus{} z \equal{} 2$ . Prove that  $ x^{2}y^{2} \plus{} y^{2}z^{2} \plus{} z^{2}x^{2} \plus{} xyz\leq 1$ . When does the equality occur?
solution_md: Let's make the inequality we have to prove homogeneous. We have to prove  $ (x\plus{}y\plus{}z)^{4}>\equal{}16(x^{2}y^{2}\plus{}y^{2}z^{2}\plus{}z^{2}x^{2})\plus{}8(x^{2}yz\plus{}xy^{2}z\plus{}xyz^{2})$ , which is equivalent to  $ (x^{4}\plus{}y^{4}\plus{}z^{4})\plus{}4(x^{3}y\plus{}xy^{3}\plus{}...)\plus{}4(x^{2}yz\plus{}zy^{2}z\plus{}xyz^{2})>\equal{}10(x^{2}y^{2}\plus{}y^{2}z^{2}\plus{}z^{2}x^{2})$ . By Muirhead inequality, we have  $ 4(x^{3}y\plus{}xy^{3}\plus{}...)>\equal{}8(x^{2}y^{2}\plus{}y^{2}z^{2}\plus{}z^{2}x^{2})$ . So we are left to prove  $ (x^{4}\plus{}y^{4}\plus{}z^{4})\plus{}4(x^{2}yz\plus{}zy^{2}z\plus{}xyz^{2})>\equal{}2(x^{2}y^{2}\plus{}y^{2}z^{2}\plus{}z^{2}x^{2})$ . We will prove the stronger inequality:  $ (x^{4}\plus{}y^{4}\plus{}z^{4})\plus{}(x^{2}yz\plus{}zy^{2}z\plus{}xyz^{2})>\equal{}2(x^{2}y^{2}\plus{}y^{2}z^{2}\plus{}z^{2}x^{2})$ . Assume wlog  $ x>\equal{}y>\equal{}z$ . Than, the last inequality is equivalent to  $ (x\minus{}y)^{2}(x\plus{}y\minus{}z) \plus{} (x\minus{}z)^{2}(x\plus{}z\minus{}y)>\equal{}(y\minus{}z)^{2}(x\minus{}y\minus{}z)$ . Obviously,  $ (x\minus{}y)^{2}(x\plus{}y\minus{}z)>\equal{}0, (x\minus{}z)^{2}(x\plus{}z\minus{}y)>\equal{}0$ . If  $ (y\minus{}z)^{2}(x\minus{}y\minus{}z)<0$ , the inequality is obviously true. Consider the case  $ (y\minus{}z)^{2}(x\minus{}y\minus{}z)>\equal{}0$ : Easy to notice that  $ (x\minus{}z)^{2}>\equal{}(y\minus{}z)^{2}$  and  $ x\plus{}z\minus{}y>\equal{}x\minus{}y\minus{}z$ . So,  $ (x\minus{}z)^{2}(x\plus{}z\minus{}y)>\equal{}(y\minus{}z)^{2}(x\minus{}y\minus{}z)$ , implying the desired inequality. So, we see that equality doesn't hold in case all of the variables  $ x,y,z$  are positive (As  $ 4(x^{2}yz\plus{}zy^{2}z\plus{}xyz^{2})>\equal{}(x^{2}yz\plus{}zy^{2}z\plus{}xyz^{2})$  where the equality doesn't hold). So we are left to consider the case when one of the variables is  $ 0$ . As  $ z$  is minimal, we have  $ z\equal{}0$ . Our inequality becomes  $ x^{2}y^{2}<\equal{}1\equal{}\frac{(x\plus{}y)^{4}}{16}$ , which is true by AM-GM inequality. Equality holds if and only if  $ x\equal{}y\equal{}1$ . So, equality cases are  $ (0,1,1)$  and all possible symmetric permutations.  Lasha Lakirbaia.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Greece National Olympiad/260607.json

stem_md: If  $a$  and  $b$  are positive integers such that  $a^2-b^4= 2009$ , find  $a+b$ .
solution_md: We use the difference of squares factorization to obtain  $(a+b^2)(a-b^2) = 2009$ . The prime factorization of  $2009$  is  $7^2 \cdot 41$ . If we choose two factors  $x$  and  $y$  such that  $xy = 2009$ ,  $a+b^2 = x$ , and  $a-b^2 = y$ , then  $2b^2 = x-y$ . If  $x = 2009$ , then  $y=1$  and  $2b^2 = 2008$ , but then  $b = \sqrt{1004}$ , which is not integral. If  $x = 287$ , then  $y = 7$  and  $2b^2 = 280$ , but then  $b = \sqrt{140}$ , which is not an integer. If  $x = 49$ , then  $y = 41$  and  $2b^2 = 8$ , so  $b = 2$ . As a result,  $a = 45$ , so  $a+b = 45+2 = \boxed{47}$ .

stem_md: Let  $S$  be the sum of all the real coefficients of the expansion of  $(1+ix)^{2009}$ .  What is  $\log_2(S)$ ?
solution_md: $z=(1+ix)^n \implies Re(z)=\frac{z+\bar{z}}{2}$ now sum of coeff means  $x=1$ ,  $Re(z)=\frac{(1+i)^n+(1-i)^n}{2}$  $1+i=1+e^{i \pi/2}=e^{i \pi/4}(e^{-i \pi/4}+e^{i \pi/4})$  $=e^{i \pi/4}(2cos(\pi/4))=e^{i \pi/4}(\sqrt{2})$ and thus  $1-i=e^{-i \pi/4}(\sqrt{2})$ now  $\frac{(1+i)^n+(1-i)^n}{2}=\frac{e^{i \pi n/4}(\sqrt{2^n})+e^{-i \pi n/4}(\sqrt{2^n})}{2}$  $=(\sqrt{2^n})(\frac{e^{i \pi n/4}+e^{-i \pi n/4}}{2})=(\sqrt{2^n})(2cos(\pi n/4)/2)=(\sqrt{2^n})(cos(\pi n/4))$ for  $n=2009, \pi n/4 =(\pi)(502+1/4)=(\pi)(2)(251)+(\pi)/4$  $ \implies cos(\pi n/4)=cos(2\pi k + \pi/4)=cos(\pi/4)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ therefore  $(\sqrt{2^n})(cos(\pi n/4))={\sqrt{2}}^{2009-1}=2^{1004} =S $  $\implies \log_2(S)=\boxed{1004}$

The binomial expansion formula is used here:
\[(1+ix)^n = \binom{n}{0}(ix)^0+\binom{n}{1}(ix)^1 + \binom{n}{2}(ix)^2 + \cdots + \binom{n}{n-1} (ix)^{n-1}+\binom{n}{n} (ix)^n.\]
If we substitute  $x = 1, -1$ , we have
\[(1+i)^n = \binom{n}{0}i^0 + \binom{n}{1}i^1+\binom{n}{2}i^2+\cdots+\binom{n}{n-1}i^{n-1}+\binom{n}{n}i^n\]\[(1-i)^n = \binom{n}{0}i^0 - \binom{n}{1}i^1+\binom{n}{2}i^2-\cdots\pm \binom{n}{n-1}i^{n-1}\pm\binom{n}{n}i^n\]
Summing these (and consequently cancelling many terms) and dividing by  $2$  gives the desired result.

stem_md: If  $\tan x + \tan y = 4$  and  $\cot x + \cot y = 5$ , compute  $\tan(x + y)$ .
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $ X = \tan x $  and let  $ Y = \tan y $ . We are given that: \[ \begin{eqnarray*} X + Y &=& 4  \dfrac {1}{X} + \dfrac {1}{Y} &=& 5. \]We want \[ \tan (x + y) = \dfrac {\tan x + \tan y}{1 - \tan x \tan y} = \dfrac {X+Y}{1 - XY}. \]From the second equation above, we have: \[ \dfrac {X+Y}{XY} = 5 \rightarrow \dfrac {4}{XY} = 5 \rightarrow XY = \dfrac {4}{5}. \]So, our answer is: \begin{align*} \tan (x+y) &= \dfrac {X+Y}{1-XY} &= \dfrac {4}{1 - \dfrac {4}{5}} &= \dfrac {4}{\dfrac {1}{5}} &= \boxed {20}. \end{align*}</details>

stem_md: Suppose  $a$ ,  $b$  and  $c$  are integers such that the greatest common divisor of  $x^2+ax+b$  and  $x^2+bx+c$  is  $x+1$  (in the set of polynomials in  $x$  with integer coefficients), and the least common multiple of  $x^2+ax+b$  and  $x^2+bx+c$   $x^3-4x^2+x+6$ .  Find  $a+b+c$ .
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Notice that   $$ (x^3-4x^2+x+6)(x+1)=(x+1)(x+1)(x-2)(x-3) $$  Therefore,   $$ x^2+ax+b=(x+1)(x-2)=x^2-x-2 $$  So,  $a=-1$  and  $b=-2$ And,   $$ x^2+bx+c=(x+1)(x-3)=x^2-2x-3 $$  So,  $c=-3$ Therefore,   $$ a+b+c=-1-2-3=\boxed{-6} $$</details>

\[\frac{\sin\theta}{x}=\frac{\cos\theta}{y}\]
and
\[
\frac{\cos^4 \theta}{x^4}+\frac{\sin^4\theta}{y^4}=\frac{97\sin2\theta}{x^3y+y^3x}.
\]

solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>From the first equation, we have  $x=k\sin\theta,y=k\cos\theta$ .  Then substitution into the second equation yields:
\begin{align*}\frac{\cos^4\theta}{\sin^4\theta}+\frac{\sin^4\theta}{\cos^4\theta}&=\frac{97\cdot2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)}=194
\end{align*}
We see that if  $t=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x}$ , then  $\frac{\cos^4\theta}{\sin^4\theta}+\frac{\sin^4\theta}{\cos^4\theta}=(t^2-2)^2-2=194$  so solving, we have  $t=\boxed4$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$  be the  $3$  roots of  $x^3-x+1=0$ .  Find  $\frac{1}{a+1}+\frac{1}{b+1}+\frac{1}{c+1}.$
solution_md: Assume the roots of the polynomial  $x^3-x+1=0.$  are  $\alpha,\beta,\gamma.$  By Vieta's Relation we get,  $\sum_{cyc}{}\alpha=0,$   $\sum_{cyc}{}\alpha\beta=-1,$  and  $\prod_{cyc}{}\alpha=-1.$  Therefore we get,  $$ \sum_{cyc}{}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha+1}\right)=\frac{\prod_{cyc}{}(\alpha+1)(\beta+1)}{\prod_{cyc}{}(\alpha+1)} $$   Also By TOR we get,   $$ \frac{1}{\alpha+1}=t\implies\boxed{\alpha=\frac{1-t}{t}.} $$   Now plug in the value of  $\alpha$  in given polynomial we get,   $$ x^3-x+1=\left(\frac{1-t}{t}\right)^3-\left(\frac{1-t}{t}\right)+1=0. $$   Therefore we get,   $$ \boxed{t^3+2t^2-3t+1=0.}\implies \sum_{cyc}{}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha+1}\right)=\boxed{-2.} $$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament/455692.json

stem_md: Let  $f(x) =x^4+14x^3+52x^2+56x+16.$   Let  $z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4$  be the four roots of  $f$ .  Find the smallest possible value of  $|z_az_b+z_cz_d|$  where  $\{a,b,c,d\}=\{1,2,3,4\}$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>First we show that all 4 roots are real and negative. Notice that \begin{align*}x^4+14x^3+52x^2+56x+16=(x^2+7x+4)^2-5x^2  \implies (x^2+(7-\sqrt{5})x+4)(x^2+(7+\sqrt{5})x+4)=0  \implies x=\left\{\frac{\sqrt{5}-7\pm \sqrt{38-14\sqrt{5}}}{2}, \frac{-\sqrt{5}-7\pm\sqrt{38+14\sqrt{5}}}{2}\right\}.\end{align*} To show that  $\frac{\sqrt{5}-7\pm \sqrt{38-14\sqrt{5}}}{2}<0$  is negative, we have to prove that  $7-\sqrt{5}>\pm\sqrt{38-14\sqrt{5}}\implies 49-10\sqrt{5}+5>38-14\sqrt{5}\implies \sqrt{5}>-4$ , which is obviously true. To show that  $\frac{-\sqrt{5}-7\pm\sqrt{38+14\sqrt{5}}}{2}<0$ , we have to prove that  $\sqrt{5}+7>\pm\sqrt{38+14\sqrt{5}}\implies 54+14\sqrt{5}>38+14\sqrt{5}$ , which is obviously true. Thus, all four roots are real and negative. 

Now, noting that  $\frac{x^4}{16}=\left(\frac{14x^3}{56x}\right)^2$ , this motivates us to find  $f(2x)$ . We find that  $\frac{1}{16}f(2x)=x^4+7x^3+13x^2+7x+1$ . Because the coefficients are symmetric and the quartic is monic, this implies that  $2x=\frac{16}{2x}\implies x=\frac{4}{x}$ . Thus, the roots come in pairs that multiply to  $4$ . Let   $$ z_1=-r_1, z_2=-r_2, z_3=-r_3, z_4=-r_4 $$   and because  $z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4$  are negative,  $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$  are positive. Now WLOG  $r_3=\frac{4}{r_1}, r_4=\frac{4}{r_2}$ . Notice that the possible values of  $|z_az_b+z_cz_d|=|(-r_a)(-r_b)+(-r_c)(-r_d)|=r_ar_b+r_cr_d$  are \begin{align*} r_1r_2+r_3r_4=r_1r_2+\frac{16}{r_1r_2},  r_1r_3+r_2r_4=4+4=8,  r_1r_4+r_2r_3=4\left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}+\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right).\end{align*} We have that that  $r_1r_2+\frac{16}{r_1r_2}\geq 8$  by AM-GM, and  $4\left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}+\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)\geq 8$  by AM-GM as well. Thus the smallest possible value of  $|z_az_b+z_cz_d|$  is  $\boxed{8}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament/455695.json

stem_md: How many ways can the integers from  $-7$  to  $7$  inclusive be arranged in a sequence such that the absolute value of the numbers in the sequence does not decrease?
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Consider  $ -7 $ . The only number that can be after  $ -7 $  is  $ 7 $ , otherwise the absolute value would decrease. But now nothing can be after  $ 7 $ , so  $ 7 $  must be the final number in the sequence (of course, we can switch the roles of  $ -7 $  and  $ 7 $ .)

Now that  $ -7 $  and  $ 7 $  are placed, we can use similar logic for  $ -6 $  and  $ 6 $ , then for  $ -5 $  and  $ 5 $ , and so on.

Thus, there is only one way to organize the numbers considering only absolute value, but we have  $ 2 $  ways to arrange  $ 7 $  and  $ -7 $ ,  $ 2 $  ways to organize  $ 6 $  and  $ -6 $ , and so on, all the way down to  $ 2 $  ways to organize  $ 1 $  and  $ -1 $ , so there are  $ 2^7=\boxed{128} $  possible arrangements.</details>

EDIT:  :wallbash_red:  :stretcher:

stem_md: Two jokers are added to a  $52$  card deck and the entire stack of  $54$  cards is shuffled randomly. What is the expected number of cards that will be strictly between the two jokers?
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Consider the probability that there are  $ n $  cards between the two jokers. There are  $ 53-n $  possible placements (the first joker can be from position  $ 1 $  to position  $ 54-(n+1) $ .) The probability that the jokers are in these positions are then  $ \left(\frac{2}{54}\right)\left(\frac{1}{53}\right) $ , since there is a  $ \frac{2}{54} $  chance that the first joker will be in one of the positions, then a  $ \frac{1}{53} $  chance that the second joker will be in the remaining position.

Therefore, the expected value is the sum of these values multiplied by  $ n $  as  $ n $  ranges from  $ 0 $  to  $ 52 $ .

\[ \sum_{n=0}^{52}{\left(n(53-n)\left(\frac{2}{54}\right)\left(\frac{1}{53}\right)\right) }\]

\[ \left(\frac{2}{54}\right)\left(\frac{1}{53}\right)\sum_{n=0}^{52}\left(-n^2+53n\right) \]

\[ \left(\frac{2}{54}\right)\left(\frac{1}{53}\right)\left(-\sum_{n=0}^{52}\left(n^2\right)+53\sum_{n=0}^{52}\left(n\right)\right) \]

\[ \left(\frac{2}{54}\right)\left(\frac{1}{53}\right)\left(-\frac{(52)(52+1)(2\cdot52+1)}{6}+53\left(\frac{(52)(52+1)}{2}\right)\right) \]

\[ \boxed{\frac{52}{3}} \]</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament/456717.json

candidates:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Expected value is linear. Therefore we just need to calculate the expected value of one card
For card  $i = 1, 2, ..., 52$ , define the function  $S_i$  to be  $$ S_i \stackrel{def}{=} 
\begin{cases} 
      1 & \small \text{card between jokers} 
      0 & \small \text{otherwise}
   \end{cases} $$    $$ \mathbb{E}(S_i) = \mathbb{P}(S_i = 1) = \frac{1}{3}  $$    $$ \mathbb{E}(S_1 + S_2 + ... + S_{52} ) = \sum{P(S_i)} = \boxed{\frac{52}{3}}  $$</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Each card has an equal likelihood of being either on top of the jokers, in between them, or below the jokers. Thus, on average,  $1/3$  of them will land between the two jokers. Multiplying this by the 52 yields our answer of  $\boxed{52/3}$ .</details>

Let  $s(n)$  denote the number of  $1$ 's in the binary representation of  $n$ . Compute
\[
\frac{1}{255}\sum_{0\leq n<16}2^n(-1)^{s(n)}.
\]
solution_md:
The key is to observe that if  $n<8$ ,  $(-1)^{s(n)}=(-1)(-1)^{s(n+8)}$ , so the sum becomes

\[\frac{1}{255}(1-2^8)\displaystyle\sum_{0\le n<8} 2^{n}(-1)^{s(n)}=\boxed{45}\]

stem_md: Paul fi lls in a  $7\times7$  grid with the numbers  $1$  through  $49$  in a random arrangement. He then erases his work and does the same thing again, to obtain two different random arrangements of the numbers in the grid. What is the expected number of pairs of numbers that occur in either the same row as each other or the same column as each other in both of the two arrangements?
solution_md:
There are  $49\choose 2$  pairs of numbers possible, each of which has a probability of 

\[\dfrac{14\times\dbinom{7}{2}}{\dbinom{49}{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\]

of being in the same row or column in one of the arrangements.

Hence, the expected number that are in the same row or column in both arrangements is

\[\dbinom{49}{2} \times \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{2}=\boxed{\frac{147}{2}}\]

stem_md: There are  $5$  students on a team for a math competition. The math competition has  $5$  subject tests. Each student on the team must choose  $2$  distinct tests, and each test must be taken by exactly two people. In how many ways can this be done?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>This is basically asking for the number of ways to have each vertex in the barpartite graph  $K_{5,5}$  be in some even cycle. Cycles of length  $2$  aren't allowed, since each person must take two tests and vice versa. Then the cycles must be split so that there is one cycle of length  $10$ , or there is one cycle of length  $4$  and one of length  $6$ .

Suppose the  $5$  team members are on the left and the  $5$  tests on the right. For the cycle of length  $10$ , there are  $5$  choices to start with some person on the left, then  $5$  choices for a test on the right, then  $4$  choices for a person on the left, and so on. But we've overcounted by a factor of  $10$ , since we're counting cycles. Then there are  $\frac{ (5!)^2 }{10} = 1440$  possibilities in this case.

For the second case, there are  ${\binom{5}{3}}^2=100$  ways to select which of the three tests and which of the three people are in the cycle of length  $6$ . Then there are  $\frac{ (3!)^2 }{6} = 6$  possible cycles of length  $6$  and  $\frac{ (2!)^2 }{4} = 1$  cycle of length  $4$ . So the total number of possibilities for this case is  $600$ .


The final answer is  $1440+600=\boxed{2040}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament/456724.json

stem_md: The squares of a  $3\times3$  grid are filled with positive integers such that  $1$  is the label of the upper- leftmost square,  $2009$  is the label of the lower-rightmost square, and the label of each square divides the  ne directly to the right of it and the one directly below it. How many such labelings are possible?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Label the cells in the grid  $C_{11}, C_{12},...,C_{33}$ . Observe that once the values of  $C_{11},C_{12}, C_{21},$  and  $C_{22}$  are determined, the values of  $C_{13}$  and  $C_{23}$  are dependent on the cells right of it and each other, and the values of  $C_{31}$  and  $C_{32}$  are dependent on the cells above it and each other. However, the values of  $C_{13}$  and  $C_{23}$  are independent of the values of  $C_{31}$  and  $C_{32}$ .  $$ \begin{bmatrix}
    C_{11} & C_{12} & C_{13} 
    C_{21} & C_{22} & C_{23} 
    C_{31} & C_{32} & C_{33} 
\end{bmatrix} $$  <details><summary>Case 1</summary>The middle square is  $1$ . In this case,  $C_{12}$  and   $C_{21}$  divide  $1$ , so they must be equal to one. 

Since  $1$  divides all integers, it only needs to be ensured that and  $C_{13}$  divides  $C_{23}$  and  $C_{31}$  divides  $C_{32}$ . The number of ways to choose an ordered pair  $(a,b)$  such that  $(a,b)\in\{1,7,41,49,287,2009\}^2$  and  $a$  divides  $b$  can be easily counted to be  $18$ . So, the total for this case is  $18^2=324$ .</details>
<details><summary>Case 2</summary>The middle square is  $7$ . In this case,  $C_{12}$  and  $C_{21}$  must be divisors of  $7$ , so they are either  $1$  or  $7$ . 

Suppose both are  $1$ . Then,  it's sufficient to ensure that  $C_{23}$  and  $C_{32}$  are multiples of  $7$ ,  $C_{13} \mid C_{23}$ , and  $C_{31} \mid C_{32}$  (which is true for all cases, so I'll stop writing this condition). Hence, we're counting pairs  $(a,b)$  of divisors of  $2009$  such that  $a \mid b$  and  $7 \mid b$ . There are  $15$  of these (again, can be counted very easily, best way is probably just to list all possible pairs  $(a,b)$  of divisors of  $2009$  such that  $a\mid b$ , that makes the process very quick). 

Now, suppose both are  $7$ . Then, we're counting pairs  $(a,b)$  such that  $7 \mid a$  and  $7\mid b$ . There are  $9$  of these. 

I claim the total in this case is  $(15+9)^2=24^2=576$ . Observe that there are two other cases possible:  $C_{12}=1$  and  $C_{21}=7$  or vice versa. However, notice that (1) these cases are identical and (2) they are included in the expansion of   $$ (15+9)^2=15^2+2\cdot 15\cdot 9 + 9^2. $$   <details><summary>Crucial observation</summary>This gives rise to a new idea: in each case, only the sub-cases where  $C_{12}=C_{21}$  need to be considered. Suppose for some value of  $C_{22}$ , there are  $k$  possible values for  $C_{12}=C_{21}$ , call these  $d_1,d_2,...,d_k$ . Now, suppose for each pair  $(d_j,C_{22})$ , there are exactly  $e_j$  ways to choose the values of  $C_{13}$  and  $C_{23}$ . Then, observe that   $$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^k e_i\right)^2=\sum_{i=1}^k e_i^2 + 2\sum_{1\leq i < j \leq k} e_ie_j $$   is exactly the number of possibilities for the particular value of  $C_{22}$ . This is because in the first sum on the right hand side, it sums over all the cases where  $C_{12}=C_{21}$ . In the second sum, it sums over the number of possibilities for all possible pairs of  $(d_i,d_j)$  with  $i\neq j$ . The factor of  $2$  in front is because you can flip the positions of  $C_{12}$  and  $C_{21}$  to achieve an identical case.</details></details>
<details><summary>Case 3</summary>The middle square is  $41$ . In this case,  $C_{12}$  and  $C_{21}$  can be  $1$  or  $41$ . Because of the observation in the last case, only the possibilities where they are equal need to be considered.

If  $C_{12}=C_{21}=1$ , then we're counting pairs  $(a,b)$  such that  $a\mid b$  and  $41 \mid b$ . There are  $12$  such pairs.

If  $C_{12}=C_{21}=41$ , then we're counting pairs  $(a,b)$  such that  $a\mid b$  and  $41 \mid a,b$ . There are  $6$  such pairs.

This gives a total of  $(12+6)^2=324$  possibilities for this case.</details>
<details><summary>Case 4</summary>The middle square is  $49$ . In this case, we can have  $C_{12}=1,7,$  or  $49$ .

If  $C_{12}=C_{21}=1$ , we're counting pairs  $(a,b)$  such that  $49 \mid b$ . There are  $9$  such pairs.

If  $C_{12}=C_{21}=7$ , we're counting pairs  $(a,b)$  such that  $7 \mid a$  and  $49\mid b$ . There are  $6$  such pairs.

If  $C_{12}=C_{21}=49$ , we're counting pairs  $(a,b)$  such that  $49\mid a,b$ . There are  $3$  such pairs.

The total for this case is  $(9+6+3)^2=324$ .</details>
<details><summary>Case 5</summary>The middle square is  $287$ . Applying the same exact logic as the past couple cases, there are  $(10+6+5+3)^2=576$  possibilities for this case.</details>
<details><summary>Case 6</summary>The middle square is  $2009$ . Applying the same logic as the past couple cases, there are  $(6+4+3+2+2+1)^2=324$  possibilities for this case.</details>

stem_md: Given a rearrangement of the numbers from  $1$  to  $n$ , each pair of consecutive elements  $a$  and  $b$  of the sequence can be either increasing (if  $a < b$ ) or decreasing (if  $b < a$ ). How many rearrangements of the numbers from  $1$  to  $n$  have exactly two increasing pairs of consecutive elements? Express your answer in terms of  $n$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The problem could be thought of visually as a graph with three sections. The first section is monotonically decreasing. The second section starts higher than the end of the first section, but is also monotonically decreasing. The third section starts higher than the end second section, but is also monotonically decreasing. Then, for each number in the set  $\{1,2,...,n\}$ , there are  $3$  ways to choose the section it goes to, giving an initial count of  $3^n$ . However, this also counts the cases where the graph has two sections, and one section (i.e. a straight line downwards that corresponds to the permutation  $n,n-1,...,1$ .

To count the number of permutations with only  $2$  sections, start with an initial count of  $2^n$  (because each element has two sections to go to). From this, you have to subtract the number of ways of choosing the point where you split into two sections that results in the permutation  $n,n-1,...,1$ . There are  $n+1$  ways of choosing this (to the left of each number, or after the  $1$ ). Hence, there are  $2^n-n-1$  permutations with only one increasing pair. However, this must be multiplied by the number of ways an invisible point where the section is split (since we're splitting the graph into three sections). There are  $(n+1)$  ways of doing this, so  $(n+1)(2^n-n-1)$  possibilities in the original count of  $3^n$  that lead to only one increasing pair.

To count the number of of ways to have one section, notice that the only possible permutation associated with this is  $n,n-1,...,1$ . Then, there are  $\binom{n+2}{2}$  ways of choosing two points where the line is being split into three sections (because of stars and bars).

Hence, the final answer is  $\boxed{3^n-(n+1)(2^n-n-1)-\binom{n+2}{2}}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament/456728.json

stem_md: Let  $f$  be a differentiable real-valued function defi ned on the positive real numbers. The tangent lines to the graph of  $f$  always meet the  $y$ -axis 1 unit lower than where they meet the function. If  $f(1)=0$ , what is  $f(2)$ ?
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Let's find the tangent line to a point  $ (x_0,f(x_0)) $ . 

The slope of the line is  $ f'(x_0) $ , so the formula in point slope form is  $ y-f(x_0)=f'(x_0)(x-x_0) $ , and in slope intercept form this is  $ y=f'(x_0)x+f(x_0)-x_0f'(x_0) $ . Therefore, the y-intercept is  $ f(x_0)-x_0f'(x_0) $ .

We're given that this is always one unit lower than where it intercepts the graph at  $ f(x_0) $ , so  $ f(x_0)-x_0f'(x_0)=f(x_0)-1 $ . Simplifying, we find that  $ f'(x_0)=\frac{1}{x_0} $ .

Integrating both sides, we get  $ f(x)=\ln(x)+C $  for some  $ C $ . We're given that  $ f(1)=0 $ , so  $ \ln(1)+C=0 $  and  $ C=0 $ . Therefore,  $ f(x)=\ln(x) $  and  $ f(2)=\boxed{\ln(2)} $ .</details>

stem_md: Compute  $e^A$  where  $A$  is defined as \[\int_{3/4}^{4/3}\dfrac{2x^2+x+1}{x^3+x^2+x+1}dx.\]
solution_md:
Not a unique solution, but I thought I would write out the complete solution here.  We can solve this using integration by parts. 
\begin{align*} 
&\int \frac{2x^2+x+1}{x^3+x^2+x+1}\,dx
&\int \frac{2x^2+x+1}{x^2(x+1)+(x+1)}\,dx
&\int \frac{2x^2+x+1}{(x^2+1)(x+1)}\,dx
&\int \frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{Bx}{x^2+1}\,dx
&\int \frac{A(x^2+1)+Bx(x+1)}{(x^2+1)(x+1)}\,dx
&\int \frac{Ax^2+A+Bx^2+Bx}{(x^2+1)(x+1)}\,dx
&\int \frac{(A+B)x^2+Bx+A}{x^3+x^2+x+1}\,dx.
\end{align*}
This makes a system of equations where  $A=1$  and  $B=1$ .  Replacing the values we get
\begin{align*}
\int \frac{1}{x+1}+\frac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx&=\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,dx+\int \frac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx
&=\log|x+1|+\frac{1}{2}\log|x^2+1|+C.
\end{align*}
Plugging in the two limits of integration, we find that  $A=\log\biggr(\frac{16}{9}\biggr)$ .  This means our final answer is  $e^A=\boxed{\frac{16}{9}}$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament/485445.json

solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Clearly this is evaluates to 0/0 if we just plug in  $h=0$ ; hence, we can use L'Hospital's rule on this limit:
\[\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{
4\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+4h)-12\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+3h)+12\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+2h)-4\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+h)
}{4h^3}\]
Canceling out the common factor of 4 gives
\[\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{
\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+4h)-3\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+3h)+3\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+2h)-\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+h)
}{h^3}\]
Obviously, this is still 0/0 if we plug in directly.  So we use L'Hospital again:
\[\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{
-4\sin(\frac{\pi}{3}+4h)+9\sin(\frac{\pi}{3}+3h)-6\sin(\frac{\pi}{3}+2h)+\sin(\frac{\pi}{3}+h)
}{3h^2}\]
And again:
\[\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{
-16\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+4h)+27\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+3h)-12\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+2h)+\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}+h)
}{6h}\]
And again:
\[\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{
64\sin(\frac{\pi}{3}+4h)-81\sin(\frac{\pi}{3}+3h)+24\sin(\frac{\pi}{3}+2h)-\sin(\frac{\pi}{3}+h)
}{6}\]
Plugging in 0 now gives  $\frac{6}{6}\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}$ .</details>

stem_md: The corner of a unit cube is chopped off such that the cut runs through the three vertices adjacent to the vertex of the chosen corner. What is the height of the cube when the freshly-cut face is placed on a table?
solution_md: The major diagonal has a length of  $\sqrt{3}$ . The volume of the pyramid is  $1/6$ , and so its height  $h$  satisfies  $\frac{1}{3}\cdot h\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(\sqrt{2})^2=1/6$  since the freshly cut face is an equilateral triangle of side length  $\sqrt{2}$ . Thus  $h=\sqrt{3}/3$ , and the answer is  $\boxed{2\sqrt{3}/3}$ .

Solution posted on the other thread, but edited due to the absence of choices
The height of the object is the difference between the space diagonal of the original cube and the altitude of the tetrahedron. The space diagonal of the cube is $\sqrt{3}$ , so we need to find the altitude of the tetrahedron. The base of the tetrahedron is an equilateral triangle with side length $\sqrt{2}$ . The slanted height of the tetrahedron is $1$ . The distance between a vertex of the base to its center is $\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3}$ . Therefore, the altitude of the tetrahedron is $\sqrt{1^2 - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3}\right)^2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ from the Pythagorean Theorem. Thus, the answer is $\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} = \boxed{\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}}$ .

stem_md: Circle  $B$  has radius  $6\sqrt{7}$ .  Circle  $A$ , centered at point  $C$ , has radius  $\sqrt{7}$  and is contained in  $B$ .  Let  $L$  be the locus of centers  $C$  such that there exists a point  $D$  on the boundary of  $B$  with the following property: if the tangents from  $D$  to circle  $A$  intersect circle  $B$  again at  $X$  and  $Y$ , then  $XY$  is also tangent to  $A$ .  Find the area contained by the boundary of  $L$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>In other words, the locus  $ L $  describes the possible centers  $ C $  such that there exists a triangle such that  $ B $  is the circumcircle and  $ A $  is the incircle.

According to Euler's Theorem, the distance between the circumcenter and the incenter of a triangle is equal to  $ \sqrt{R(R-2r)} $ , where  $ R $  is the circumradius and  $ r $  is the inradius. Since both  $ R $  and  $ r $  are given in the problem, this distance is constant, so the locus is a circle. The radius of the circle is this distance between the centers, which is  $ \sqrt{(6\sqrt{7})(6\sqrt{7}-2\sqrt{7})}=\sqrt{168} $ . 

Therefore, the area of this circle locus is  $ (\sqrt{168})^2\pi=\boxed{168\pi} $ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be a triangle in the coordinate plane with vertices on lattice points and with  $AB = 1$ .  Suppose the perimeter of  $ABC$  is less than  $17$ .  Find the largest possible value of  $1/r$ , where  $r$  is the inradius of  $ABC$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>We have  $ A=\frac{1}{2}rp $ , where  $ A $  is the area,  $ r $  is the inradius, and  $ p $  is the perimeter. Therefore,  $ r=\frac{2A}{p}\implies\frac{1}{r}=\frac{p}{2A} $ . Now we see that we want to maximize the perimeter while minimizing the area.

WLOG, let  $ A $  be on  $ (0,0) $  and let  $ B $  be on  $ (1,0) $ . Since this base length is set, to minimize the area, we need to minimize the height. Since  $ C $  must be on a lattice point, we can let it be on the line  $ y=1 $ , say,  $ (c,1) $  for some integer  $ c $ . Notice that we can make the perimeter arbitrarily large by making  $ c $  arbitrarily large, so this is the best case scenario. We now only have to find  $ c $  such that the perimeter is as large as possible without being greater than or equal to  $ 17 $ .

Since we're given that  $ AB=1 $ , we just need to have  $ BC+CA<16 $ . Since  $BC $  and  $ CA $  are close in length, we try  $ c=\frac{16}{2}=8 $ . Then, from the distance formula,  $ BC+CA=\sqrt{65}+\sqrt{50} $ .  $ \sqrt{65} $  is slightly more than  $ 8 $  and  $ \sqrt{50} $  is slightly more than  $ 7 $ , so  $ \sqrt{65}+\sqrt{50} $  is slightly more than  $ 15 $ . Clearly, if we try to go one unit more to the right, then  $ BC+CA $  will be more than  $ 16 $ .

Therefore,  $ A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot1\cdot1=\frac{1}{2} $  and  $ p=1+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{65} $ , so the largest value of  $ \frac{1}{r} $  is  $ \frac{1+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{65}}{2\cdot\frac{1}{2}}=\boxed{1+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{65}} $ .</details>

Let the points be labeled as above. Notice that  $ P $  is the incenter, and so  $ AP $  is also an angle bisector of  $ \angle A $ . Let  $ BD=x $ . From the Angle Bisector Theorem on  $ \triangle ABC $  with respect to  $ A $ , we have  $ \frac{DC}{x}=\frac{5}{16} $ , so  $ DC=\frac{5x}{16} $ . Now using the Angle Bisector Theorem on  $ \triangle ABD $  with respect to  $ B $ , we have  $ \frac{DP}{4}=\frac{x}{16} $ , so  $ DP=\frac{x}{4} $ .

Now we'll use Stewart's Theorem on  $ \triangle ABC $  and cevian  $ AD $ .

\begin{align*} (16)\left(\frac{5x}{16}\right)(16)+(5)(x)(5)&=\left(4+\frac{x}{4}\right)\left(x+\frac{5x}{16}\right)\left(4+\frac{x}{4}\right)+(x)\left(\frac{5x}{16}\right)\left(x+\frac{5x}{16}\right)105x&=\left(4+\frac{x}{4}\right)^2\left(\frac{21x}{16}\right)+(x)\left(\frac{5x}{16}\right)\left(\frac{21x}{16}\right)105&=\left(4+\frac{x}{4}\right)^2\left(\frac{21}{16}\right)+\left(\frac{5x}{16}\right)\left(\frac{21x}{16}\right)105\cdot256&=(16+x)^2(21)+(5x)(21x)5\cdot256&=(x+16)^2+5x^25(16-x)(16+x)&=(x+16)^280-5x&=x+166x&=64x&=\frac{32}{3} \end{align*}

Therefore,  $ BC=\frac{21x}{16}=\frac{21\left(\frac{32}{3}\right)}{16}=\boxed{14} $ .</details>

solution_md:
Suppose N is a $6$ -digit number having base- $10$ representation $\underline{a}\text{ }\underline{b}\text{ }\underline{c}\text{ }\underline{d}\text{ }\underline{e}\text{ }\underline{f}$ . If $N$ is $6/7$ of the number having base- $10$ representation $\underline{d}\text{ }\underline{e}\text{ }\underline{f}\text{ }\underline{a}\text{ }\underline{b}\text{ }\underline{c}$ , find $N$ .
Solution$N$ can be expressed as $1000A + B$ , where $A = \overline{abc}$ and $B = \overline{def}$ We know $1000A + B = \dfrac{6}{7}(1000B + A)$ or $7000A + 7B = 6000B + 6A$ or $6994A = 5993B$ A and B are both 3 digit numbers. We can use the Euclidean Algorithm to calculate the greatest common divisor of 6994 and 5993: $\gcd (6994, 5993) = \gcd (5993, 1001) = \gcd (1001, 988) = \gcd (1001, 13) = 13$ Now we can deduce that $A = \dfrac{5993}{13} = 461$ and $B = \dfrac{6994}{13} = 538$ , so $N = \overline{AB} = 461538$

stem_md: find all pairs of non-negative integer pairs  $(m,n)$ ,satisfies $107^{56}(m^{2}-1)+2m+3=\binom{113^{114}}{n}$
solution_md:
It is well known that  $\frac{n}{gcd(n,k)}|{n\choose k}$   $\implies$  for all  $0 < n < 113^{114}$ ,  $113|{113^{114}\choose n}$ Now, let  $(\frac{a}{b})$  denote the Legendre symbol
We have  $(\frac{107}{113})(\frac{113}{107}) = 1$ and  $(\frac{113}{107}) = (\frac{6}{107}) = (\frac{2}{107})(\frac{3}{107})$ and  $(\frac{3}{107})(\frac{107}{3}) = (\frac{3}{107})(\frac{2}{3}) = -(\frac{3}{107}) = -1$  $\implies (\frac{3}{107}) = 1$ and  $(\frac{2}{107}) = -1^{\frac{107^2-1}{8}} = -1$  $\implies (\frac{113}{107}) = -1$  $\implies (\frac{107}{113}) = -1$  $\implies 107^{56} \equiv 107^\frac{113-1}{2} \equiv -1 \pmod {113}$ Now, if  $0 < n < 113^{114}$ then  $107^{56}(m^2-1) + 2m + 3 \equiv 1-m^2+2m+3 \equiv 0 \pmod {113}$  $\implies m^2-2m-4 \equiv (m-1)^2 -5 \equiv \pmod {113}$  $\implies (m-1)^2 \equiv 5 \pmod {113}$  $\implies (\frac{5}{113}) = 1$  $\implies (\frac{113}{5}) = (\frac{3}{5}) = 1$  which is a contradiction
so there are no solutions if  $0< n < 113^{114}$ if  $0 = n$  or  $n \geq 113^{114}$ then we have  $107^{56}(m^2-1) + 2m + 3 = 0$ It is easy to see that there are no non-negative solutions to this
So there does not exist such non-negative pairs (m,n) that satisfies the given equation

stem_md: For a given prime  $ p > 2$  and positive integer  $ k$  let \[ S_k \equal{} 1^k \plus{} 2^k \plus{} \ldots \plus{} (p \minus{} 1)^k\] Find those values of  $ k$  for which  $ p \, |\, S_k$ .
solution_md:
Let  $g$  be a primitive root  $\pmod{p}$ . Then we make two cases:

Case 1:  $p-1\mid k$ .
Then  $S_k \equiv p-1 \pmod{p}$ , so it doesnt hold.
Case 2:  $p-1 \nmid k$ .

We claim that $S_k \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ if and only if $p-1 \, |\, k$ . As $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ for $a = 1, 2, \ldots, p-1$ , $p | S_k$ if and only if $p | S_{k\pm (p-1)}$ . Let $e_n$ be the $n$ th elementary symmetric polynomial evaluated at the numbers $1,2,\ldots,p-1$ , and let $P(x) = x^{p-1} - 1$ . By Fermat's little theorem, $x-a$ is a root of $P(x)$ for $a = 1, 2, \ldots, p-1$ . Therefore $P(x)$ factors as $(x-1)(x-2) \ldots (x-(p-1))$ modulo $p$ , which expands as $x^{p-1} - e_1 x^{p-2} + e_2 x^{p-3} - \ldots + e_{p-1}$ . Comparing coefficients, we find that $e_i \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ for $1 \leq i \leq p-2$ . As $e_i \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ for $1 \leq i \leq p-1$ , the result follows immediately.

(a) Do there exist 2009 distinct positive integers such that their sum is divisible by each of the given numbers?

(b) Do there exist 2009 distinct positive integers such that their sum is divisible by the sum of any two of the given numbers?
solution_md:
(a) Do there exist 2009 distinct positive integers such that their sum is divisible by each of the given numbers?
Suppose it exists $ n$ distinct positive integers $ a_i$ such that $ \sum\frac{1}{a_i}\equal{}1$ , then let $ b_k\equal{}\frac{\prod a_i}{a_k}$ : $ \{b_k\}$ are $ n$ distinct positive integers whose sum is $ S\equal{}\sum b_k\equal{}\prod a_i\sum\frac{1}{a_k}\equal{}\prod a_i$ and each $ b_k$ divides $ S$ . In order to end the demonstration, it's easy to show with induction that it is always possible, when $ n>2$ , to find $ n$ distinct positive integers $ a_i$ such that $ \sum\frac{1}{a_i}\equal{}1$ : It's true for $ n\equal{}3$ : $ 1\equal{}\frac 12\plus{}\frac 13\plus{}\frac 16$ If it's true for $ n$ , just replace $ \frac 1a$ , for the greatest $ a$ with $ \frac 1{a\plus{}1}\plus{}\frac 1{a(a\plus{}1)}$ and so it's true for $ n\plus{}1$ Hence the result.

stem_md: Denote the three real roots of the cubic  $ x^3 \minus{} 3x \minus{} 1 \equal{} 0$  by  $ x_1$ ,  $ x_2$ ,  $ x_3$  in order of increasing magnitude. (You may assume that the equation in fact has three distinct real roots.) Prove that  $ x_3^2 \minus{} x_2^2 \equal{} x_3 \minus{} x_1$ .
solution_md:
Let  $f(x)=x^3 - 3x -1$ .  Examining the values of f(1), f(0), f(-1) and f(-2), we can see that  $x_1 < x_2 < 0 < x_3$ . 

Note that if  $z$  is a root of  $f(x)=0$ , then  $1/z$  and  $(-1-z)$  are both roots of  $g(x) = x^3+3x^2-1=0$ .  But  $1/x_2 <1/x_1 < 0 < 1/x_3$  and  $-1-x_3 < -1-x_2 < -1-x_1$ , so we must have  $x_3+1/x_2= -1 = x_1+1/x_3$ .  Since  $f(z)=0$  implies  $z^2 = 3 + 1/z$ , we can substitute and rearrange to get the required equality.

stem_md: Does there exist a pair  $ (f; g)$  of strictly monotonic functions, both from  $ \mathbb{N}$  to  $ \mathbb{N}$ , such that \[ f(g(g(n))) < g(f(n))\] for every  $ n \in\mathbb{N}$ ?
solution_md:
Assume that such functions exist. Since the functions are increasing, by simple induction we get  $ f(n),g(n)\ge n$  for all  $ n\in\mathbb{N}$ . If  $ f(n)\equal{}n$  for some  $ n\in\mathbb{N}$ , subsituting to the given inequality, we get  $ g(g(n))<g(n)$ , contradicting the hypothesis that  $ g$  is increasing. Similarly, if  $ g(n)\equal{}n$  for some  $ n\in\mathbb{N}$ , we get  $ f(n)<f(n)$  which is impossible. Therefore  $ f(n),g(n)>n$ .

We now have  $ f(g(g(n)))<g(f(n))<f(g(f(n)))$ . We get  $ f(g(g(n)))<f(g(f(n)))$ , so  $ g(n)<f(n)$ . Now,  $ f(g(g(n)))<g(f(n))<f(f(n))$ , so  $ g(g(n))<f(n)$ . By induction, we get that  $ f(n)>g(g(...(n)...))$ . This is impossible because  $ g(n)<g(g(n))<...<g(g(...(n)...))$ . Therefore no such functions exist.

stem_md: Given is the convex quadrilateral  $ ABCD$ . Assume that there exists a point  $ P$  inside the quadrilateral for which the triangles  $ ABP$  and  $ CDP$  are both isosceles right triangles with the right angle at the common vertex  $ P$ . Prove that there exists a point  $ Q$  for which the triangles  $ BCQ$  and  $ ADQ$  are also isosceles right triangles with the right angle at the common vertex  $ Q$ .
solution_md:
Assuming  $ AB \parallel CD$   $ \Longrightarrow$  isosceles  $ \triangle ABP \sim \triangle CDP$  are centrally similar with center  $ P$   $ \Longrightarrow$   $ ABCD$  is isosceles trapezoid with diagonal intersection  $ P,$  with perpendicular diagonals  $ AC \perp BD,$  cyclic, and  $ Q$  is obviously its circumcenter. Assuming  $ BC \parallel DA$   $ \Longrightarrow$  isosceles  $ \triangle ABP \cong \triangle CDP$  are congruent  $ \Longrightarrow$   $ ABCD$  is isosceles trapezoid with circumcenter  $ P,$  with perpendicular diagonals  $ AC \perp BD$  and  $ Q$  is obviously its diagonal intersection. Hence, we can assume  $ AB, CD$  are not parallel and  $ BC, DA$  are also not parallel. Let  $ K, M$  be midpoints of  $ AB, CD.$  Let  $ X \equiv AB \cap CD,$  WLOG on the same side of  $ KM$  as  $ B, C.$  Quadrilateral  $ PKXM$  is cyclic on account of the right angles at  $ K, M$ ; let  $ (S)$  be its circumcircle.

Let  $ PB, PC$  cut  $ (S)$  again at  $ B', C'.$  By Pascal theorem for cyclic hexagon  $ PKB'XC'M,$  the intersections  $ B \equiv PB' \cap KX,$   $ C \equiv PC' \cap MX,$   $ L \equiv KC' \cap MB'$  are collinear  $ \Longrightarrow$   $ L \in BC.$  Then
 $ \angle KML \equal{} \angle KMB' \equal{} \angle KPB' \equal{} \angle KPB \equal{} 45^\circ$  $ \angle MKL \equal{} \angle MKC' \equal{} \angle MPC' \equal{} \angle MPC \equal{} 45^\circ$ 

Let  $ PA, PD$  cut  $ (S)$  again at  $ A', D'.$  By Pascal theorem for cyclic hexagon  $ PKD'XA'M,$  the intersections  $ A \equiv PA' \cap KX,$   $ D \equiv PD' \cap MX,$   $ N \equiv KD' \cap MA'$  are also collinear  $ \Longrightarrow$   $ N \in DA.$  Then
 $ \angle KMN \equal{} 180^\circ \minus{} \angle KMA' \equal{} 180^\circ \minus{} \angle KPA' \equal{} \angle KPA \equal{} 45^\circ$  $ \angle MKN \equal{} 180^\circ \minus{} \angle MKD' \equal{} 180^\circ \minus{} \angle MPD' \equal{} \angle MPD \equal{} 45^\circ$ 

Combining,  $ \triangle KLM \cong \triangle KNM$  are isosceles right and congruent  $ \Longrightarrow$   $ KLMN$  is a square. Assume that  $ L' \not\equiv L, N'\not\equiv N$  are midpoints of  $ BC, DA.$  Since  $ KLMN, KL'M'N'$  are both parallelograms  $ \Longrightarrow$   $ KL \equal{} MN, KL' \equal{} MN', \angle LKL' \equal{} \angle NMN'$   $ \Longrightarrow$   $ \triangle LKL' \cong \triangle NMN'$  are centrally congruent by s.a.s. and  $ (BC \equiv LL') \parallel (NN' \equiv DA),$  which is a contradiction. Therefore,  $ L, N$  are midpoints of  $ BC, DA$  and the square  $ KLMN$  is Varignon parallelogram of the quadrilateral  $ ABCD.$  Consequently,  $ ABCD$  has perpendicular diagonals  $ (AC \parallel KL) \perp (LM \parallel BD).$ 

The diagonal intersection  $ E \equiv AC \cap BD$  is the 2nd intersection of the circles  $ (K) \equiv \odot (ABP), (M) \equiv \odot (CDP).$  Let  $ Q$  be the 2nd intersection of the circles  $ (L) \equiv \odot(BCE), (N) \equiv \odot (DAE)$   $ \Longrightarrow$  the angles  $ \angle BQC, \angle DQA$  are right. Radical axis  $ EQ$  of  $ (L), (N)$  is perpendicular to their center line,  $ EQ \perp LN.$  Moreover,  $ (LN \parallel BD) \perp AC$  or  $ LN \perp (PC \equiv PA)$   $ \Longrightarrow$ 
 $ \angle QBC \equal{} \angle QEC \equal{} \angle MLN \equal{} 45^\circ$   $ \Longrightarrow$   $ \triangle BCQ$  is isosceles right. $ \angle QAD \equal{} \angle QED \equal{} \angle MNL \equal{} 45^\circ$   $ \Longrightarrow$   $ \triangle ADQ$  is isosceles right.

Let  $ C_1$  and  $ C_2$  be two congruent circles centered at  $ O_1$  and  $ O_2$ , which intersect at  $ A$  and  $ B$ . Take a point  $ P$  on the arc  $ AB$  of  $ C_2$  which is contained in  $ C_1$ .  $ AP$  meets  $ C_1$  at  $ C$ ,  $ CB$  meets  $ C_2$  at  $ D$  and the bisector of  $ \angle CAD$  intersects  $ C_1$  and  $ C_2$  at  $ E$  and  $ L$ , respectively. Let  $ F$  be the symmetric point of  $ D$  with respect to the midpoint of  $ PE$ . Prove that there exists a point  $ X$  satisfying  $ \angle XFL \equal{} \angle XDC \equal{} 30^\circ$  and  $ CX \equal{} O_1O_2$ .
*Author: Arnoldo Aguilar (El Salvador)*
solution_md:
let  $ \alpha=\angle PAB$  and  $ \theta=\frac{1}{2}\angle AO_1B$ ...

note that  $ ADC$  is isosceles, so  $ AL$  is perpendicular to  $ CD$ ... also note that  $ \angle EDC=\angle ECB=\angle EAB=90-\alpha-\theta$ , and since  $ \angle ABD=\alpha+\theta$  it follows that  $ DE$  is perpendicular to  $ AB$ , or  $ DE$  is parallel to  $ O{}_1O{}_2$ ... 
this implies that  $ DEO{}_1O{}_2$  is a parallelogram, therefore,  $ FPO{}_2{}_O{}_1$  is a parallelogram too, and this implies that  $ F$  lies in  $ C_1$ ... 

note that symmetry arguments imply that  $ \angle PFB=\angle PAB=\alpha$ , son this implies that  $ AC$  is perpendicular to  $ BF$ ...
since  $ \angle CAL+\angle ALB=(90-\theta)+\theta=90$  it follows that  $ AC$  is also perpendicular to  $ BL$ , which implies that  $ F,B,L$  are collinear...

note that  $ \angle PFB=\angle CFB=\alpha$  and  $ AC$  is perpendicular to  $ BF$ , therefore  $ FP=FC$ ... also since  $ AFL$  is isosceles we have that  $ FP=PL$ , so  $ FPLC$  is a kite (rhombus)... this implies that  $ CL=CF$ ... let  $ l$  be a line through  $ F$  such that  $ l$  and  $ FL$  form an angle of  $ 30$ , and let  $ X$  be another point on  $ l$  such that  $ CF=CX$ ... (in at least one of the two possible lines  $ l$   $ X$  and  $ F$  are different)... then,  $ C$  is the circumcenter of triangle  $ FLX$  and since  $ \angle XFL=30$  we have that  $ \angle XCL=60$ , which implies that  $ XLC$  is equilateral... we can prove that this point  $ X$  satisfies the other two conditions as well ( $ CL=CF=O{}_1O{}_2$  and the other one is similar), and we're done  :D

stem_md:
Given a positive integer  $ n\geq 2$ , consider a set of  $ n$  islands arranged in a circle. Between every two neigboring islands two bridges are built as shown in the figure.

Starting at the island  $ X_1$ , in how many ways one can one can cross the  $ 2n$  bridges so that no bridge is used more than once?

**Attachments:**

![islas.jpg](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/d/3/c95b4630a562fe2053ee9ecd74a01a1b9d98e7.jpg)
solution_md: I claim that there are $\boxed{n \cdot 2^{n + 1}}$ total sequences. Let $a_n$ be the number of distinct bridge sequences. Then we prove the following by induction:**Claim:** $a_n = n \cdot 2^{n + 1}$ , for $n \geq 3$ . *Proof:* The base case for $n = 3$ is trivial. Assume the statement is true for all $k \leq n$ , and now we prove for the $(n + 1)$ -st case: Consider player $X_{n + 1}$ , and observe that for every path consisting of $n$ people, we must pass through $X_{n + 1}$ and further every path through $X_{n + 1}$ has an additional two bridge options. (Also observe that the symmetry in whichever way we began with - clockwise or counterclockwise - is accounted for, as in this case every path is dependent on the paths from $a_n$ ). Now we have yet to count the fully clockwise and fully counterclockwise paths with $X_{n + 1}$ as an island, and so accounting for these final paths, one obtains; \[a_{n + 1} = 2a_n + 2(2^{n + 1}) = 2a_n + 2^{n + 2} = (n + 1) \cdot 2^{n + 2}, \] as claimed. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Consider the sequence  $ \{a_n\}_{n\geq1}$  defined as follows:  $ a_1 \equal{} 1$ ,  $ a_{2k} \equal{} 1 \plus{} a_k$  and  $ a_{2k \plus{} 1} \equal{} \frac {1}{a_{2k}}$  for every  $ k\geq 1$ . Prove that every positive rational number appears on the sequence  $ \{a_n\}$  exactly once.
solution_md:
Consider the sequence $ \{a_n\}_{n\geq1}$ defined as follows: $ a_1 \equal{} 1$ , $ a_{2k} \equal{} 1 \plus{} a_k$ and $ a_{2k \plus{} 1} \equal{} \frac {1}{a_{2k}}$ for every $ k\geq 1$ . Prove that every positive rational number appears on the sequence $ \{a_n\}$ exactly once.
It is easy to prove by induction that $a_{2^k}=k+1\cdots \cdots (1) $ . In the same we can prove that if $a_m=\frac{a}{b} \iff a_{2^k\cdot m}=k+\frac{a}{b}$ . For any $n \in \mathbb{N}$ we have $a_{2^{n-1}+1}=\frac{1}{n}$ . So If we can prove that we can construct $\frac{a+1}{b}$ from any fraction $\frac{a}{b}$ we are done. We consider 3 cases: 1. $b|a+1$ . In this case we can easily construct this from $(1)$ . 2. $ba+1$ In case 2 we can write $a+1=bq+r$ . So we have $\frac{a+1}{b}=q+\frac{r}{b}$ , which yields that it is enough to prove case 3. For case 3, if we have $a_m=\frac{r}{b}$ , we can say that $m$ is odd and $a_{m-1}=\frac{b}{r}$ . Now using the same argument (Euclidean Algorithm) of case 2, and of case 1; we can conclude that we shall get some $a_i=r_j$ , Now we prove the uniqueness of every term. If $a_i=a_j$ with $i>j$ . We can can infer from the previous argument that $(a_i,a_j) \to (a_p,a_q)$ for some $p,q$ with $p\not=q$ (because we need the same number of steps for this transformation), and $a_p=a_q=n \in \mathbb{N}$ . But from $(1)$ we get that $p=q$ , which is a contradiction.

stem_md: Six thousand points are marked on a circle, and they are colored using 10 colors in such a way that within every group of 100 consecutive points all the colors are used. Determine the least positive integer  $ k$  with the following property: In every coloring satisfying the condition above, it is possible to find a group of  $ k$  consecutive points in which all the colors are used.
solution_md:
The answer is 89.

Firstly, we will make some assumptions and conventions. A  $ L$ -arc is a set of  $ L$  consecutive points. The orientation is clockwise.

Suppose that, for some coloring, no 89-arc has all 10 colors. So we will prove these facts:

1 - For each 11-arc there is one color that doesn't appear among the 89 following points;
2 - Each 12-arc has just 2 colors.

If 1) is not valid for some 11-arc, then the 89 next points has all 10 colors (all 100-arc has all colors), contradiction!

For 2): split any 100-arc in eight 11-arcs ( $ A_1,A_2, \ldots,A_8$ ) and a 12-arc  $ A_9$ . Using 1), we know that for the arcs  $ A_i, i\equal{}1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8$  there is a color  $ i$  that doesn't appear at  $ A_{i\plus{}1},\ldots,A_9$ .  Clearly all colors  $ 1,2,\ldots,8$  are distinct, so there is just 2 colors at  $ A_9$ . 
This argument works for any 12-arc. So, that there is at most 2 color at any 12-arc. Now we need to prove that the "at most" is, in fact, "exactly".

If we get a monochromatic 12-arc, just see the 88-arc following it. The 100-arc obtained "glue-ing" them has 10 colors, so the last point of the 12-arc and all 88-arc form a 89-arc with all 10 colors, contradiction!

Let it  $ X_0$  a point with color 0, this color not appear at the 89-arc following it. The 11-arc following  $ X_0$  form the arc  $ A_1$ . The arc  $ X_0\plus{}A_1$  is a 12-arc, with 2 colors, namely 0 (the color of  $ X_0$ ) and 1. By the way,  $ X_0$  is the only point at this arc with the color 0. So the 11-arc  $ A_1$  has color 1. 
If  $ X_1$  is the latest point of  $ A_1$ , the 89-arc following doesn´t have the 1 color at it. Applying the same reasoning above, we can see a beautiful pattern: monochromatic 11-arcs alternating this colors. But hey!, 6000 is not a multiple of 11. It is impossible!

So, we always obtain a 89-arc with all 10 colors.

The problem now is to exhibit a colouring such that a 88-arc does not have the property. I will do it later(sloth...)

stem_md:
A line through a vertex of a non-degenerate triangle cuts it in two similar triangles with  $\sqrt{3}$  as the ratio between correspondent sides.
Find the angles of the given triangle.
solution_md: Let the line  $AD$  divide  $\triangle ABC$  into 2 parts with  $D$  on  $BC$ . If  $\angle ADB\neq \angle ADC$ , then WLOG let  $\angle ADC>90$ . If  $\angle ABD=\angle ADC$ , we get  $BA\parallel DA$ , which fails. Now if  $\angle BAD=\angle ADC$ , we get  $BA\parallel BC$  which also fails. Thus we must have  $\angle ADB=\angle ADC=90$ . Now if  $\angle ABD=\angle ACD$ , both triangles are congruent, a contradiction. Thus the only way is when  $\angle ABD=\angle DAC$ . Thus  $\frac{BD}{DA}=\frac{DA}{DC}=\sqrt3 \text{ or } \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ . Either way, we get the angles of  $\triangle ABC$  to be  $30,60,90$ .

stem_md:
Let  $x_1,\cdots, x_n$  be nonzero vectors of a vector space  $V$  and  $\varphi:V\to V$  be a linear transformation such that  $\varphi x_1 = x_1$ ,  $\varphi x_k = x_k - x_{k-1}$  for  $k = 2, 3,\ldots,n$ .
Prove that the vectors  $x_1,\ldots,x_n$  are linearly independent.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 IberoAmerican Olympiad For University Students/350191.json

candidates:
Assume the contrary, we may find  $m\ge 2$  such that  $x_1,...,x_{m-1}$  are linearly independent, but  $x_1,...,x_m$  linealy dependent. Then we can write  $x_m=a_1 x_1+\cdots+a_{m-1}x_{m-1}$ , the coeficients being uniquely determined. Applying  $\varphi$  to this equation, we have $x_m-x_{m-1}=a_1 x_1+a_2 (x_2-x_1)+\cdots+a_{m-1}(x_{m-1}-x_{m-2})
=*x_1+*x_2+\cdots+*x_{m-2}+a_{m-1}x_{m-1}$ , 
( $*$  are non-important coefficients)
or  $x_m=*x_1+*x_2+\cdots+*x_{m-2}+(a_{m-1}+1)x_{m-1}$ .
So the coefficient before  $x_{m-1}$  changed to  $a_{m-1}+1$ , which is impossible.

If W denotes the subspace of V generated by  $x_1, x_2, ..., x_n$ , then we can see that W is an invariant subspace for  $\varphi$ . We can thus consider the restriction  $\phi$  of  $\varphi$  to W,  $\phi: W \longrightarrow W$ . Now we can consider the matrix  $A \in M_n$  whose column  $j$  is made up of the coordinates of  $\phi(x_j)$  relative to  $\{x_1, x_2, ..., x_n \}$ . If these vectors were linearly dependent, then this matrix would be singular, since there would be at least one column which could be written as a linear combination of the other columns. But for this  $\phi$ , A is upper triangular with  $a_{ii} = 1$  (and  $a_{i, i+1} = -1$ ) for all i, and so A is non-singular: therefore, the vectors  $x_1, x_2, ..., x_n$  are linearly independent.

For  $n=1$ , it's trivial. Suppose the vectors  $x_1,\cdots,x_n$  are linearly independent. Let  $a_1,\cdots,a_{n+1}$  be scalars such that  $\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}a_kx_k=0$ .
Therefore  $0=\varphi(0)=\varphi\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}a_kx_k\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}a_k\varphi(x_k)=a_1x_1+\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}a_k(x_k-x_{k-1})=$  $=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}a_kx_k-\sum_{k=1}^na_{k+1}x_k=0$ , which means  $\sum_{k=1}^na_{k+1}x_k=0$ , and since the vectors  $x_1,\cdots,x_n$  are linearly independent and nonzero, we have  $a_k=0,\forall k\in\mathbb{Z}:2\le k\le n+1$ , which means  $a_1x_1=0$ , and since  $x_1$  is nonzero, we have  $a_1=0$ , therefore the vectors  $x_1,\cdots,x_{n+1}$  are linearly independent and, by induction, the statement is proven.

stem_md:
Let  $a, b, c, d, e \in \mathbb{R}^+$  and  $f:\{(x, y) \in (\mathbb{R}^+)^2|c-dx-ey > 0\}\to \mathbb{R}^+$  be given by  $f(x, y) = (ax)(by)(c- dx- ey)$ . 
Find the maximum value of  $f$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We have that  $f(x,y)=\frac{a}{d}\frac{b}{e}(dx)(ey)(c-dx-ey)\leq \frac{a}{d}\frac{b}{e}\left(\frac{c}{3}\right)^3$  by the AM-GM inequality.

Equality holds iff  $dx=ey=c-dx-ey\Leftrightarrow (x,y)=(\frac{c}{3d},\frac{c}{3e})$ . Since  $(\frac{c}{3d},\frac{c}{3e})\in \{(x, y)\in (\mathbb{R}^{+})^{2}|c-dx-ey > 0\}$ , equality holds.
We conclude that the maximum of  $f$  is  $ \frac{a}{d}\frac{b}{e}\left(\frac{c}{3}\right)^3$</details>

solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim that the answer is that there is a  $(n,m)$ -slippery function iff  $\gcd(m,n)=1$ .**For all such pairs there is such a function:**
If  $\gcd(m,n)=1$ , let  $f(x)=\frac{n}{m}x$ . Then  $f(t_2)-f(t_1)=\frac{n}{m}(t_2-t_1)$ , from where we conclude that  $m\mid n(t_2-t_1)\Rightarrow m\mid t_2-t_1$  (because  $\gcd(m,n)=1$ ). This implies  $t_2-t_1\in \{0,m\}$  because  $t_2\geq t_1$  and  $t_1,t_2\in[0,m]$ , as desired.**If  $\gcd(m,n)>1$  there is no such function:**
Suppose now that  $d=\gcd(m,n)>1$ . Let  $g(x)=f\left(x+\frac{m}{d}\right)-f(x)$ . Obviously  $g$  is also continuous.
We have that: $n=f(m)-f(0)=$  $=\left(f\left(\frac{m}{d}\right)-f(0)\right)+\left(f\left(\frac{2m}{d}\right)-f\left(\frac{m}{d}\right)\right)+\ldots+\left(f(m)-f\left(\frac{(d-1)m}{d}\right)\right)=$  $=g(0)+\ldots+g\left(\frac{(d-1)m}{d}\right)$ . 
If any of this summands is equal to  $\frac{n}{d}$  we are done, because  $\frac{n}{d}\in\mathbb{Z}$  and  $m>\frac{m}{d}=t_2-t_1\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ .
If there is no summand equal to  $\frac{n}{d}$ , then there is one summand that is greater that  $\frac{n}{d}$  and one that is smaller. But if  $g\left(i \frac{m}{d}\right)>\frac{n}{d}>g\left(j\frac{m}{d}\right)$  for some  $0\leq i\neq j\leq d-1$ , then by the Intermediate Value Theorem there exists an  $x$  such that  $f\left(x+\frac{m}{d}\right)-f(x)=g(x)=\frac{n}{d}$ . Putting  $t_2=x+\frac{m}{d}$ ,  $t_1=x$  we obtain the desired.</details>

stem_md:
Let  $\mathbb{N}$  and  $\mathbb{N}^*$  be the sets containing the natural numbers/positive integers respectively.

We define a binary relation on  $\mathbb{N}$  by  $a\acute{\in}b$  iff the  $a$ -th bit in the binary representation of  $b$  is  $1$ .

We define a binary relation on  $\mathbb{N}^*$  by  $a\tilde{\in}b$  iff  $b$  is a multiple of the  $a$ -th prime number  $p_a$ .

i) Prove that there is no bijection  $f:\mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}^*$  such that  $a\acute{\in}b\Leftrightarrow f(a)\tilde{\in}f(b)$ .
ii) Prove that there is a bijection  $g:\mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}^*$  such that  $(a\acute{\in}b \vee b\acute{\in}a)\Leftrightarrow (g(a)\tilde{\in}g(b) \vee g(b)\tilde{\in}g(a))$ .
solution_md:
Question i) seems me to be much more simple than question ii). Or, at least, my answer to question i) is much more simple than my answer to question ii).
<details><summary>Solution to question i)</summary>Suppose that you have a bijection  $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^\ast$  such that  $a\acute{\in}b\Leftrightarrow f(a)\tilde{\in}f(b)$ . Consider  $A = f(0)$ ,  $B = f^{-1}(p_A)$  and  $C = f^{-1}(p_A^2)$ . Since  $f$  is bijective and  $\{A\} = \{i \mid p_A \in p_i \mathbb{Z}\} =  \{i \mid p_A^2 \in p_i \mathbb{Z}\}$ , it follows that only  $1$  of the binary representation of  $B$  (resp.  $C$ ) is the  $0$ -bit, and therefore that  $B = 1 = C$ , which is absurd.</details>
<details><summary>Solution to question ii)</summary>We build inductively sets  $A_n \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ ,  $B_n \subseteq \mathbb{N}^\ast$  and integers  $a_n \in \mathbb{N}$ ,  $b_n \in \mathbb{N}^\ast$ ,  $c_n \in \mathbb{N}^\ast$  as follows:


<u>**At the step  $\#0$**</u>
we define  $A_0 = \{0\}$ ,  $B_0 = \{b_0\}$  and  $a_0 = 0$ ,  $b_0 = 1$ ,  $c_0 = 1 + \max A_0 + \max B_0$ .

<u>**At the step  $\#2n+1$**</u>
we define  $a_{2n+1} = \min(\mathbb{N} \backslash A_{2n})$ . Consider the set  $S_{2n+1} = \{i \leq 2n \mid a_i \acute{\in} a_{2n+1} \wedge a_{2n+1} \acute{\in} a_i\}$ . Then, we define  $b_{2n+1} = p_{c_{2n}} \prod_{i \in S_{2n+1}} p_{b_i}$ ,  $A_{2n+1} = A_{2n} \cup \{a_{2n+1}\}$ ,  $B_{2n+1} = B_{2n} \cup \{b_{2n+1}\}$  and  $c_{2n+1} = 1 + \max A_{2n+1} + \max B_{2n+1}$ .
Note that  $S_{2n+1} = \{i \leq 2n \mid b_i \acute{\in} b_{2n+1}\} = \{i \leq 2n \mid b_i \acute{\in} b_{2n+1} \wedge b_{2n+1} \acute{\in} b_i\}$  and that  $b_{2n+1} \geq p_{c_{2n}} > c_{2n} > \max B_{2n}$ .

<u>**At the step  $\#2n+2$**</u>
we define  $b_{2n+2} = \min(\mathbb{N}^\ast \backslash B_{2n+1})$ . Consider the set  $S_{2n+2} = \{i \leq 2n+1 \mid b_i \tilde{\in} b_{2n+2} \wedge b_{2n+2} \tilde{\in} b_i\}$ . Then, we define  $a_{2n+2} = \sum_{i \in S_{2n+2}} 2^{a_i} + 2^{c_{2n+1}}$ ,  $A_{2n+2} = A_{2n+1} \cup \{a_{2n+2}\}$ ,  $B_{2n+2} = B_{2n+1} \cup \{b_{2n+2}\}$  and  $c_{2n+2} = 1 + \max A_{2n+2} + \max B_{2n+2}$ .
Note that  $S_{2n+2} = \{i \leq 2n+1 \mid a_i \acute{\in} a_{2n+2}\} = \{i \leq 2n+1 \mid a_i \acute{\in} a_{2n+2} \wedge a_{2n+2} \acute{\in} a_i\}$  and that  $a_{2n+2} \geq 2^{c_{2n+1}} > c_{2n+1} > \max A_{2n+1}$ .


It follows that  $\bigcup A_n = \mathbb{N}$  and that  $\bigcup B_n = \mathbb{N}^\ast$ ; moreover, the  $a_i$ 's are pairwise different, and so are the  $b_i$ 's. Therefore, the function  $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^\ast$  the maps each  $a_i$  to  $b_i$  is bijective. In addition, for every pair  $i < j$ , we just built  $a_j$  and  $b_j$  so that  $(a_i\acute{\in}a_j \vee a_j\acute{\in}a_i)\Leftrightarrow (b_i\tilde{\in}b_j \vee b_j\tilde{\in}b_i)$ . Therefore, the bijection  $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^\ast$  satisfies  $(a\acute{\in}b \vee b\acute{\in}a)\Leftrightarrow (g(a)\tilde{\in}g(b) \vee g(b)\tilde{\in}g(a))$ , which closes the proof.</details>

stem_md:
Let  $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_e\in\mathbb{C}$  be such that the polynomials $f_1(x) =\prod_{i=1}^d(x-\alpha_i)$  and  $f_2(x) =\prod_{i=1}^e(x-\beta_i)$ have integer coefficients.

Suppose that there exist polynomials  $g_1, g_2 \in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  such that  $f_1g_1 +f_2g_2 = 1$ .

Prove that  $\left|\prod_{i=1}^d \prod_{j=1}^e (\alpha_i - \beta_j)      \right|=1$
solution_md:
Another solution. (Somehow the same.)
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>The polynomial  $f_1$  is monic, so it factors as the product of irreducible monic polynomials with integer coeficients. Let  $F(x)=\prod{(x-a_i)}$  be one of this irreducible factors, and let  $a$  be root of  $F$ . In the number field  $\mathbb{Q}(a)$ , the numbers  $a, b=f_2(a), g_2(a)$  are algebraic integers:  $a$ , because its minimal polynomial has integer coeficients; b and  $g_2(a)$ , because the algebraic integers in  $Q(a)$  form a ring. Moreover,  $b$  is unit of  $Q[a]$  since  $bg_2(a)=1$ , so its norm in  $Q(a)$  is  $N(b)=\pm 1$ . 

Apply division algorithm in  $Q(x)$  to obtain  $f_2(x)=q(x)F(x)+r(x)$ , note that  $r(a)$  is the only polynomial in  $a$ , with rational coeficients, degree less than  $\deg F$  and value  $b$ . So the field conjugates of  $b$  in  $Q(a)$  are the numbers  $f_2(a_i)=r(a_i)$ , and we have \[\pm 1=N(b)=\text{product of field conjugates}=\prod{f_2(a_i)}=\prod_{F(\alpha_i)=0}\prod_{j=1}^{e}{(\alpha_i-\beta_j)}\]

Now, if  $f_1=\prod{F_l^{k_l}}$  apply the previous result to each irreducible factor  $F_l$  and note that \[\prod_{i=1}^d\prod_{j=1}^e{(\alpha_i-\beta_j)}=\prod_{F_l}\left(\prod_{F_l(\alpha_i)=0}\prod_{j=1}^e(\alpha_i-\beta_j)\right)^{k_l}=\pm 1\]

Which implies what we wanted.</details>

stem_md: Prove for the sidelengths  $a,b,c$  of a triangle  $ABC$  the inequality  $\frac{a^3}{b+c-a}+\frac{b^3}{c+a-b}+\frac{c^3}{a+b-c}\ge a^2+b^2+c^2$
solution_md:
Prove for the sidelengths $a,b,c$ of a triangle $ABC$ the inequality $\frac{a^3}{b+c-a}+\frac{b^3}{c+a-b}+\frac{c^3}{a+b-c}\ge a^2+b^2+c^2$
**Tangent Line Method**: For $ 0 \leq x < \frac{3}{2}$ , we have: $$ \frac{x^3}{3-2x} - x^2 \geq 3(x-1) $$ WLOG, we can assume $a+b+c=3$ . Therefore, we get: $$ \sum_{cyc}\left(\frac{a^3}{b+c-a}-a^2\right)=\sum_{cyc}\left(\frac{a^3}{3-2a}-a^2\right) \geq 3\sum_{cyc}(a-1)=0 $$ The proof is complete.

stem_md:
Let  $m,n \in Z, m
e n, m 
e 0, n 
e 0$  . 
Find all  $f: Z 	o R$  such that   $f(mx+ny)=mf(x)+nf(y)$  for all   $x,y \in Z$  .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Answer</summary>If  $m + n\neq 1$ , the solutions are given by  $f(x) = Cx\; \forall x\in \mathbb{Z}$  for some constant  $C$ .
If  $m + n = 1$ , the solutions are given by  $f(x) = Cx + D\; \forall x\in \mathbb{Z}$  for some constant  $C$  and  $D$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $P(x, y)$  be the proposition  $f(mx + ny) = mf(x) + nf(y)$ . The left hand side of  $P(x+n, y)$  and  $P(x, y+m)$  are equal, so we can compare the right hand side to obtain:  $$  mf(x+n) + nf(y) = mf(x) + nf(y+m)  $$    $$  \frac{f(y + m) - f(y)}{m} = \frac{f(x + n) - f(x)}{n} \ldots (1) $$  In particular, there exists a fixed constant rational number  $C$  such that  $\frac{f(x+m) - f(x)}{m} = \frac{f(x+n) - f(x)}{n} = C$  for all  $x\in \mathbb{Z}$ .  <details><summary>(Here is the proof if this is confusing)</summary>Take  $C = \frac{f(m) - f(0)}{m} = \frac{f(n) - f(0)}{n}$  (valid by  $x = y = 0$  into  $(1)$ ). Then, plugging  $y = 0$  into  $(1)$  gives us  $\frac{f(x+n) - f(x)}{n} = C$  while plugging in  $x = 0$  gives us  $\frac{f(x+m) - f(x)}{m} = C$ .</details> As a result, by simple induction, for all  $k, m\in \mathbb{Z}$  we obtain  $f(x + km) = f(x) + Ckm$  and  $f(x+kn) = f(x) + Ckn$ . The original equation then becomes:  $$  C(mx + ny) + f(0) = mf(x) + nf(y)  $$    $$  m(f(x) - Cx) + n(f(y) - Cy) = f(0)  $$  for all  $x, y\in \mathbb{Z}$ . Now, let  $g(x) = f(x) - Cx$  for all  $x\in \mathbb{Z}$ . This equation now reads as  $mg(x) + ng(y) = g(0)$ . If  $m + n = 1$ , plugging in  $y = 0$  gives us  $mg(x) = (1 - n) g(0) = mg(0)$  and thus  $g(x) = g(0)$ , implying  $\boxed{f(x) = Cx + D\; \forall x\in \mathbb{Z}}$ , where  $D = g(0)$ . Otherwise, setting  $x = y = 0$  gives us  $g(0) = 0$  and plugging in  $y = 0$  gives  $g\equiv 0$ , so  $\boxed{f(x) = C\; \forall x\in \mathbb{Z}}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 IMAC Arhimede/1834058.json

candidates:
Straightforward, but very good for  $\mathbb{Z}$  FE introductions. 

To begin with,  $x=y=0$  gives  $(m + n - 1)f(0) = 0$ . Hence if  $m+n\neq 1$ , then  $f(0) = 0$ . But for if  $m+n=1$  we can note that if  $f(x)$  is a solution, then so if  $f(x) - c$  for any constant  $c$  - hence we may assume  $f(0) = 0$  as well and take it into account for the answer at the end.

Set  $y=0$  to get  $f(mx) = mf(x)$  for all  $x$  and  $x=0$  to get  $f(ny) = nf(y)$  for all  $y$ . But by replacing  $x$  and  $y$  with  $nx$  and  $my$  in the initial equation we get \[ mnf(x+y) = f(mn(x+y)) = f(mnx + nxy) = mf(nx) + nf(my) = mn(f(x) + f(y)) \]
and so (cancelling  $mn\neq 0$ ) yields  $f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)$  for any integers  $x,y$ . This is Cauchy's equation, so (by a well known two-sided induction) it follows that  $f(x) = f(1)x$  for all  $x\in \mathbb{Z}$ . 

Taking into account the argument for  $m+n=1$  in the first paragraph, we conclude that all solutions are  $f(x) = f(1)x$  if  $m+n\neq 1$  and  $f(x) = Ax + B$  for arbitrary integer constants  $A$  and  $B$  if  $m+n = 1$ .
