We will prove the claim with strong induction on  $n$ . The claim is trivial for  $n=1,2$ , and suppose it is also true for any number of positive integers less than  $n$ . For convenience, if a point is  $M$ , we call it "marked", and suppose that the  $\{a_i\}$  are sorted in increasing order.

Now, assume the contrary, namely that there exists a *bad* marking scheme  $S$  such that the grasshopper cannot land on  $s$ . For convenience, denote the set of positions achievable by the grasshopper if there were no marked integers as  $T$ . We can WLOG that  $S\subset T$ .**Claim:**There exist at most  $i$  numbers in  $S$  under  $a_n+a_{n-1}+\ldots +a_{n-i}$ . Furthermore, the grasshopper can reach any position in  $T\setminus S$  which is at most  $a_n+\ldots+a_{n-i}$ .**Proof:**We use induction on  $i$ . When  $i=0$ , suppose that  $S$  does contain an element  $<a_n$ . Then, if  $a_n\not\in S$ , the grasshopper hops to  $a_n$  and can complete its journey by induction. Hence, as  $S$  is bad,  $a_n\in S$ . Thus,  $S$  contains at least two elements  $\le a_n$ . Now, we consider the pairs  $(a_1,a_1+a_n), (a_2,a_2+a_n),\ldots (a_{n-1},a_{n-1}+a_n)$ . Note that these pairs are disjoint, and if there exists any pair  $(a_i,a_i+a_n)$  which has both elements unmarked, then the grasshopper can follow this route. Beyond  $a_i+a_n$ , there are at most  $n-3$  unmarked points, so the grasshopper can finish by induction.

Hence, every pair has a marked element. So, the pairs account for  $n-1$  marked elements and there is an additional one from  $a_n$ , and  $|S|>n-1\implies$  contradiction. So, our original assumption was wrong, and there exist no marked elements  $<a_n$ . Note that this immediately implies the second part of the claim for  $i=0$  as well. So, our base case is complete.

Now, we continue with the inductive step for our claim. We already have that there are at most  $i$  elements of  $S$  less than or equal to  $a_n+\ldots + a_{n-i+1}$ . Now, suppose the contrary, namely that there are  $>i$  marked elements less than  $v=a_n+\ldots+a_{n-i}$ . If  $v$  is unmarked, note that one of  $v-a_j$  for  $n-i\le j\le n$  must be unmarked since there are  $i+1$  of them and  $v-a_j\le a_n+\ldots +a_{n-i+1}$ . So, by inductive hypothesis, we can get to this  $v-a_j$ , and consequently get to  $v$ . Now, the grasshopper has jumped  $i+1$  times and there are at least  $i+1$  marked elements behind it. So, the grasshopper can finish by our overarching strong induction, violating the fact that  $S$  is bad. Hence,  $v$  is marked. 

Now, we can do exactly what we did in the base case. In particular, consider the pairs  $(v-a_j+a_k,v+a_k)$  for  $n-i\le j\le n$ ,  $1\le k\le n-i-1$ . By a similar argument to  $v$ , we have that  $v-a_j+a_k$  is always reachable if it is unmarked. So, if any of these   $(i+1)(n-i-1)$  pairs are unmarked, then the grasshopper can get to  $v+a_k$  in  $i+2$  jumps, and since there are at least  $i+2$  marked numbers behind it, it can get to the end by induction  $\implies$  contradiction. Suppose that, out of the all  $1\le k\le n-i-1$ , only those in set  $K$  have the property that  $v+a_k$  is marked. Then, we must have  $v-a_j+a_k$  is marked for all  $k\not\in K$ .

Clearly,  $K\neq [n-i-1]$ , or else there are at least  $n-i-1$  marked elements  $>v$  and at least  $i+1$  less than  $v$ , which totals to more than  $n$  marked elements. So, choose the minimal element  $k_0\not\in K$ . Now,  $a_k-a_j$  can achieve the values  $a_{k_0}-a_n, a_{k_0}-a_{n-1},\ldots, a_{k_0}-a_{n-i}$ , and  $a_{k'}-a_{n-i}$  for any  $k'\in [n-i-1]\setminus\left( K\cup\{k_0\}\right)$ . These  $n-1-|K|$  values are all distinct, so in total we have at least  $n-1-|K|+|K|+1=n$  marked elements (where the  $+1$  comes from  $v$ ), which is once again a contradiction. Hence, the first claim is proven.

For the second part, suppose the contrary. Namely, assume there exists a first unmarked element,  $e$  in  $T\setminus S$  between  $a_n+\ldots +a_{n-i+1}+1$  and  $a_n+\ldots a_{n-i}$  inclusive which can be expressed as  $e=\sum_{j\in A} a_j$  for some set  $A$  but is unreachable. As ourlower bound represents one more than the maximum element of  $T$  expressible as the sum of  $i$  jumps, we have  $|A|> i$ . If  $e$  is unreachable, then that means  $e-a_j$  is not either for any  $j\in A$ . This value is unique for distinct  $j$ , and it corresponds to a marked value by inductive hypothesis and minimality, since we assumed all previous nonmarked squares were reachable. However, this means there exists  $|A|>i$  marked squares less than  $a_n+\ldots +a_{n-i}$  and we showed that there were at most  $i$ , so contradiction. Hence,  $e$  does not exist and the second part of the induction is complete.

With our claim, we have that the largest marked number should be at least  $a_n+\ldots +a_2$ , or at most  $a_1$  away from  $s$ . At the same time, our logic holds backwards, so the largest marked number should be at least  $a_n$  away from  $s$ . As  $a_1<a_n$ , we have a contradiction, and hence  $S$  does not exist, as desired.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Refer to the points in  $M$  as stones. We use strong induction on  $n$ . The base case  $n  =1$  is obvious since there are no stones, and  $n = 2$  follows from not having a stone at both  $a_1$  and  $a_2$ . Assume it is true for all  $m < n$ . (Also, the inductive hypothesis can be used as  $m$  jumps and at most  $m - 1$  stones, since deleting stones only makes our task easier.)

Call the jump lengths  $a_1 > a_2 > \ldots > a_n$  with sum  $S$ , and suppose stones are at  $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1}$  in order from left to right. 

We will show that we can jump over at least  $k$  stones in  $k$  turns (from the front), which would mean we are done by the induction hypothesis. **Claim:** There is some  $k < n$  for which  $a_1 + a_2 + \ldots + a_k > s_k$ , or we can reverse the number line and then there will exist such a  $k$ . 

*Proof:* Note that for each  $k$ , either  $k$  works from the left or  $n - k$  works from the right -- otherwise, we would have  $a_1 + \ldots + a_k \leq s_k$  and  $a_1 + \ldots + a_{n - k} \leq S - s_k$  (since  $s_k$  is the  $(n - k)$ th stone from the right end). But then  $S \geq a_1 + \ldots + a_k + (a_1 + \ldots + a_{n - k}) >( a_1 + \ldots + a_k) + (a_{k + 1} + \ldots + a_n)$ , contradiction. 

Now flip if necessary, so that there exists  $k$  from the front. Take the minimal  $k$ , and let  $x = a_1 + \ldots + a_k$ . 

First suppose  $k = 1$ . If jumping by  $a_1$  doesn't land on a stone, then we can just do it. So suppose that jumping  $a_1$  lands on a stone  $s_r$ . Then we can jump  $a_i, a_1$  in that order for each  $i \geq 2$  -- this crosses at least  $s_1$  and  $s_r$ . If all of these fail, then for each  $i \geq 2$ , we have a stone at  $a_i$  or  $a_1 + a_i$ . This gives us  $n - 1$  stones, and all of these are distinct and not equal to  $s_r = a_1$  (because  $a_1 + a_i > a_j$ ). So then if all of them failed, we would have at least  $n$  stones, contradiction. So one of them must work, and then we can jump over at least  $2$  stones with  $2$  jumps. 

So now we assume  $k \geq 2$ . **Claim:** If  $x$  doesn't have a stone, then we can take jumps of lengths  $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$  from the start and jump over at least  $k$  stones. 

*Proof:* This must jump over at least  $k$  stones ( $s_1, \ldots, s_k$ ), so it suffices to show that we can order them in a way that doesn't land on any stones in between. We perform jumps from  $x$  to  $0$ . 

First we jump backwards by  $a_i$  for some  $1 \leq i < k$ . No new blocked stops can appear since all changed stops are smaller than  $m$ . Finally, if in the current path after the  $a_n$  jump we have the  $a_i$  jump, swap them to get a path without any blocked numbers.

Induct. Assume  $a_k$  is strictly increasing. Call each element of  $M$  a mine. Let  $x=s-a_n$ . Consider four cases based on whether  $x$  has a mine and whether there is a mine past  $x$ .



- $x$  has no mine, there is a mine past  $x$ . By induction hypothesis, we can jump to  $x$ , then jump from  $x$  to  $s$ .
- $x$  has no mine, no mine past  $x$ . Let  $x$  be the biggest mine. By induction on  $M$  excluding  $m$ , there is a path to  $x$  which avoids mines other than maybe  $m$ . If it hits  $m$  on the hop of length  $a_k$ , swap it with the hop of length  $a_n$  and finish.
- $x$  is a mine, no mine past  $x$ . Do case 2 with  $m=x$ .
- $x$  is a mine, there is a mine past  $x$ . There exists an  $1 \le i \le n-1$  such that  $s-a_i$  and  $y=s-a_i-a_n$  are both mineless. By induction, jump to  $y$  in  $n-2$  stops, then  $y \rightarrow s-a_i \rightarrow s$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ ABC$  be a triangle with  $ AB \equal{} AC$  . The angle bisectors of  $ \angle C AB$  and  $ \angle AB C$  meet the sides  $ B C$  and  $ C A$  at  $ D$  and  $ E$  , respectively. Let  $ K$  be the incentre of triangle  $ ADC$ . Suppose that  $ \angle B E K \equal{} 45^\circ$  . Find all possible values of  $ \angle C AB$  .

*Jan Vonk, Belgium, Peter Vandendriessche, Belgium and Hojoo Lee, Korea*
solution_md:
I bashed this on paper so I'll just post the highlights here (I know that this wouldn't be a valid writeup but I'm not going to type up the same bash I did by hand). Swap the names of points  $B$  and  $D$ .

Note that  $\angle ABK=45^{\circ}$  so quadrilateral  $DBKE$  is cyclic. We employ barycentric coordinates wrt  $ABC$ . $D=(0,2,-1)$ ,  $E=(2a:0:b)$ ,  $K=(a:b:c)$ ,  $B=(0,1,0)$ . The circle has equation  $-a^2yz-b^2xz-c^2xy+(ux+vy+wz)(x+y+z)=0$ . Plug in  $B$  to get  $v=0$ , plug in  $D$  to get  $w=2a^2$ , plug in  $E$  to get
\[u=\frac{b^3-2a^2b-ab^2}{2a+b}.\]
Plug in  $K$ , immediately we can cancel out a factor of  $a+b+c$ . Eventually we get
\[(c-a)(c^2+2ac-a^2)=b(c-a)(c+a).\]
So  $c=a$  or we can square both sides and cancel stuff out to get  $a=\sqrt3 c$ , so the answers are  $\boxed{60^{\circ},90^{\circ}}$ . These both work because the steps are reversible to show that  $K$  lies on  $(BDE)$ , which implies the angle condition.  $\blacksquare$

Let  $ K,H$  be the incenter of triangle  $ ADC, ABC.AK\cap HE = O$ . Put  $ AB = AC = x, BC = y$  $ \angle AKH = \angle HEK = 45^o$  then  $ HK^2 = HO.HE$ 
But  ${ \frac {HO}{HE} = \frac {AH}{AH + AE}, \frac {HK^2}{HC^2} = \frac {HD^2}(HD + DC)^2}$ 
We get  $ \frac {HC^2.HD^2}{(HD + DC)^2} = \frac {HE^2.AH}{AH + AE}$  $ \Rightarrow \frac {HD^2}{(HD + DC)^2} = \frac {HE^2}{HC^2}.\frac {AH}{AH + AE} = \frac {AE^2}{AB^2}.\frac {AH}{AH + AE}$  $ \Rightarrow \frac {HD}{(HD + DC)^2} = \frac {AE^2}{AB^2}.\frac {AH}{HD(AH + AE)}$  $ \Rightarrow \frac {HD}{(HD + DC)^2} = \frac {AE^2}{AB^2}.\frac {AB}{BD(AH + AE)} = \frac {AE^2}{AB.BD.(AH + AE)}$  $ \Rightarrow AE^2.(HD + DC)^2 = HD.AB.BD.(AH + AE)$  $ \Rightarrow \frac {x^4}{(x + y)^2}.(\frac {1/2y.AD}{1/2y + x} + 1/2y)^2 = \frac {1/2y.AD}{1/2y + x}.x.1/2y.(\frac {x.AD}{1/2y + x} + \frac {x^2}{x + y})$  $ \Rightarrow \frac {x^2}{(x + y)^2}.(\frac {1/2AD}{1/2y + x} + 1/2)^2 = \frac {1/2AD}{1/2y + x}.1/2.(\frac {AD}{1/2y + x} + \frac {x}{x + y})$ 
Then set  $ x = ky$  and note that  $ AD = \sqrt {k^2 -1/4}y$  we can easy find  $ k$ . $ \Rightarrow \angle A = 60^o$  or  $ 90^o$ .

Let  $ D$  be the midpoint of  $ BC$ ;  $ I$  be the incenter  of  $ \triangle ABC$ .  $ DK$  meets  $ AC$  at
point  $ T$ .Let  $ AB=AC=a$ ; $ BC=2$ . It means  $ CD=DB=1$ 
Firstly, triangle  $ IEK$  and triangle  $ CDT$  are similar (since  $ \angle IED=\angle EDC = 45^o$ ). Thus  $ \frac{IE}{IK}=\frac{CD}{CT}$ .
We have: $ \frac{IK}{ID}=\frac{IC}{ID+1} \rightarrow \frac{1}{IK}=\frac{ID+1}{ID.IC}$  $ \frac{IE}{EC}=\frac{IB}{2}\rightarrow IE=\frac{EC.IC}{2}$  (notice that  $ IB=IC)$ .
Thus  $ \frac{IE}{IK}=(1+\frac{1}{ID})\frac{EC}{2}$ 
In triangle  $ ABC$  :  $ \frac{EC}{BC}=\frac{EC}{2}=\frac{AC}{AB+BC}=\frac{a}{a+2}$ .
But  $ \frac{ID}{DC}=\frac{AD}{AC+DC}=\frac{AD}{a+1}$ 
Hence  $ \frac{IE}{IK}=\frac{(AD+a+1)a}{AD(a+2)}$ .
On other hand;  $ \frac{CD}{CT}=\frac{AD}{AT}=\frac{1+AD}{a}$ .
It implies 
\[ \frac{(AD+a+1)a}{AD(a+2}=\frac{1+AD}{a}\]
\[ \leftrightarrow AD.a^2+a^3+a^2=a.AD+a.AD^2+2.AD+2.AD^2\]
\[ \leftrightarrow AD.a^2=a.AD-a+2AD+a^2-2\]
(since  $ AD^2=a^2-1$ )
\[ \leftrightarrow 
AD(a^2-a-2)=a^2-a-2\]
Thus either  $ AD=1$  or  $ a^2-a-2=0$ . $ AD=1$  implies  $ \angle A =90^o$  $ a^2-a-2=0$  implies  $ a=2$  thus  $ A=60 ^o$ .
We have done!.

Simple solution by trigonometry calculation :)

Let  $ \alpha = \measuredangle DAC$ , and consider triangle  $ %Error. "traingel" is a bad command.
EJC$ , where  $ J$  is the incenter of  $ \triangle ACD$ .
According to the assumption, this triangle has angles  $ \frac{3\alpha}{2}, 45^\circ - \frac{\alpha}{2}, 135^\circ - \alpha$ .
From Sine law in  $ \triangle BEC$ , we have
\[ \frac{EC}{\sin 45^\circ - \alpha/2} = \frac{2R \sin 2 \alpha}{\sin {45^\circ - 3\alpha/2}}.\]
From Sine law in  $ \triangle AJC$ , we have
\[ \frac{JC}{\alpha/2} = \frac{2R \sin {90^\circ - \alpha}}{\sin 135^\circ}.\]

Finally, in triangle  $ \triangle EJC$ , we have
\[ \frac{EC}{\sin{135^{\circ} - \alpha}} = \frac{JC}{\sin {3 \alpha / 2}}.\]

After simplification, we have following identity
\[ \frac{\sin {45^\circ + \alpha}}{\sin \alpha} \cdot \frac{\sin {45^\circ + 3\alpha/2}}{\sin {3 \alpha/2}} = 
\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{\sin {45^\circ - \alpha/2}}{\sin {\alpha/2}}.\]

Now, set  $ x = \cot \frac{\alpha}{2}$  and using formulas for double and triple angle, it follows
\[ \left(\frac{x^2-1}{2x}+1\right)\left(\frac{3x-x^3}{1-3x^2}+1\right)=2(x-1).\]

This equation is equivalent to  $ (x-1) (x^2-4x+1) (x^2-2x-1)=0$ .
It follows that  $ \cot 2x = \ctg \alpha = \sqrt{3}$  or  $ \cot 2x = \ctg \alpha = 1$ . This brings us to  $ \alpha = 45^\circ$  or  $ \alpha = 30^\circ$ , and finally  $ \measuredangle CAB = 90^\circ$  or  $ \measuredangle CAB = 60^\circ$ .

My trigonometric solution:

Note  $ \angle BCI \equal{} \mathbb\alpha$ 
So  $ \angle CIE \equal{} 2\mathbb\alpha$  and  $ \angle DIK \equal{} 90 \minus{} \mathbb\alpha$ 

By sine law in triangle  $ EIK$ , we have:  $ \frac {IK}{\sin 45} \equal{} \frac {EK}{\sin (2\mathbb\alpha)}$ 

By sine law in triangle  $ DIK$ , we have:  $ \frac {IK}{\sin 45} \equal{} \frac {DK}{\cos\mathbb\alpha}$ 

So  $ \frac {EK}{DK} \equal{} 2\sin\mathbb\alpha$           $ (1)$ 
 $ \angle KEA \equal{} 3\mathbb\alpha \plus{} 45$ . So  $ \sin\angle KEC \equal{} \sin\angle KEA \equal{} \sin(3\mathbb\alpha \plus{} 45) \equal{} \sin45(\sin(3\mathbb\alpha) \plus{} \cos(3\mathbb\alpha))$ 

Sine law in triangle  $ CEK$  implies  $ \frac {EK}{\sin\mathbb\alpha} \equal{} \frac {KC}{\sin45(\sin(3\mathbb\alpha) \plus{} \cos(3\mathbb\alpha))}$ 

By sine law in triangle  $ CKD$ , we have:  $ \frac {DK}{\sin\mathbb\alpha} \equal{} \frac {KC}{\sin 45}$ 

So  $ KC \equal{} \frac {EK \sin45(\sin(3\mathbb\alpha) \plus{} \cos(3\mathbb\alpha))}{\sin\mathbb\alpha} \equal{} \frac {DK\sin 45}{\sin\mathbb\alpha}.$ 

So  $ \frac {DK}{EK} \equal{} \sin(3\mathbb\alpha) \plus{} \cos(3\mathbb\alpha)$ 

Multiplying this with  $ (1)$ , we get:
 $ 1 \equal{} 2\sin\mathbb\alpha(sin(3\mathbb\alpha) \plus{} cos(3\mathbb\alpha))$ 

Transforming product to sum we get:
 $ 1 \equal{} \cos(2\mathbb\alpha) \minus{} \cos(4\mathbb\alpha) \minus{} \sin(2\mathbb\alpha) \plus{} \sin(4\mathbb\alpha)$  
 $ 1 \equal{} \cos(2\mathbb\alpha) \minus{} 2\cos ^2(2\mathbb\alpha) \plus{} 1 \minus{} \sin(2\mathbb\alpha) \plus{} 2\sin(2\mathbb\alpha)\cos(2\mathbb\alpha)$ 

Factorizing the equation we get:
 $ (2\cos(2\mathbb\alpha) \minus{} 1)(\sin(2\mathbb\alpha) \minus{} \cos(2\mathbb\alpha)) \equal{} 0$ 

So  $ \angle BAC \equal{} 60$  or  $ 90$

stem_md:
Determine all functions  $ f$  from the set of positive integers to the set of positive integers such that, for all positive integers  $ a$  and  $ b$ , there exists a non-degenerate triangle with sides of lengths
\[ a, f(b) \text{ and } f(b \plus{} f(a) \minus{} 1).\]
(A triangle is non-degenerate if its vertices are not collinear.)

*Proposed by Bruno Le Floch, France*
solution_md:
The answer is $\boxed{f \equiv x},$ which clearly works, as we obtain a triangle of side lengths $a, b, a+b-1.$ **Claim:** $f$ is unbounded.
ProofAssume for the sake of contradiction that $f$ is bounded above by some $C.$ Take an $a \ge 2C.$ By the Triangle Inequality, we obtain that $a < f(b) + f(b+f(a)-1) \le 2C,$ a contradiction. $\square$
So, clearly, $f$ attains infinitely many values. **Claim:** $f(1) = 1.$
ProofAssume for the sake of contradiction that $f(1) \neq 1.$ Then, taking $a = 1,$ we get that $|f(b+f(1)-1)-f(b)| < 1$ by Triangle Inequality, so $f(b+f(1)-1) = f(b).$ We assumed that $f(1) > 1,$ so $f$ cycles, and thus obtains finitely many values, a contradiction. This implies $f(1) = 1,$ as desired. $\square$
Next, we will use this to figure out a bunch of stuff about $f.$ **Claim:** $f(f(a))=a,$ and $f$ is bijective.
ProofBy plugging in $b = 1,$ we obtain that $1, a, f(f(a))$ forms a triangle, so $|f(f(a))-a| < 1,$ or $f(f(a)) = a.$ Clearly this implies that $f$ is surjective. Now assume that $f(a) = f(b).$ We get that $a = f(f(a)) = f(f(b)) = b,$ so $f$ is indeed bijective. $\square$
Now, by plugging in $f(b)$ instead of $b$ (we can do this since $f$ is bijective), we get that $a, b, f(f(a)+f(b)-1)$ form a triangle, or $f(f(a)+f(b)-1) \le a+b-1.$ **Claim:** $f(3) = 2f(2)-1.$
ProofPlug in $a = 2$ and $b=2$ into the equation above (we will call the assertion above $Q(a,b);$ i.e. $Q$ denotes $f(f(a)+f(b)-1) \le a+b-1$ ). We get $4 > f(2f(2)-1),$ so $f(2f(2)-1) = 1, 2, 3.$ Thus, $2f(2)-1 = f(1), f(2), f(3).$ The first two give $f(2) = 1,$ which is impossible, so $f(3) = 2f(2)-1,$ as desired. $\square$
**Claim:** $f(n) = (n-1)f(2)-(n-2).$
ProofWe use induction on $n$ ; the base cases $n = 1, 2, 3$ we already did. Now assume that $f(k) = (k-1)f(2)-(k-2)$ for all $k \le n$ . By $Q(n,2),$ we get that $f(f(2)+f(n)-1) \le n+1.$ If $f(f(2)+f(n)-1) \le n,$ then $f(2)+f(n)-1 = f(k),$ for some $k \le n$ , and by the inductive hypothesis, $f(k) \le f(n),$ while $f(2)+f(n)-1 > f(n).$ So, $f(2)+f(n)-1 = f(n+1),$ completing the induction. $\square$
Now, if $f(2) \ge 3,$ then $f(n) \equiv 1 \pmod f(2),$ so $f$ cannot be surjective. Thus, $f(2)=2$ ( $f(2) \neq 1$ by injectivity), so $f(n) = n,$ as desired.

Determine all functions $ f$ from the set of positive integers to the set of positive integers such that, for all positive integers $ a$ and $ b$ , there exists a non-degenerate triangle with sides of lengths \[ a, f(b) \text{ and } f(b \plus{} f(a) \minus{} 1).\] (A triangle is non-degenerate if its vertices are not collinear.) *Proposed by Bruno Le Floch, France*
It's easy to see that $f(n)=n$ is indeed such a function. We will prove that it's the only such function. Let $P(a,b)$ denote the assertion that $a,f(b),f(b+f(a))-1)$ are side lengths of a non-degenerate triangle. $P(1,1)\implies f(1)=f(f(1))$ . Let $f(1)=c\implies f(c)=c$ . $$ P(1,c)\implies f(2c-1)=c $$ $$ P(1,2c-1)\implies f(3c-2)=c $$ $$ \vdots $$ Thus we can create an infinite sequence(if $c\ge 2$ ) of integers $\{a_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ such that $f(a_n)=c$ . $$ P(a_n,b)\implies a_n+f(b)>f(+f(a_n)-1) $$ Keeping $b$ fixed we can choose $a_n$ to be arbitrarily large. The inequality obviously fails for large enough value of $n$ forcing $f(1)=1$ . Now $P(a,1)\implies f(f(a))=a\qquad (1)$ . Let $f(2)=n$ . By $(1)$ we have $f(n)=2$ . $(1)$ also implies $f$ is bijective. $$ P(2,n)\implies 2+f(n)\ge f(n+f(2)-1)\implies 3\ge f(2n-1) $$ Because $f$ is bijective we must have $f(2n-1)=3\implies f(3)=2n-1$ by $(1)$ . $$ P(3,n)\implies 3+f(n)>f(n+f(3)-1)\implies 4\ge f(3n-2)\implies f(3n-2)=4 $$ because $f$ is bijective. We can inductively prove that $f(kn-k+1)=k+1$ . Unless $n=2$ , the sequence $\{kn-k+1\}_{k\ge 1}$ is going to skip infinitely many values and because $f$ is bijective we can't assign any value to these skipped values. Hence $n=2$ and $f(k+1)=k+1$ for all $k$ . Thus the only function such is $f(n)=n$ .

Let  $P(a,b)$  be the given functional inequality. We'll write  $T(x,y,z)$  if  $x,y,z$  are the sides of a non-degenerate triangle. Note that \[P(1,b)\implies f(b)=f(b+f(1)-1).\] Let  $k=f(1)-1$ , so we have  $f(b)=f(b+k)$ . Now, \[P(1+nk,b)\implies T(1+nk,f(b),f(b+k))\implies T(1+nk,f(b),f(b)).\] Making  $n$  very large gives a contradiction if  $k\ge 1$ , so we have  $k=0$ , and thus  $f(1)=1$ . Now, \[P(a,1)\implies a=f(f(a)),\] so in particular,  $f$  is injective and surjective. Call  $Q(a,b)$  the modified functional inequality \[T(a,b,f(f(a)+f(b)-1)),\] which is true by  $P(a,f(b))$ .

Note that \[Q(a,2)\implies T(2,a,f(f(a)+\ell)),\] where  $\ell:=f(2)-1$ . Thus, \[f(f(a)+\ell)\in\{a-1,a,a+1\}.\] We can't have  $f(f(a)+\ell)=a$ , as that would imply  $f(a)+\ell=f(a)$ , or  $\ell=0$ , or  $f(2)=1=f(1)$ . Thus,  $f(f(a)+\ell)\in\{a-1,a+1\}$ , so \[f(a)+\ell\in\{f(a-1),f(a+1)\}.\] We are now able to solve the problem by induction.**Claim:**  We have  $f(x)=1+\ell(x-1)$ .

*Proof:*  The proof is induction  $x$ , with the  $x=1$  case trivially holding, and the  $n=2$  case holding by definition of  $\ell$ . Now, suppose we know the claim is true for numbers  $x=1,\ldots,n$  where  $n\ge 2$ , and we wish to show that  $f(n+1)=1+\ell n$ . Note that we have \[f(n)+\ell\in\{f(n-1),f(n+1)\},\] so \[1+\ell n\in\{1+\ell(n-2),f(n+1)\}.\] Thus,  $f(n+1)=1+\ell n$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$ The claim combined with  $f(f(x))=x$  easily implies that  $\boxed{f(x)=x}$ , which can be checked to work.

Call a triple  $[x,y,z]$  good if they are the sides of a triangle. Let  $A(a,b)$  be the assertion that  $[a,f(b),f(b+f(a)-1)]$  is good.  $A(1,b)$  gives  $[1,f(b),f(b+f(1)-1)]$  is good, which means  $f(b)=f(b+f(1)-1)$ . Hence  $f$  is periodic with period  $f(1)-1$ . But  $A(a,1)$  gives  $[a,f(1),f(f(a))]$  is good. Since  $f$  is periodic, it is bounded above, and hence taking arbitrarily large  $a$  gives a contradiction. Hence  $f(1)-1=0$ , i.e.  $f(1)=1$ . So  $a,1,f(f(a))$  is good, which means  $f(f(a))=a$ . So  $f$  is an involution; in particular it is bijective. 

Let  $c=f(2)-1$ . We claim that  $f(a)=1+(a-1)c$ . We induct on  $a$ , the base case  $a=2$  trivial. Note  $A(a,f(2))$  gives  $[a,2,f(f(a)+c)]$  is good. Hence there are 3 possibilities for each  $a$ :


- Case 1:  $a=f(f(a)+c)$ . Since  $f$  is an involution,  $f(a)=f(a)+c$ , which implies  $f(2)=1$ . But  $f(1)=1$ , contradicting injectivity.
- Case 2:  $a-1 = f(f(a)+c)$ . Since  $f$  is an involution,  $f(a-1) = f(a)+c$ . By induction,  $f(a-1)=1+(a-2)c$ . So  $f(a)=1+(a-3)c$ . But by induction,  $f(a-2) = 1+(a-3)c$ , contradicting injectivity.
- Case 3:  $a+1 = f(f(a)+c)$ . This is the only possibility left. Again, since  $f$  is an involution,  $f(a+1) = f(a)+c = 1+ac$  by induction.

This completes the induction. So  $f(a)=1+(a-1)c$  for some constant  $c$ . Since  $f$  is an involution,  $a=f(1+(a-1)c) = 1+(a-1)c^2$ , so  $c=1$ . Hence  $f(a)=a$ . It is easy to see that this works.

Let $P(a,b)$ denote the assertion that there exists a non-degenerate triangle with sides of lengths $$ a, f(b), f(b+f(a)-1). $$ **Claim:** $f(1)=1.$ *Proof.* Assume for the sake of contradiction that $f(1)>1.$ Observe then that $P(1,n)$ implies that $$ 1+f(n)>f(n+c), $$ where $c=f(1)-1>0.$ Thus, $f(n+c)\leq f(n),$ implying that $f$ is non increasing. Moreover, for any $n\in\mathbb{N}, f(1)\ge f(n).$ However, note that $P(2f(1)+1, n)$ gives that $$ 2f(1) + 1 < f(n) + f(n+c), $$ yet $f(1)\ge f(n), f(n+c).$ Contradiction. Hence, we conclude $f(1)=1,$ as desired. $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** $f$ is bijective. *Proof.* From claim 1, $f(1)=1,$ so $P(n, 1)$ gives the two inequalities by triangle inequality: - $n+1 > f(f(n))$ - $f(f(n)) > n-1.$ Hence, these two inequalities imply $n+1 > f(f(n)) > n-1,$ giving $f(f(n))=n$ . It is well known that if $f$ is an involution, then it is a bijection. $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** $f(n)$ is increasing. *Proof.* Let $c=f(2)-1 > 0$ (since $f$ is bijective). Observe that $P(2,f(n))$ asserts that $$ n+2 > f(f(n)+c) > n-2. $$ Note that since $f$ is bijective, then $f(f(n)+c)$ is either equal to $n+1$ or $n-1.$ Or, since $f$ is an involution, $$ f(f(f(n)))=f(n)+c = f(n+1) \quad\quad \text{or}\quad\quad f(n)+c = f(n-1). $$ However, also note that $$ f(1)+c=f(2), $$ so since $f$ is injective, $$ f(3)+c=f(4), $$ and by induction, it is clear that if $f(2k+1)+c=f(2(k+1))$ for $k\in\mathbb{N},$ then $f(2(k+1)+1)+c = f(2(k+2)).$ Similarly, since $f(2)\neq f(1),$ then $$ f(2)+c=f(3), $$ and since $f$ is injective, $$ f(4)+c=f(5), $$ and it can also be easily shown by induction that if $f(2k)+c=f(2k+1)$ for $k\in\mathbb{N},$ then $f(2(k+1))+c=f(2(k+1)+1).$ Hence, we conclude that for all $n$ , $f$ is an increasing arithmetic progression with positive difference $c.$ $\blacksquare$ However, since $f$ is surjective, then $c=1,$ so $f(n)=f(1)+n-1=n,$ giving the sole solution $f(x)=x$ as desired. $\square$

Let  $P(a,b)$  denote the functional assertion. The only solution is  $f(a) \equiv a$  for all  $a \in \mathbb{N}$ . This obviously works. Now we show that this is the only solution.
-----**Claim 1.**  $f(1) = 1$ . 
*Proof.* Note that if a triangle has integer side lengths  $1,a,b$  then  $a = b$ . Hence  $(1,a)$  implies that  $f(b) = f(b + f(a) - 1)$ . Suppose that  $f(1) > 1$  and write  $k = f(1)  - 1$ . By induction  $f(1 + kn) = f(1) = k+1$  for all non-negative integers  $n$ . Taking  $P(3k+1, k+1)$  gives that  
\[ k+1, k+1, 3k+1 \text{ are the side lengths of a triangle } \]
which is evidently not possible. Hence  $f(1) = 1$ . 
------**Claim 2.**  $f(f(a)) = a$  for all positive integers  $a$ . As an immediate corollary,  $f$  is bijective.
*Proof.*  This is immediate from  $P(a,1)$  since  $1,a,$  and  $f(f(a)$  are the side lenghts of a triangle. Then since  $f \circ f$  is bijective,  $f$  must also be bijective. (This fact is well-known, but the basic sketch is to prove surjectivity and injectivity separately by looking at  $f \circ f$ .)
------**Claim 3.**  $f(a) = (a-1)(f(2) - 1) + 1$ .
*Proof.* Since  $f$  is bijective  $f(2) > 1$ . For brevity's sake. let  $f(2) - 1 = k$ . From  $P(a,f(2))$ , we get that  $ f(f(a)+ k) \in \{ a-1, a, a+1 \}.$ Since  $f$  is involutive, we can conclude 
\[f(a) + k \in \{ f(a-1), f(a), f(a+1) \} \tag{1} \] 
Moreover, because  $k \neq 0$ , we can immediately discard  $f(a)$ . 

By strong induction, we shall show that  $f(a) = (a-1)k + 1$ . The bases cases  $a=1$  and  $a=2$  are trivial. For the inductive step, we attempt to extend to  $f(a+1)$ . By the inductive hypothesis, 
\[ f(a) = (a-1)k + 1 \neq (a-2)k + 1 = f(a-1) .\]
Therefore  $(1)$  implies that  $f(a) + k = f(a+1)$ , so we are done.
-----**Claim 4.**  $f(a) = a$  for all  $a$ . 
*Proof.* By  $P(a, f(b))$ , we have that  $a,b, f(f(a) + f(b) - 1)$  are the sides of a triangle. By **Claim 3**, 
\[ f(f(a) + f(b) - 1) = k(ka + kb + 1) + 1 = k^2(a+b) + k + 1 < a+b \]
Obviously, this is only possible where  $k=1$ , so  $f(a) = (a-1) +1 = a$ .

MotivationShow that if there exists some $f(k) > k$ , then we can bound $f(n)$ for large values of $n$ by taking $P(k, b)$ . **This is a generalization of the $P(1, b)$ + periodic modulo $N$ argument in other solutions.** After that, it is easy to show that if there exists some $f(k) < k$ , then this contradicts $P(k, 1)$ .
SolutionThe only solution is $f(n) \equiv n$ . Let $P(a,b)$ denote the given assertion. **Claim:** $f(n) \le n \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$ *Proof.* Suppose for contradiction that there exists some natural number $k$ such that $f(k) > k$ . Let $d = f(k)-1 \ge k$ . By $P(k, b)$ , we have that $$ f(b+d) \le f(b)+ k-1 $$ This implies that for $n \ge k$ , $f(n)$ increases with order at most $O\left(\frac{k-1}{d} \cdot n\right) \le O\left(\frac{k-1}{k} \cdot n\right)$ while $n$ increases with order $O(n)$ . Thus we can take $P(a, k)$ with $a$ arbitrarily large and $k$ as before. Thus we have that $a >> f(k) + f(k + f(a)-1)$ , as $a >> f(a)$ , contradiction. **Claim:** $f(n) \nless n \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$ *Proof.* From the first claim, $f(1) = 1$ is immediate. Suppose for contradiction that there exists some index $\ell$ such that $f(\ell) < \ell$ . However, taking $P(\ell, 1)$ yields \begin{align*} f(1) + f(1+f(\ell)-1) &> \ell f(f(\ell)) \ge \ell \end{align*} However, from the first claim and the contradiction assumption, we have that $f(f(\ell)) \le f(\ell) < \ell$ , contradiction. Thus from both claims, we have that $f(n) = n$ , as desired.

Note that if one side of an integer-side triangle has length 1, then the triangle inequality forces the other two sides to be equal. Further, if one side has length 2, then the other sides are either equal or differ by 1. Also, let  $P(a,b)$  denote the assertion.

From  $P(1,b)$  we get that  $f(b)=f(b+f(1)-1)$ , so  $f$  has period  $f(1)-1$ . If  $f(1)-1>0$  then this means that  $f$  is bounded. Then taking  $P(a,b)$  with  $a$  much larger than the maximum value which  $f$  can attain creates a contradiction, which implies that  $f(1)=1$ .
From  $f(1)=1$ ,  $P(a,1)$  gives that  $1,a,f(f(a))$  form the sides of a triangle, so  $f(f(a))=a$ . Hence  $f$  is bijective.
Now  $P(2,b)$  gives that  $2,f(b),f(b+f(2)-1)$  form the sides of a triangle. Since  $f$  is bijective and therefore injective, we have  $f(2) \geq 2$ , so  $b \neq b+f(2)-1$ . This means that  $f(b) \neq f(b+f(2)-1)$ . So, we must have:  $$ f(b) \pm 1 = f(b+f(2)-1) $$  Now let  $f(2)-1=c$ . We claim that  $$ f(b),f(b+c),f(b+2c),\ldots $$  must be an arithmetic sequence for any value of  $b$ . Suppose that there exists a  $k$  such that  $f(b+(k-1)c)-1=f(b+kc)$  and  $f(b+kc)+1=f(b+(k+1)c)$ . This implies that  $f(b+(k-1)c)=f(b+(k+1)c)$ , but since  $c$  is positive and  $f$  is injective, this is impossible. Similarly there does not exist  $k$  such that  $f(b+(k-1)c)+1=f(b+kc)$  and  $f(b+kc)-1=f(b+(k+1)c)$ . Therefore, the difference between consecutive terms in this sequence is always  $+1$  or  $-1$ , and thus is an arithmetic sequence.
However, note that if  $f(b+kc)-1=f(b+(k+1)c)$  for all  $k$  given a specific value of  $b$ , then the sequence decreases unboundedly. In particular, we can take  $k$  massive and get that  $f$  is negative, which doesn't work since the codomain is positive. Therefore we conclude that:  $$ f(b)+1=f(b+f(2)-1) $$  for all  $b$ .
Now suppose that  $f(2)-1>1$ . Then the sequence:  $$ f(1),f(1+c),f(1+2c),\ldots $$  covers all positive integers, since  $f(1)=1$ . However, this sequence does not include values of  $f$  such as  $f(2)$ . Since  $f$  is injective, this means that we can't assign any values to  $f(2)$  without breaking this injectivity: a contradiction. This means that  $f(2)-1=1$ , so:  $$ f(b)+1=f(b+1) $$  after which easy induction gives us  $f(a)=a$  as the only solution.  $\blacksquare$

We'll prove  $k=1$ . Call a triple  $(a,b,c)$  *good*, if we can form a non-degenerated triangle with side lengths  $a,b,c$ . We'll show that  $(b_{2009},r_{2009},w_{2009})$  is good. Then we'll easily get \begin{align*} b_{2009}+r_{2009} &\geq b_w,r_w > w_{2009},
 r_{2009}+w_{2009} &\geq r_b+w_b > b_{2009},
 w_{2009}+b_{2009} &\geq w_r+b_r > r_{2009}.
\end{align*} Thus,  $(b_{2009},r_{2009},w_{2009})$  is good, indeed.
Now, it suffices to construct  $2009$  triangles, such that  $(b_i,r_i,w_i)$  isn't good for all  $1 \leq i \leq 2008$ . Let the triangles have side lengths \[ (b_1,r_1,w_2), (b_2,r_2,w_3), \dots, (b_{2008},r_{2008},w_{2009}), (b_{2009},r_{2009},w_1). \] Take  $b_1=b_2=\dots=b_{2008}=1$  and  $b_{2009}=2009$ . It is easy to see that  $(b_1,r_1,w_1)= \left(1,\tfrac32,2 \right)$  is good. It is also easy to see that  $(b_i,r_i,w_{i+1})=(1,i+1,i+1)$  for  $2 \leq i \leq 2008$  is good. And of course the triple  $(b_{2009},r_{2009},w_{2009})= \left(2009,2009, \tfrac25 \right)$  is good. But \[ b_1+w_1 = 1+\tfrac25 < \tfrac32 = r_1, \] so  $(b_1,r_1,w_1)$  is not good. Also \[ b_i+w_i=1+i=r_i \] for  $2 \leq i \leq 2008$ , so  $(b_i,r_i,w_i)$  is not good either.

Let  $f$  be any function that maps the set of real numbers into the set of real numbers. Prove that there exist real numbers  $x$  and  $y$  such that \[f\left(x-f(y)\right)>yf(x)+x\]

solution_md:
It's a nice problem in my opinion. It's sad though, as there is no elegant proof without contradiction.
Let $f$ be any function that maps the set of real numbers into the set of real numbers. Prove that there exist real numbers $x$ and $y$ such that \[f\left(x-f(y)\right)>yf(x)+x\] *Proposed by Igor Voronovich, Belarus*
Solution: For the sake of contradiction, suppose there exists a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $$ f(x-f(y)) \le yf(x)+x, $$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ . Denote the above property of $f$ by $P(x, y)$ ; then, $$ P(x+f(0),0) \implies f(x) \le x+f(0), $$ and $$ P(f(y), y) \implies y\cdot \left(f(f(y))+1\right) \ge 0, $$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ . Call the previous two relations $(1)$ and $(2)$ respectively. Let $C=-(1+f(0))$ and consider the subsequent claim.**Claim 1:** For all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ we have $t>0 \implies f(t) \ge C$ . (Proof) Evidently, $(2)$ implies for all $t>0$ we have $f(f(t)) \ge -1$ so $(1)$ yields $f(t)+f(0) \ge -1 \implies f(t) \ge C$ as stated. $\square$ Now, we define the set $$ \mathcal{S} \overset{\text{def}}{:=} \left \{ x>0: f(x)<0 \right \}. $$ **Claim 2:** $\mathcal{S}$ is bounded above. (Proof) Assume to the contrary; let $s \in \mathcal{S}$ . By our assumption, there exists $t \in \mathcal{S}$ such that $$ t>\frac{C-s}{f(s)}, $$ then we have $$ f(s-f(t)) \le tf(s)+sf(t) \ge s>0$ , a contradiction! Hence, the claim must hold. $\square$ Thus, there exists an $N>0$ for which $x>N \implies f(x) \ge 0$ . Now, we consider the next crucial step; define the set $$ \mathcal{P} \overset{\text{def}}{:=} \left \{ x>N: f(x)>0 \right \}. $$ **Claim 3:** $\mathcal{P}$ is unbounded. (Proof) Else, we have $M>N>0$ such that $x>M \implies f(x)=0$ . If there exists $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x_0)<0$ then plug in $x=x_0, y>M$ to get $$ P(x_0, y) \implies f(x_0)=f(x_0-f(y)) \le yf(x_0)+x_0, $$ which fails for $y \rightarrow \infty$ . Therefore, $f(x) \ge 0$ always holds. However, $$ P(x, y) \implies 0 \le f(x-f(y)) \le yf(x)+x, $$ which fails if for any fixed $x$ we have $f(x)>0$ ; by setting $y \rightarrow -\infty$ . Since $f \not \equiv 0$ , we get the desired contradiction! $\square$ Finally, we fix an $x$ sufficiently large, so that $f(x)>0$ and take any $y$ with $$ y<\frac{C-x}{f(x)}, $$ to get $$ f(x-f(y)) \le yf(x)+x

Plugging  $y=0$ \[f(x-f(0))\le x\implies f(x)\le x+f(0)\]
Plugging  $x=f(y)$ \[f(0)\le yf(f(y))+f(y)\le y(y+2f(0))+(y+f(0))\implies y(y+2f(0)+1)\ge 0\]
As  $y$  is any real number, hence  $f(0)=-1/2$ .

Thus  $f(x)\le x-\dfrac12$ .
Notice that  $f(x) < 0$  for all  $x<1/2$ . We assume there is  $x>0$  such that  $f(x)\ge 0$ Take some  $x\ge 0$  and  $y\le 0$  such that  $f(x)\ge 0$  ,  $x-f(y)>0$  ,  $f(x-f(y))\ge 0$  and  $x+yf(x) < 0$ Thus  $0>x+yf(x)\ge f(x-f(y))\ge 0$ .

Hence for any  $x\ge 0$  and   $y\le 0$  we have  $f(x-f(y))<0$  or  $x+f(x)y\ge 0$  but not both.
We get  $f(x-f(y))(x+f(x)y)\ge 0$ .
Plugging  $y=0$  
\[f\left(x+\dfrac12\right)x\ge 0\]
Thus  $f(x)\ge 0$  for  $x>\dfrac12$ .

Take a pair of  $x>0$  and  $y<0$  such that  $x-f(y)\ge\dfrac12$ Hence  $yf(x)+x\ge 0\implies y\left(x-\dfrac12\right)+x\ge 0\implies (y+1)\left(x-\dfrac12\right)\ge\dfrac12$ . But this can't be true for all such  $x,y$ .
Hence we have a contradiction.

Thus  $f(x)\le 0$  for all  $x$ .

Again take  $x>0$  and  $y<0$  such that  $f(x-f(y))-x>0$ . Then we get  $f(x)\ge 0$ . Thus  $f(x-f(y))\le x\implies f(x)\le x+f(y)$ .
Therefore  $f(x)\le x+y-\dfrac12$ .
Hence we arrive at a contradiction and no such  $f(x)$  exists.

Assume the contrary, that  $f(x-f(y))\leq yf(x)+x$  for any  $x, y\in\mathbb{R}$ . Let  $P(x, y)$  denote this assertion.  $P(x+f(0), 0)$  gives  $$ f(x)\leq x+f(0) $$  for any  $x\in\mathbb{R}$ . Now we prove the following double claim:**Claim:** We have
 :arrow: *(i)*  $\lim_{y\rightarrow -\infty}f(y)=-\infty$ ;
 :arrow: *(ii)*  $\lim_{y\rightarrow +\infty}f(y)=+\infty$ .

*Proof:* Part *(i)* is an immediate corollary of  $f(y)\leq y+f(0)$ , so let's focus on the latter. Let  $y\in\mathbb{R}^+$ ;  $P(x+f(y), y)$  yields  $$ f(x)\leq yf(x+f(y))+x+f(y)\leq y(x+f(y)+f(0))+x+f(y)=(y+1)x+(y+1)f(y)+yf(0) $$  for every real  $x$ . Our aim is to prove that for any real  $t$  there is an  $y_0$  such that for any  $y\geq y_0$ ,  $f(y)\geq t$ . If we can find arbitrarily large  $y$  such that  $f(y)<t$ , then for arbitrarily large  $y$  we have  $$ (y+1)f(y)+yf(0)\leq (y+1)t+yf(0)\leq (y+1)(t+|f(0)|) $$  and, by fixing  $x<-t-|f(0)|$ , for arbitrarily large  $y$  we have the inequality  $$ f(x)\leq (y+1)(x+t+|f(0)|) $$  however the last factor is negative, implying that this expression may attain arbitrarily small values when we increase  $y$ . This is a contradiction.  $\square$ Now it's easy to devise a contradiction. Choose  $x$  such that  $f(x)>0$  (it trivially exists by our claim). Then  $\lim_{y\rightarrow -\infty}(yf(x)+x)=-\infty$ , implying that  $\lim_{y\rightarrow -\infty}f(x-f(y))=-\infty$ . But  $\lim_{y\rightarrow -\infty}(x-f(y))=+\infty$ , therefore  $\lim_{y\rightarrow -\infty}f(x-f(y))=+\infty$ . This is a contradiction, establishing the problem statement.

Putting  $y = -\frac{2c+1}{2}$  gives that  $0 \geq (\frac{2c+1}{2})^2$ , which is only possible if  $f(0) = c = -\frac{1}{2}$ .
Now, we will prove that for all positive  $x$ ,  $f(x) \leq 0$ . Assume FTSOC that there exists  $x > 0$  such that  $f(x) > 0$ . 
Then, take  $y$  to be a sufficiently small negative number, and note that  $x - f(y) \geq x - y + \frac{1}{2}$ , so we can assume that  $x - f(y) > 0$ .
Then, by taking  $y$  to be sufficiently small, we can make the right hand side be sufficiently small, which leads us to the conclusion that there doesn't exist $N < 0$  such that there doesn't exist positive  $z$  such that  $f(z) < N$ .

Now, let  $y$  be a positive number such that  $f(y)$  is sufficiently small (and negative). Also, let  $x$  be a negative number. Note that $yf(x) + x \leq xy - \frac{x}{2} + x = xy + \frac{x}{2} < 0$  for any such  $x$ . Since we can make  $f(y)$  sufficiently negative, we can choose  $x - f(y)$  to be any number we want.
Therefore,  $f(x)$  is negative for all  $x$ , including the  $x$  we originally chose so that  $f(x) > 0$ , giving the required contradiction.

Now, note that  $-\frac{1}{2} \leq yf(f(y)) + f(y)$  for all  $y$ . However, letting  $x$  be positive and  $y$  be sufficiently negative in the original equation gives that since $x-f(y)$  is positive and  $yf(x)$  is non-negative,  $yf(x) + x$  can be made sufficiently large unless  $f(x) = 0$ . However, if there exists positive  $y$  such that $f(y) < -\frac{1}{2}$ , then since  $yf(f(y)) \leq 0, yf(f(y)) + f(y) < -\frac{1}{2}$ , a contradiction. Suppose that  $f(x-f(y)) \leq yf(x)+x$ . Setting  $y=0$  implies that  $f(x) \leq x+f(0)$  (shift  $x$  with  $f(0)$ ) and  $x=f(y)$  combined with the previous inequality gives that  $yf(f(y))+y+f(0) \geq yf(f(y))+f(y) \geq f(0)$ , so  $f(f(y)) \geq -1$  for  $y>0$ . Combining with the first inequality again, we obtain  $f(y)+f(0) \geq -1$ , so  $f(x) \geq c$  for all  $x>0$  (for some constant  $c=-1-f(0)$ ).

If there is some  $t$ , such that  $f(t)>0$ , take  $x=t$  and  $y \rightarrow -\infty$  to get that  $c \leq f(t-f(y)) \leq yf(t)+t \rightarrow -\infty$ , contradiction (obviously  $f(y) \leq y+f(0) \leq t$  would be satisfied for small enough  $y$ ). Hence  $f(x) \leq 0$  for all  $x$ .

We show that there are no functions  $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  satisfying \[f(x - f(y)) \le yf(x) + x \] Let  $P(x,y)$  denote the given assertion. 

Claim:  $f(0) = -\frac{1}{2}$ Proof:  $P(x+f(0),0): f(x)\le x + f(0)$ .  $P(f(x),x): f(0)\le xf(f(x)) + f(x)$ . This implies that  $f(0)\le x(x + 2f(0) + 1) + f(0)\implies x(x + 2f(0) + 1) \ge 0$  since  $f(f(x))\le x + 2f(0)$ . 

Taking  $x>0$  gives that  $x + 2f(0) + 1 \ge 0$ , so  $f(0)\ge -\frac{1}{2}$ . 

Taking  $x<0$  gives that  $x + 2f(0) + 1\le 0$ , so  $f(0)\le - \frac{1}{2}$ . 

Thus,  $f(0) = -\frac{1}{2}$ .  $\square$ So  $f(x)\le x  - 1/2$ . We get \[f(0)\le xf(f(x)) + f(x)\le xf(f(x)) + x + f(0),\] so  $x(f(f(x)) + 1) \ge 0$ , which implies  $f(f(x))\ge -1\forall x>0$ , so  $f(x) + f(0)\ge -1\implies f(x) \ge -1/2$ . 


Claim:  $f(x) \le 0\forall x\in \mathbb{R}$ . 
Proof: Clearly we only need to prove this for  $x>1/2$ . 

Suppose some  $k>1/2$  satisfied  $f(k)>0$ .  $P(k,x): f(k - f(x)) \le xf(k) + k$ . Fix  $x$  arbitrarily small. Since  $f(x) \le 0$ , we have  $k-f(x)>0$ , so the LHS is at least  $-1/2$ . However, the RHS approaches  $-\infty$ , contradiction.  $\square$  $P(1434,x): f(1434 - f(x)) \le xf(1434) + 1434$ . Fix  $x$  arbitrarily large. Since  $f(x)\le 0$ , the LHS is at least  $-1/2$ . If  $f(1434) = 0$ ,  $P(f(1434),1434)$  gives that  $-1/2 \le -517$ , which is absurd. Thus,  $f(1434) < 0$ , which implies that the RHS gets arbitrarily small, contradiction.

Assume otherwise that  $f(x-f(y))\le yf(x)+x$  for all  $x$  and  $y$ . Then, let this be  $P(x,y)$ .

Let  $c=f(0)$ .  $P(x,0)$  gives  $f(x-c)\le x$  so  $f(x)\le x+c$  for all  $c$ .  $P(f(y),y)$  gives \[c\le yf(f(y))+f(y)\le y(y+2c)+y+c\implies 0\le y(y+(2c+1)).\] If we pick  $y=-\tfrac{2c+1}{2}$  then this becomes  $0\le -\tfrac{(2c+1)^2}{4}$  which implies  $c=-\tfrac12$ . But also,  $y(f(f(y))+1)\ge 0$  so for  $y\ge 0$  we have  $f(f(y))\ge -1$  and so \[-y\ge yf(f(y))\ge c-f(y)\] so  $y\le f(y)-c$  so  $f(y)\ge y+c$ . Therefore,  $f(x)=x+c$  for all  $x$ . In the original inequality this becomes  $-y\le y(x+c)$  which is clearly false.

Find all functions $f$ from the set of real numbers into the set of real numbers which satisfy for all $x$ , $y$ the identity \[ f\left(xf(x+y)\right) = f\left(yf(x)\right) +x^2\] *Proposed by Japan*

Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(xf(x+y))=f(yf(x))+x^2$ 1) $f(x)=0$ $\iff$ $x=0$ ============== If $f(0)\ne 0$ , then $P(0,\frac x{f(0)})$ $\implies$ $f(x)=f(0)$ constant, which is not a solution. So $f(0)=0$ If $f(u)=0$ , then $P(u,-u)$ $\implies$ $u^2=0$ Q.E.D. 2) $f(x)$ is a bijection ============= $P(x,0)$ $\implies$ $f(xf(x))=x^2$ and so $\mathbb R^+\cup\{0\}\subseteq f(\mathbb R)$ $P(x,-x)$ $\implies$ $f(-xf(x))=-x^2$ and so $\mathbb R^-\cup\{0\}\subseteq f(\mathbb R)$ And so $f(x)$ is a surjection Let then $a<0$ and $u$ such that $f(u)=a$ : $P(\sqrt{-a},\frac u{f(\sqrt{-a})})$ $\implies$ $f(\sqrt{-a}f(\sqrt{-a}+\frac u{f(\sqrt{-a})}))=0$ So (using 1. above) : $f(\sqrt{-a}+\frac u{f(\sqrt{-a})})=0$ So (using again 1) above) : $\sqrt{-a}+\frac u{f(\sqrt{-a})}=0$ and $u=-\sqrt{-a}f(\sqrt{-a})$ And so a unique $u$ for any $a<0$ Let then $a>0$ and $u\ne 0$ such that $f(u)=a$ and $v$ such that $f(v)=\frac u{\sqrt a}$ : $P(\sqrt a,v-\sqrt a)$ $\implies$ $f((v-\sqrt a)f(\sqrt a))=0$ So (using 1. above) : $(v-\sqrt a)f(\sqrt a)=0$ and so $v=\sqrt a$ and $u=\sqrt af(\sqrt a)$ And so a unique $u$ for any $a>0$ And so $f(x)$ is an injection. Q.E.D. 3) $f(x)$ is an odd function ================= Let $x\ne 0$ $P(x,0)$ $\implies$ $f(xf(x))=x^2$ $P(-x,0)$ $\implies$ $f(-xf(-x))=x^2$ And so $f(xf(x))=f(-xf(-x))$ and so, since injective, $xf(x)=-xf(-x)$ and $f(-x)=-f(x)$ (true also if $x=0$ ) Q.E.D. 4) $f(2x)=2f(x)$ ========= Let $x\ne 0$ : $P(x,-2x)$ $\implies$ $-f(xf(x))=-f(2xf(x))+x^2$ $P(-x,-x)$ $\implies$ $f(xf(2x))=f(xf(x))+x^2$ Subtracting, we get : $f(xf(2x))=f(2xf(x))$ and, since injective : $xf(2x)=2xf(x)$ and so $f(2x)=2f(x)$ (true also if $x=0$ ) Q.E.D. 5) $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ $\forall x,y$ ===================== $P(x,y)$ $\implies$ $f(xf(x+y))=f(yf(x))+x^2$ $P(x+y,-x)$ $\implies$ $f((x+y)f(y))=-f(xf(x+y))+(x+y)^2$ Subtracting, we get a new assertion $Q(x,y)$ : $f((x+y)f(y))+f(yf(x))=y^2+2xy$ $Q(x-y,y)$ $\implies$ $f(xf(y))+f(yf(x-y))=2xy-y^2$ $Q(x-y,2y)$ $\implies$ $f((x+y)f(y))+f(yf(x-y))=2xy$ Subtracting, we get $f(xf(y)+yf(y))-f(xf(y))=y^2$ And so $f(xf(y)+yf(y))=f(xf(y))+f(yf(y))$ (remember that $P(y,0)$ $\implies$ $f(yf(y))=y^2$ ) And so $f(x+yf(y))=f(x)+f(yf(y))$ $\forall x,y$ And so $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ $\forall x\in\mathbb R,\forall y\in f^{[-1]}(\mathbb R^+\cup\{0\})$ But then $f(-x+y)=-f(x)+f(y)$ and so $f(x-y)=f(x)+f(-y)$ And so $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ $\forall x\in\mathbb R,\forall y\in f^{[-1]}(\mathbb R^-\cup\{0\})$ Q.E.D. 6) either $f(x)=x$ $\forall x$ , either $f(x)=-x$ $\forall x$ ================================ Using $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ , $P(x,y)$ becomes $f(xf(x))+f(xf(y))=f(yf(x))+x^2$ and so $f(xf(y))=f(yf(x))$ $P(x+y,0)$ $\implies$ $f(xf(x))+f(xf(y))+f(yf(x))+f(yf(y))=(x+y)^2$ and so $f(xf(y))=xy$ Setting $y=f(1)$ and using $f(yf(y))=y^2$ , we get $f(x)=xf(1)$ Plugging this in original equation, we get $f(1)^2=1$ Hence the two solutions : either $f(1)=1$ and so $\boxed{f(x)=x}$ $\forall x$ either $f(1)=-1$ and so $\boxed{f(x)=-x}$ $\forall x$

Therefore  $$ P(k,b)\implies f(kf(k+b)) = f(a)+k^2=0 $$  hence  $kf(k+b)=0\implies f(k+b)=0\implies b=-k$  or  $a=kf(-k)$ This conclude that  $f$  must be injective.

\[ P(\alpha,0) \implies 0 = \alpha^2 \implies \alpha = 0 \] **Claim 3:**  $f$  is injective. 
Proof: let  $f(a) =f(b)$ .
\[ P(x,0) \implies xf(x) = x^2 \] 
So 
\[ P(a,b-a) \implies f(af(b)) = f((b-a)f(a))  + a^2 \]
As  $f(a) =f(b)$  
\[ a^2 = f(af(a)) = f(af(b)) = f((b-a)f(a))  + a^2 \]
So after cancelling we get that 
\[ f((b-a)f(a))  = 0 \] 
So we get that  $a=0$  or  $b=a$ .  Hence proved.**Claim 4:**  $f(1)^2 = 1$ Proof:  $P(x,0)\implies f(xf(x))=x^2$  $x=1\implies f(f(1))=1$  $x=f(1)\implies f(f(1)))=f(1)^2$ so  $f(1)=1$  or  $-1$ .**Claim 5:**  $f(2x) = 2f(x)$ Proof: this is clear for  $x=0$ , so take  $x\neq0$ . Once again  $f(xf(x))=x^2$  by  $P(x,0)$  and now also  $f\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}f\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right)=\frac{x^2}{2}$  by  $P\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}},0\right)$ . Take  $P\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ . This gives  $$ f\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}f\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right)=f\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}f\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right)+\frac{x^2}{2}=x^2 $$  Comparing with  $P(x,0)$ , we get by 4. that  $$ \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}f\left(\sqrt{2}x\right)=xf(x) $$  or equivalently,  $f\left(\sqrt{2}x\right)=\sqrt{2}f(x)$  for  $x\neq0$ . By applying it twice, it follows that  $f(2x)=\sqrt{2}f\left(\sqrt{2}x\right)=2f(x)$ , as desired.

Now simply use  $P(1,y)$  and  $P(\sqrt{2},y)$  to finish.

Let  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  be positive real numbers such that  $\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = a+b+c$ . Prove that:
  \[\frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a+2b+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a+b+2c)^2}\leq \frac{3}{16}.\] 
*Proposed by Juhan Aru, Estonia*
solution_md:
Let $a$ , $b$ , $c$ be positive real numbers such that $\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = a+b+c$ . Prove that: \[\frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a+2b+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a+b+2c)^2}\leq \frac{3}{16}\] *Proposed by Juhan Aru, Estonia*
By the AM-HM inequality,\[(a+b+c)^2\ge9\] and by the Cauchy Schwarz inequality \[\sum a^2\ge 3\]. By Titu's lemma or Cauchy Schwarz, $\sum_{cyc} \frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2} \leq \frac{9}{\sum{(2a+b+c)^2}}$ .( $\dots \boxed{1}$ ) \[\sum(2a+b+c)^2=\sum_{cyc}a^2+2\sum a(a+b+c) + \sum_{cyc} (a+b+c)^2\] \[=\sum_{\cyc}a^2+2(a+b+c)^2 + 3(a+b+c)^2\ge 3+2\cdot 9+3\cdot 9\ge 48\]..Putting this in the inequality $\boxed{1}$ , we get what we wanted to prove.

\[ (2a+b+c)^2 = \big((a+b)+(a+c)\big)^2 = 4\left(\frac{(a+b)+(a+c)}{2}\right)^2 \ge 4(a+b)(a+c) \]
by AM-GM. Hence, 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2} &\le \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{1}{4(a+b)(a+c)} = \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{b+c}{4(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)} = \frac{a+b+c}{2(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}.
\end{align*}
Since  $abc(a+b+c) = ab+bc+ca$  by the condition, we homogenize the above; we want to show
\begin{align*}
    &\frac{abc(a+b+c)^2}{2(ab+bc+ca)(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)} \le \frac{3}{16} 
    \iff &8abc(a+b+c)^2 \le 3(ab+bc+ca)(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) 
    \iff & 8(a^3bc+ab^3c+abc^3 + 2a^2b^2c+2a^2bc^2+2ab^2c^2) 
    &\le 3(a^3 b^2 + 2 a^3 b c + a^3 c^2 + a^2 b^3 + 4 a^2 b^2 c + 4 a^2 b c^2 + a^2 c^3 + 2 a b^3 c + 4 a b^2 c^2 + 2 a b c^3 + b^3 c^2 + b^2 c^3) 
    \iff &2(a^3bc+ab^3c+abc^3)+4(a^2b^2c+a^2bc^2+ab^2c^2) \le 3(a^3b^2+a^3c^2+a^2b^3+a^2c^3+b^3c^2+b^2c^3) 
    \iff &2\sum_{\text{cyc}} a^3bc + 4\sum_{\text{cyc}} ab^2c^2 \le 3\sum_{\text{cyc}} a^3(b^2+c^2). 
\end{align*}

Therefore, this is true, so therefore  $f''(a)\geq0$  for  $0<a<1.$ Finally, since  $f''(a)\geq0$  on the interval  $0<a<1$ , by Jensen,   $$ f(a)+f(b)+f(c)\geq 3f(1/3)=0, $$   so we are done.

The condition is so ugly that we want to get rid of it immediately. Doing so, it suffices to prove that  $$ \sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} \frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2}\leq \frac{3(\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c})}{16(a+b+c)}, $$  which is homogeneous. Thus drop the original condition and impose  $a+b+c=3$ , which makes the inequality  $$ \sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} \frac{1}{(a+3)^2}\leq \frac{1}{16a}+\frac{1}{16b}+\frac{1}{16c} \iff \sum_\mathrm{cyc} \frac{(a+3)^2-16a}{16a(a+3)^2} \geq 0. $$  We will use the "tangent line trick" and prove the inequality  $$ \sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} \frac{(x+3)^2-16x}{16x(x+3)^2}\geq -\frac{1}{32}(x-1) $$  for  $x>0$ , which is equivalent upon cross-multiplication and factorization to the true inequality  $(a-1)^2(a^2+7a+18) \geq 0$ . Thus we have  $$ \frac{(a+3)^2-16a}{16a(a+3)^2} \geq -\frac{1}{32}(a+b+c-3)=0, $$  and we are done.  $\blacksquare$

Let $a$ , $b$ , $c$ be positive real numbers such that $\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = a+b+c$ . Prove that: \[\frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a+2b+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a+b+2c)^2}\leq \frac{3}{16}.\] *Proposed by Juhan Aru, Estonia*
Usually try to homogenize inequalities, so let’s try that here. We want to prove $\sum_{cyc}\frac{a+b+c}{(2a+b+c)^2}\leq \frac{3}{16}\sum_{cyc}\frac{1}{a}$ . Now, let a+b+c=3 to quickly rid ourselves of the 3. It suffices, then, to prove that $\sum_{cyc}\frac{16a-(a+3)^2}{16a(a+3)^2}\leq 0\iff\sum_{cyc}\frac{10a-a^2-9}{a^2+6a+9}\leq \sum_{cyc}\frac{a-1}{2}=0$ , where the last step is because we can expand simply and note the preserved a=b=c=1 equality case (so there must be a factor of a-1, and we see it is a double root by easy factoring) that gives the true $(a-1)^2(a^2+7a+18) \geq 0$ . I dislike these kinds of problems, because at some point there is no motivation to have an intermediate step, other than lucky guess (to be specific, that (a-1)/2). Luckily, it isn’t too out of reach, since we want something that is equal to 0 cyclically, which relates to a-1 (an equality case), and then multiply by some constant (1/2). I had to use WolframAlpha along with a friend to test a bunch of values, but since this was untimed it worked. :) Edit: Actually, I can apply the tangent line trick to get this conjecture much, much easier, and I just learned how to take derivatives. :P

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Firstly, we have
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a+2b+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a+b+2c)^2}\leq \frac{3}{16} &\implies \sum_{\text{cyc}} \left(\frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2}-\frac{1}{16}\right) \le 0 
&\implies \sum_{\text{cyc}} \left(\frac{1}{(2a+b+c)^2}-\frac{1}{16} \cdot \frac{\tfrac{1}{a}+\tfrac{1}{b}+\tfrac{1}{c}}{a+b+c}\right) \le 0 
&\implies \sum_{\text{cyc}} \left(\frac{16}{(2a+b+c)^2}-\frac{1}{a(a+b+c)}-\frac{1}{b(a+b+c)}-\frac{1}{c(a+b+c)}\right) \le 0 
&\implies \sum_{\text{cyc}} \left(\frac{16}{(2a+b+c)^2}-\frac{3}{a(a+b+c)}\right) \le 0.
\end{align*}
Now, let  $a+b+c=3.$  Then, we wish to show that   $$ \sum_{\text{cyc}} \left(\frac{16}{(a+3)^2}-\frac{1}{a}\right) \le 0. $$   Let us define the function   $$ f(x) \coloneq \frac{16}{(x+3)^2}-\frac{1}{x}, $$   i.e. so that we wish to prove   $$  \sum_{\text{cyc}} f(a) \le 0. $$   By Jensen's Inequality, since  $f(1)=0,$  it suffices to prove that  $f(x)$  is concave on the interval  $[0,3].$  We have
\begin{align*}
f''(x) \ge 0 &\iff \frac{96}{(x+3)^4}-\frac{2}{x^3} \le 0 
&\iff 96x^3-2(x+3)^4 \le 0 
&\iff 2x^4-72x^3+108x^2+216x+162 \ge 0 
&\iff (x-3)(x^3-33x^2-45x-27) \ge 0.
\end{align*}
Observe that  $x-3 \le 0$  for all  $x$  in the interval  $[0,3],$  and it is also not difficult to see that   $$ x^3<33x^2 \implies x^3-33x^2-45x-27 \le 0 $$   on this interval as well, concluding the proof.  $\square$</details>

We have $(2a+b+c)^2=[(a+b)+(c+a)]^2\ge 4(a+b)(c+a)$ Similarly, we have $\textbf{LHS}\le \frac{1}{4(a+b)(a+c)}+\frac{1}{4(b+c)(a+b)}+\frac{1}{4(b+c)(c+a)}=\frac{a+b+c}{2(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}$ Proving the $\frac{8}{9}$ inequality: Let's prove $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\ge \frac{8}{9}(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)\Leftrightarrow 9(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\ge 8(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)$ $\Leftrightarrow 9[ab(a+b)+bc(b+c)+ca(c+a)]+18abc\ge 8[ab(a+b)+bc(b+c)+ca(c+a)]+24abc$ $\Leftrightarrow ab(a+b)+bc(b+c)+ca(c+a)\ge 6abc\Leftrightarrow ab(a+b)+bc(b+c)+ca(c+a) +3abc\ge 9abc$ $\Leftrightarrow (a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)\ge 9abc$ which is true because $a+b+c\ge 3\sqrt[3]{abc}$ and $ab+bc+ca\ge 3\sqrt[3]{a^2b^2c^2}$ Using this inequality, we have $\textbf{LHS}\le \frac{a+b+c}{\frac{16}{9}(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)}=\frac{9}{16(ab+bc+ca)}$ $\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = a+b+c\Leftrightarrow ab+bc+ca=abc(a+b+c)\le \frac{(ab+bc+ca)^2}{3}\Rightarrow ab+bc+ca\ge 3$ $\Rightarrow \textbf{LHS}\le \frac{3}{16}$ Equality at $a=b=c=1$

Let  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  be positive real numbers such that  $ab+bc+ca\leq 3abc$ . Prove that
 \[\sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}}+\sqrt{\frac{b^2+c^2}{b+c}}+\sqrt{\frac{c^2+a^2}{c+a}}+3\leq \sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{a+b}+\sqrt{b+c}+\sqrt{c+a}\right)\]

*Proposed by Dzianis Pirshtuk, Belarus*
solution_md:
Quite an awesome inequality!
Let $a$ , $b$ , $c$ be positive real numbers such that $ab+bc+ca\leq 3abc$ . Prove that \[\sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}}+\sqrt{\frac{b^2+c^2}{b+c}}+\sqrt{\frac{c^2+a^2}{c+a}}+3\leq \sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{a+b}+\sqrt{b+c}+\sqrt{c+a}\right)\] *Proposed by Dzianis Pirshtuk, Belarus*
Notice that for all real numbers $x>y>0$ we have $$ \sqrt{x-y} \le \sqrt{2x}-\sqrt{y} \iff x^2 \ge 4y(x-y) \iff (x-2y)^2 \ge 0. $$ Write $$ \sqrt{\frac{x^2+y^2}{x+y}}=\sqrt{(x+y)-\frac{2xy}{x+y}} \le \sqrt{2(x+y)}-\sqrt{\frac{2xy}{x+y}}, $$ so our given inequality is equivalent to $$ \sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}} \ge 3. $$ Apply Holder's inequality to get $$ \left(\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}\right)^2 \left(\sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{a+b}{2ab} \right) \ge 27. $$ However, since $$ \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{a+b}{2ab}=\sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{1}{a} \le 3, $$ we get the desired bound. Equality occurs when $a=b=c=1$ . $\blacksquare$

Hi, I'm very glad to see that my problem was included in IMO Shortlist :) , because I was in Spain yet as a contestant. 

Originally I proposed this problem with the following proof. As I now this version was sent by out team leader without any corrections to IMO 2009 Problem Selection Committee:

We have \[\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \leq \sqrt{2}(x+y-\sqrt{xy}) \quad \forall x ,y >0 \eqno (*),\]  
because  $(*) \Leftrightarrow x^2+y^2 \leq 2(x^2+y^2+xy +2xy-2x\sqrt{xy}-2y\sqrt{xy}) \Leftrightarrow (\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^4 \geq 0,$  which is clearly. 

Therefore
\[\sqrt{\frac{x^2+y^2}{x+y}} \leq \frac{\sqrt{2}(x+y-\sqrt{xy})}{\sqrt{x+y}}=\sqrt{2(x+y)}-\frac{\sqrt{2xy}}{\sqrt{x+y}} \quad \forall x ,y >0. \]

This implies that \[\sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}}+\sqrt{\frac{b^2+c^2}{b+c}}+\sqrt{\frac{c^2+a^2}{c+a}} \leq \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{a+b}+\sqrt{b+c}+\sqrt{c+a})-\sqrt{2}\left( \frac{\sqrt{ab}}{\sqrt{a+b}}+ \frac{\sqrt{bc}}{\sqrt{b+c}}+\frac{\sqrt{ca}}{\sqrt{c+a}} \right). \]

Then, it is enough to prove that 
\[\frac{\sqrt{ab}}{\sqrt{a+b}}+ \frac{\sqrt{bc}}{\sqrt{b+c}}+\frac{\sqrt{ca}}{\sqrt{c+a}} \geq \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}.\]

Denote by  $x=\frac{1}{a},$   $y=\frac{1}{b},$  и  $z=\frac{1}{c}.$  We have  $ab+bc+ca \leq 3abc \Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{a}+
\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c} \leq 3 \Leftrightarrow x+y+z \leq 3.$ It is easy to see that 
\[
\frac{\sqrt{ab}}{\sqrt{a+b}}+ \frac{\sqrt{bc}}{\sqrt{b+c}}+\frac{\sqrt{ca}}{\sqrt{c+a}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}}}+
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{a}}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{a}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}}+
\frac{1}{\sqrt{y+z}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z+x}} \geq 
\left[ AM-HM \right] \geq \frac{9}{\sqrt{x+y}+\sqrt{y+z}+\sqrt{z+x}} \geq \left[ AM-QM \right] \geq 
\frac{9}{\sqrt{3((x+y)+(y+z)+(z+x))}}=
\frac{9}{\sqrt{6(x+y+z)}}=\left[ x+y+z \leq 3 \right] \geq \frac{9}{\sqrt{6 \cdot 3}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}},
\]
and we are done. Equality occurs if and only if  $a=b=c=1.$ P.s. The best way to prove (*)  is to say that it's equiv to the inequality  $\sqrt{x^{2}+{y^2}}+\sqrt{2xy} \leq \sqrt{2(x+y)^2}=\sqrt{2}(x+y)$ , which is true by AM-QM.

We first prove a well-known inequality.

Claim:  $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}\leq \sqrt{2(x+y)}$ .

Proof: The claim follows directly from AM-GM. We have that  $x+y\geq 2\sqrt{xy}\leftrightarrow 2x+2y\geq x+y+2\sqrt{xy}=(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})^2\leftrightarrow \sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}\leq \sqrt{2(x+y)}.$ From the claim, we have that   $$ \sum_{cyc} \sqrt{2(a+b)}\geq \sum_{cyc} \sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}}+\sum_{cyc}\sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}. $$  Hence, in order to prove the problem, we just have to show that  $\sum_{cyc} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}\geq 3$ . Luckily, this is easy by Holder:  $$ (\sum_{cyc} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}})^2(\sum_{cyc} \frac{4a+4b}{ab})\geq (2+2+2)^3=6^3\implies $$    $$ \sum_{cyc} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}\geq \sqrt{\frac{216}{4(2)(3)}}=3. $$  We are done!

By Hölder:   $$ (\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}) (\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}) (\sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{a+b}{2ab})\geq 27 $$     $$ \iff (\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}})(\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}) (\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{1}{a}) \geq 27 $$     $$ \iff (\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}) \geq 3 $$  By AM-QM:   $$ \sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{2}\sqrt{a+b} \geq \sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{2a}{a+b}} +\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}} $$   Q.E.D.

Note that  $a+b+2\sqrt{ab}\le 2a+2b$  which means  $\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}\ge\sqrt{2}\le \sqrt{a+b}$ , so \[\sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}}\le \sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{a+b}-\sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}\right)\] so it remains to show that  $\left(\sum_{cyc}\sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}\right)\le 3$ By Holder's \[\left(\sum_{cyc}\sqrt{\frac{2ab}{a+b}}\right)^2(\sum_{cyc}\frac{a+b}{2ab})\ge 27\], but  $\sum_{cyc}\frac{a+b}{2ab}=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}\le 3$  which implies the result.

stem_md:
Consider  $2009$  cards, each having one gold side and one black side, lying on parallel on a long table. Initially all cards show their gold sides. Two player, standing by the same long side of the table, play a game with alternating moves. Each move consists of choosing a block of  $50$  consecutive cards, the leftmost of which is showing gold, and turning them all over, so those which showed gold now show black and vice versa. The last player who can make a legal move wins.
(a) Does the game necessarily end?
(b) Does there exist a winning strategy for the starting player?

*Proposed by Michael Albert, Richard Guy, New Zealand*
solution_md:
$\color{green} \boxed {\textbf{SOLUTION}}$  $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{A}}$  
Let,  $N$  denotes the total number of cards. 

For  $N=1$  the game ends.

Assume the game ends for  $1,2,3,...N$  cards. Consider Cards numbered  $1,2,3,...N,N+1$  $\textbf{Case 1 :}$  If  $1$  is black sided then we can choose the other  $N$  cards and from inductive hypothesis it is true that the game will end $\textbf{Case 2 :}$  If  $1$  is gold sided then - $\textbf{Sub-Case 1 :}$  We never choose  $1$  then by inductive hypothesis the game ends $\textbf{Sub-Case 2 :}$  If we choose  $1$  then it becomes black sided and we again left with  $N$  cards and we are done  $\blacksquare$  $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{B}}$  
Consider the cards  $50,100,150,...2000$  At the beginning, all of them are gold sided, After first player's move, no matter how he chooses  $50$  cards consecutively, there must be one card from  $50,100,150,...2000$  and it turns into black. So, When second player moves, there stays odd number of cards and he always finds a move, but as the game finishes, there must be a position when the first player will not find any move, So first player don't have any winning strategy  $\blacksquare$

We number the cards left to right  $1,2,\dots$ , and say that we choose card  $n$  if we choose the block of  $50$  cards from  $n$  to  $n+49$ .

a) We show that the game necessarily ends for any positive number  $N$  of cards, regardless of how may are initially with their golden side up:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>If  $N<50$  or  $N=50$  and the first card is initially black side up, the game ends before it can begin because no move is possible.  If  $N=50$  and the first card is golden side up, there is exactly one possible move that produces the previous situation, or the game finishes in exactly one move.
Assume now that the game ends for  $1,2,3,\dots,N-1$  cards, and consider a game with  $N$  cards.  If the first one is black side up, then we can never choose card  $1$ , it is equivalent to playing with  $N-1$  cards, and the game finishes.  If the first one is golden side up and it is never chosen, then it is also equivalent to playing with  $N-1$  cards, and the equivalent game finishes, or we are forced to choose card  $1$ , which becomes black side up, reverting to the previous situation and the game finishes.</details>

b) We show now that the first player ALWAYS looses, independently on how each player ends, when the game has  $2009$  cards:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Note that for each two times that we choose card  $n$ , the net result is doing nothing, since cards  $n$  to  $n+49$  are reversed each time that card  $n$  is chosen. Hence the game always finishes after an even number of moves, ie the first player is always the one that runs out of possible moves, and the first player always looses, independently on how the game is played.</details>

Here I present the generalization of this problem, where we're given a pair  $(n,k) \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}^2, n\geq k$ , and we have  $n$  cards and we can flip a block with  $k$  cards where the leftmost is showing its gold side. $\textbf{Claim:}$  The game always end.
It can be done by many ways as you can see above, but I'll present another way to define a monovariant. Attribute the weight  $(k+i)!$  to the  $i$ -th card <u>from the right to the left</u>. And let  $S_i$  be the sum of the numbers of the cards showing its gold side after  $i$  moves. 
Note that  $S_i$  can increase in at most   $$ \sum_{p=j+1}^{k+i+i} p! < k\cdot (k+j)! $$   but it will necessarily decrease in at least  $(k+i+1)!>k\cdot (k+i)!$ , so  $\{S_i\}$  is descending, therefore, since it can't be negative, sometime we'll not be able to operate anymore  $\blacksquare$ Now, let us define  $m_i$  to be movement where the  $i$ -th card <u>from the left to the right</u> is the leftmost one which is showing its gold side. Then, for each multiset  $J$  of positive integer whose elements are less than  $n+1-k$  , let  $\sum_{j \in J} m_j$  to be the operation of performing all movements  $m_j$ ,  $j \in J$  and when  $J=\emptyset $ ,  $\sum m_j = 0$ . Then, let  $V$  be the set of all possible moves.  $\textbf{Claim:}$   $V$  is a vector space over  $\mathbb{F}_2$  
It's obvious since whenever we can sum each  $m_i$  an even number of times, it's easy to see that it's equivalent to do none of those  $m_i$  and whenever we can operate a sum  $m_i+m_j$  as  $m_j+m_i$ , those two will lead to the same cards configuration as the parity of flips for each card is preserved.  $\blacksquare$ Then, let  $G=(m_{a_1}, m_{a_2}, ..., m_{a_T})$  be a game that ended. Note that if we delete all the movements that appeared an even number of times in  $G$  and make all the moves that appeared an odd number to appear just one time, the winner will be preserved and we'll get into a new set of moves  $G'$  that will have the same ending position. Finally, note that necessarilly  $m_1 \in G'$ , and, if  $m_i,1<i\leq k \in G'$  it'll need to appear more than one time in  $G'$ , contradiction. Inductively, we can conclude that  $G' = \{m_1, m_{k+1}, m_{2k+1}, ..., m_{k\lfloor \frac{n-k}k \rfloor +1}\}$  and, once the winner is preserved from  $G$  to  $G'$ , we can conclude that the winner will be   $$ \text{The first player, if  $\lfloor \frac{n-k}k \rfloor$  is even and the second player otherwise.} $$  Hence we conclude that once defined the parity of  $\lfloor \frac{n-k}k \rfloor$ , the winner is defined, and, no matter how he plays, he will win the game in  $100\%$  of the times and the game will always end with the same cards showing their gold faces.  :o  $\textbf{Remark:}$  This generalization is inspired by @jonh_malkovich 's generalization for the [Brazil - TST Cone 2021/P2](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c2525019h2751885p28146268).

For any integer  $n\geq 2$ , let  $N(n)$  be the maxima number of triples  $(a_i, b_i, c_i)$ ,  $i=1, \ldots, N(n)$ , consisting of nonnegative integers  $a_i$ ,  $b_i$  and  $c_i$  such  that the following two conditions are satisfied:

- $a_i+b_i+c_i=n$  for all  $i=1, \ldots, N(n)$ ,
- If  $i\neq j$  then  $a_i\neq a_j$ ,  $b_i\neq b_j$  and  $c_i\neq c_j$

Determine  $N(n)$  for all  $n\geq 2$ .

*Proposed by Dan Schwarz, Romania*
solution_md:
For any integer $n\geq 2$ , let $N(n)$ be the maxima number of triples $(a_i, b_i, c_i)$ , $i=1, \ldots, N(n)$ , consisting of nonnegative integers $a_i$ , $b_i$ and $c_i$ such that the following two conditions are satisfied: - $a_i+b_i+c_i=n$ for all $i=1, \ldots, N(n)$ , - If $i\neq j$ then $a_i\neq a_j$ , $b_i\neq b_j$ and $c_i\neq c_j$ [/list] Determine $N(n)$ for all $n\geq 2$ . *Proposed by Dan Schwarz, Romania*
Answer: $\boxed{N(n)=\left \lfloor \frac{2n}{3} \right \rfloor +1}.$ For brevity, let $k=N(n)$ . To see $k \le \left \lfloor \frac{2n}{3} \right \rfloor+1$ notice that $$ kn=\left(\sum^k_{i=1} a_i \right)+\left(\sum^k_{i=1} b_i \right)+\left(\sum^k_{i=1} c_i \right) \ge 3 \left(0+1+\dots +(k-1) \right)=\frac{3k(k-1)}{2} \implies k \le \left( \frac{2n}{3}+1\right). $$ We shall provide a construction for each of the cases $n \equiv \{0, 1, 2\} \pmod{3}$ separately. [list] - $\boxed{n=3m}$ : Consider all triples $(k, 2m-1-2k, m+1+k)$ for $0 \le k \le m-1$ and $(k, 4m-2k, k-m)$ for $m \le k \le 2m$ ; they work. - $\boxed{n=3m+1}$ : Consider all triples $(k, 2m-2k, m+1+k)$ for $0 \le k \le m$ and $(k, 4m+1-2k, k-m)$ for $m+1 \le k \le 2m$ ; they work. - $\boxed{n=3m+2}$ : Consider all triples $(k, 2m-2k, m+2+k)$ for $0 \le k \le m$ and $(k, 4m+3-2k, k-m-1)$ for $m+1 \le k \le 2m+1$ ; they work. From the previous analysis, we conclude that the bound actually occurs, hence it is the desired maximum. $\blacksquare$

ConstructionFirst we will consider $n= m\cdot \ell$ for $m\in \mathbb{N}$ . Clearly we must have $\ell > 1$ for the bound to be sharp. 1) $\ell = 2 \Longrightarrow$ we have $\{(a,2m-a) |\, a \in [0,2m]\}$ 2) $\ell = 3 \Longrightarrow$ we have $\{(a,m+a,2m-2a) | \, a \in [0,m]\} \cup \{(m+a,a-1,2m-2a+1)|\, a \in [1,m]\}$ 3) $\ell \ge 4$ . We are after $2m+1$ , $\ell$ -tuples that sum to $\ell \cdot m$ . So for even $\ell$ we can take $\textstyle\frac{\ell}{2}$ sets of $2$ -tuples and make an $\ell$ tuple. If $\ell$ odd we can take one set of $3$ -tuple and $\textstyle\frac{\ell -3}{2}$ sets of $2$ -tuples to make an $\ell$ tuple. All of which summ to $m\cdot \ell$ . Furthermore, because of how appended $2,3$ -tuples together we can assume that in the set of $\ell$ -tuples there is one tuple with exactly $\lfloor \textstyle\frac{\ell}{2} \rfloor$ zeros $(*)$ For the above construction we will define $M_{m,\ell}$ to be the $(2m+1)\times \ell$ matrix, where each row sums to $m\cdot \ell$ and no column contains two of the same number. Now consider a general $n$ and $\ell$ . Find $m$ such that $2m+1 \le \left\lfloor \frac{2n}{\ell}\right\rfloor +1< 2m+3$ . Case 1: $\left\lfloor \frac{2n}{\ell}\right\rfloor +1 = 2m+1$ . Take $M_{m,\ell}$ and add $(n-m\cdot \ell)$ to every entry in one column. Then all rows sum to $n$ and we have $2m+1$ of them, so we are done. Case 2: $\left\lfloor \frac{2n}{\ell}\right\rfloor +1 = 2m+2$ . First notice we must have $2n \ge 2m\ell + \ell \Leftrightarrow (m+1)\ell - n \le \lfloor \textstyle\frac{\ell}{2} \rfloor$ . So take $M_{m+1,\ell}$ . From $(*)$ we know there is some row with $\lfloor \textstyle\frac{\ell}{2} \rfloor$ zeros. For $(m+1)\ell - n$ of these zeros take their corresponding column and subtract $1$ from each entry. Then delete the row which had $\lfloor \textstyle\frac{\ell}{2} \rfloor$ zeros (because some entries are now $-1$ ). Now we have $2m+2$ rows that all sum to $n$ and we are done.

stem_md:
For an integer  $m\geq 1$ , we consider partitions of a  $2^m\times 2^m$  chessboard into rectangles consisting of cells of chessboard, in which each of the  $2^m$  cells along one diagonal forms a separate rectangle of side length  $1$ . Determine the smallest possible sum of rectangle perimeters in such a partition.

*Proposed by Gerhard Woeginger, Netherlands*
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Let the diagonal span from top left to bottom right. Consider the rectangle that contains the bottom left square; call this rectangle the *foundation*.
Lemma: the minimal tiling has the top right corner of the foundation touching the diagonal of 1 by 1 squares.
Proof: Suppose not. If the foundation's corner is touching a corner of a 1 by 1 square, then we may extend the foundation up one or right one to obtain a smaller perimeter. WLOG let the foundation extend one extra unit right. To see that the rectangles that get cut off are still rectangles, note that the sections remaining are the same as if a line was drawn down the vertical line a distance one to the right of the foundation. To see that the total perimeter is decreased, note that the perimeter of the foundation increases by 2, while the perimeter of the rectangles that were cut short each decrease by at least 2. Since at least one rectangle was cut, the total perimeter decreases. This shift brings the main rectangle's top right corner to touch the 1 by 1 squares, so done.
Otherwise, if the foundation's corner is not touching a corner of the 1 by 1 square, then there must exist a rectangle covering the square immediately to the top right of the top-right corner of the foundation; call this square the *key square*. WLOG all of the rectangle containing the key square is above the foundation. Then since all rectangles containing squares immediately below the key square cannot contain squares in the row of the key square and above, shifting the right side of the foundation right one unit does not turn any of these rectangles into non-rectangles. 
Repeating the process using the new key square each time, we can eventually arrive at the situation described in the previous case, so the lemma is proved.  $\blacksquare$ Let  $a_n$  be the minimal total perimeter of the rectangles that are strictly below the diagonal of 1 by 1 squares in a  $n\times n$  chessboard. Note that the foundation's perimeter is always  $2n$ , using the previous lemma. Thus,  $a_n = \min_{1\le i\le n-1} \{a_i+a_{n-i} + 2n\}$ .
Claim:  $a_{2^m-c} = 2^{m+1}m-c(2m+2)$  for  $0 \le c\le 2^{m-1}$ .
Proof:
We use strong induction. The base case of  $m=0$  is just  $a_1 = 0$ , which is trivially true, as there are no rectangles. Now we assume the statement true for  $m$  and all  $0 \le c\le 2^{m-1}$ , (and smaller values of  $m$  with corresponding ranges of  $c$  as well), and prove it for  $m+1$  and all  $0 \le c\le 2^{m}$ .
First, it is easy to see that  $a_n$  is a convex function as it consists of a series of linear functions with increasing slope; thus  $ \min_{1\le i\le n-1} \{a_i+a_{n-i} + 2n\} = 2a_{n/2}+2n$  if  $n$  is even, and  $a_{(n-1)/2}+a_{(n+1)/2}+2n$  if  $n$  is odd.
Notice that for  $2^{m-1} \le n\le 2^m-1$ ,   $$ a_{2n+1}-a_{2n}  =a_{n+1}+a_n-2a_n= a_{n+1}-a_n+2 =2m+4 $$   and  $a_{2n+2}-a_{2n+1}= a_{n+1}-a_n+2 = 2m+4$  similarly. Since  $a_{2^{m+1}} = 2a_{2^m} + 2^{m+2} = 2^{m+2}(m+1)$ , it follows that  $a_{2^{m+1}-c} = 2^{m+2}(m+1) - c(2m+4)$  for  $0 \le c\le 2^m$  and the induction is complete.   $\blacksquare$ In particular, by induction  $a_{2^m} = 2^{m+1}m$ . Since the problem asks for  $2a_{2^m} + 4\cdot 2^m$ , the answer is  $2^{m+2}m+2^{m+2} = \boxed{2^{m+2}(m+1)}$  and we're done.  $\Box$</details>

We say that a *ladder* of size  $n$  is the figure formed by all squares below one of the diagonals of an  $n\times n$  square partitioned in  $n^2$  unit squares.  Clearly any partition considered in the problem is the union of the partition of two ladders of size  $2^m$ , plus the  $2^m$  unit squares in the diagonal.

*Claim:* A ladder of size  $n$  can be partitioned in rectangles consisting of unit squares whose perimeter is at least  $p_n=2n\log_2n$ .

*Proof:* The result is clearly true for  $n=2$ , since the ladder consists of exactly one unit square with perimeter  $4=2\cdot2\cdot\log_22$ .  For larger ladders, wlog the ladder has a leftmost column of  $n-1$  squares and a bottom row of  $n-1$  squares.  Number the rows and columns such that the bottom row is  $1$  and the top row (consisting of exactly one square) is  $n-1$ , and the leftmost column is  $1$  and the rightmost column is  $n-1$ .  The squares forming the border of the ladder are  $(i,j)$  ( $i$  is the row,  $j$  is the column) such that either  $i=1$ , or  $j=1$ , or  $i+j=n$ .  Assume the perimeter of the partition is minimum, and consider the rectangle  $R$  that contains the square  $(1,1)$ ; its top right square is  $(i,j)$ , and assume that  $i+j<n$ .  Consider the rectangles (possibly only one) to the right of  $R$  having a (possibly partially) common side with  $R$ .  If these rectangles span exactly the right side of  $R$ , we may move the side of  $R$  one square to the right, mantaining the perimeter if there is exactly one rectangle having a partially common side with the right side of  $R$ , and decreasing it if there are more than one of them; the second case is then absurd since the partition considered has minimum perimeter, while in the first case, we take  $R$  and the rectangle to its right, and since they have a common side, we remove this common side transforming the two rectangles into one, absurd since the perimeter would decrease.  We conclude that there is at least one rectangle having a side that overlaps partially with the right side of  $R$ , but continues upwards.  Then, the rectangles on top of  $R$  have bottom sides overlaping with the top side of  $R$ , hence the perimeter may be reduced by moving upwards the top side of  $R$  (if there are more than one rectangles on top of  $R$ ), or joining  $R$  and the rectangle on top of it by removing the top side of  $R$  (if there is exactly one rectangle on top of  $R$ ).  Contradiction, hence  $i+j=n$ .  The minimum perimeter is then equal, for some  $i,j$ , to the perimeter of a ladder of size  $n-i$ , plus the perimeter of a ladder of size  $n-j$ , plus the perimeter of a rectangle of size  $i\times j$ , ie, since the claim is true for  $n=2$ , using  $p_k=2k\log_2k$  for all  $k<n$  for the inductive step, we find that
\[p_n\geq2i+2j+p_{n-i}+p_{n-j}=2i+2j+2(n-i)\log_2(n-i)+2(n-j)\log_2(n-j)\geq
2n+4\frac{n}{2}\log_2\frac{n}{2}=2n+2n\log_2n-2n=2n\log2n,\]
where we have used Jensen's inequality since  $f(x)=x\log_2x=\frac{x\ln x}{\ln2}$  has second derivative positive  $\frac{1}{x\ln2}$  for all  $x>0$ , and that  $\frac{2n-i-j}{2}=\frac{n}{2}$  because  $i+j=n$  for minimum partition perimeters.  Equality occurs when  $i=j$ .

When  $n=2^m$  is a power of  $2$ ,  $p_{2^m}=2m2^m$ , hence the total perimeter for the partition of the  $2^m\times2^m$  square is at least  $2p_{2^m}+4\cdot2^m=(m+1)2^{m+2}$ .  This minimum can be achieved as follows: partition first the  $2^m\times2^m$  square in four  $2^{m-1}\times2^{m-1}$  squares, two of them contain as diagonals half the diagonal that is formed by individual unit squares of the partition, two of them do not.  Take the two squares that do not contain unit squares as rectangles of the partition, and set them as rectangles of the partition, and partition recursively in the same way, the two   $2^{m-1}\times2^{m-1}$  squares that have in their diagonals unit squares that are rectangles of the partition.

Let  $C_{ij}$  denote the cell on the  $i$ -th row and the  $j$ -th row. Assume  $C_{ii}$  are the unit cells which form separate rectangles. Now we find the lower bound of the sum of perimeters in partition of  $\bigcup_{1\le j<i\le 2^m}C_{ij}$  (the lower part of the figure).

Assume that there are  $n$  rectangles altogether. Also assume that  $r_i$  rectangles contain some cell of the  $i$ -th row, and  $c_j$  rectangles contain some cell of the  $j$ -th row. In the  $i$ -th row, each of the  $r_i$  rectangles traces 2 unit vertical segments. So the total length of the vertical sides is  $2\sum r_i$ , and hence the total perimeter is  $p=2\sum(r_i+c_i)$ .

Now we classify subsets of the rectangles as follows. Subset  $S$  is of type  $i$  if  $S$  contains all rectangles which cover some cell of the  $i$ -th row but do not cover any cell of the  $i$ -th column. The number of subsets of type  $i$  is  $2^{n-r_i-c_i}$ . No subset  $S$  can belong to 2 different types  $i>j$  (otherwise  $C_{ij}$  belongs to  $S$  but doesn't belong to  $S$ ). Hence we have \[2^n\ge\sum2^{n-r_i-c_i}\implies 1\ge\sum\frac1{2^{r_i+c_i}}\] Since the function  $\frac1{2^x}$  is convex, then \[\sum\frac1{2^{r_i+c_i}}\ge2^m\cdot\frac1{2^{\frac{\sum(r_i+c_i)}{2^m}}}=\frac{2^m}{2^{\frac{p}{2^{m+1}}}}\] Therefore  $1\ge\frac{2^m}{2^{\frac{p}{2^{m+1}}}}$ , and we get  $p\ge m\cdot2^{m+1}$ .

Hence the total perimeter in the whole figure is at least  $2\cdot(m\cdot2^{m+1})+4\cdot2^m=2^{m+2}(m+1)$ .
