stem_md: A natural number  $k$  is said  $n$ -squared if by colouring the squares of a  $2n \times k$  chessboard, in any manner, with  $n$  different colours, we can find  $4$  separate unit squares of the same colour, the centers of which are vertices of a rectangle having sides parallel to the sides of the board. Determine, in function of  $n$ , the smallest natural  $k$  that is  $n$ -squared.
solution_md:
Well, that is not correct at all. The least  $n$ -squared number  $k$  is  $\boxed{2n^2 - n + 1}$ . 

Let us first prove that  $k=2n^2 - n + 1$  is  $n$ -squared. Consider any of the  $k$  columns; consider on it a maximal set of squares colored with different colors - there will be at most  $n$  such squares (since we have in all  $n$  colors available). Therefore any of the other at least  $n$  squares will belong to a pair of squares of same color with one of the set considered. So the array contains at least  $kn$  pairs of squares situated on a same column, and colored with a same color. By an averaging argument, there will exist some color that colors (at least)  $k$  such pairs.

But there are  $\binom {2n} {2} = n(2n-1)$  possible pairs of squares on a same column; when  $k\geq 2n^2 - n + 1$ , it follows there will be a repetition for the position of a colored pair on two columns, and the centres of these four squares will make up a rectangle as described.

If we manage to color with  $n$  colors an array  $2n \times n(2n-1)$  we will have succeeded. This is done by coloring arrays  $2n\times (2n-1)$  for each of the  $n$  colors in such a way that no pair of squares on a same column and colored with the same color does repeat on another column. This is done by the well-known method of scheduling a round-robin between  $2n$  teams in  $2n-1$  rounds.

stem_md: In every  $1\times1$  cell of a rectangle board a natural number is written. In one step it is allowed the numbers written in every cell of arbitrary chosen row, to be doubled, or the numbers written in the cells of the arbitrary chosen column to be decreased by 1. Will after final number of steps all the numbers on the board be  $0$ ?
solution_md:
Your solution is wrong because you misunderstood problem statement. For example, if we have a number  $a$  in a random cell of our table and we do an operation on its row, its value becomes  $2a$  and if after that we do an operation on its column, its value becomes  $2a-1$ . I think you misunderstood this part!

The answer is **yes**. You can always change table to all  $0$  with an algorithm which I will describe below.**Lemma** : If there is only  $1$  column, we can perform our operations in such a way so that column becomes all  $1$ .**Proof** : Consider we have a column of size  $n$ . Let's name its cells from top to down starting with  $1$ . Let  $a_{i}$  be the value of  $i$ -th cell. As the order of values doesn't matter, we can simply assume that the sequence of values is increasing :  $a_{1} \le a_{2} \le ... \le a_{n}$ . If  $a_{n} = 1$  we're simply done, else assume that all  $a_{j}$ 's such that  $1 \le j \le i$  equal to 1 and  $i < n$ . Now consider  $a_{j+1}$ . We will give an algorithm to change its value to  $1$ , having all its upper cells keeping their old value which was  $1$  and increase number of cells with value  $1$  as when  $n$  is finite, our procedure runs finitely and results in a column of all  $1$ . We use induction on  $a_{j+1}$ . If  $a_{j+1} = 2$  then just double all its upper cells then decrease  $1$  from all column's cells. This was basis of induction. Now consider  $a_{j+1} > 2$ . Just double all its upper cells so they all will be  $2$  as they were previously  $1$ . Now decrease  $1$  from all cells. Now, all its upper cells remain  $1$  while  $a_{j+1}$  is decreased by  $1$  so we can apply induction hypothesis to make  $a_{j+1} = 1$  and increase number of cells with value  $1$  and as this number is finite, our process terminates when all cells are equal to  $1$ . Recall that in each step in our algorithm, all values stay natural numbers which is a mandatory condition to be fulfilled.  $\blacksquare$ **Main proof** : Let's just use induction on number of columns, for  $1$  column, use **Lemma** and then decrease its cells by  $1$  to get all  $0$  table. Now consider more than  $1$  columns, apply **Lemma** on first column, after that, change it to all  $0$ . Now you can easily neglect this column and simply continue process and apply induction hypothesis as we have less columns which completes our proof.  $\blacksquare$

Let  $r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_m$  be the number of row operations done for each row and  $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$  be the number of column operations done for each column. Then the cell  $a_{ij}$  gives an equation  $a_{ij} + 2r_i - c_j = 0$ . So we have  $mn$  linear equations with  $m+n$  variables. Cleaning the table can be done iff the system has at least one integer solution (and actually should be infinite, since from a solved board we can apply one row operation to each row and two column operations to each column, cleaning everything again). This infinite solution property is not generally possessed for the system since the number of equations is larger than the number of variables. (Even if there is only one column and hence  $n = 1$ , if not all cells are of the same parity you cannot have an integer solution. If there is only one row it can always be solved though.)

stem_md: Each one of 2009 distinct points in the plane is coloured in blue or red, so that on every blue-centered unit circle there are exactly two red points. Find the gratest possible number of blue points.
solution_md:
I see no-one hurries to post a solution :o Suppose there are $ r$ red points among some $ n$ points. Since any pair of them can lie on at most two blue-centered unit circles, it means that the number $ b$ of blue points can be at most $ 2\genfrac {(} {)} {0pt} {} {r} {2} \equal{} r(r \minus{} 1)$ . Since $ b \plus{} r \equal{} n$ , this leads to condition $ r \plus{} r(r \minus{} 1) \equal{} r^2 \geq n$ , i.e. $ r \geq \left \lceil \sqrt{n} \ \right \rceil$ , so $ b \leq n \minus{} \left \lceil \sqrt{n} \ \right \rceil$ . A simple model is given by $ r \equal{} \left \lceil \sqrt{n} \ \right \rceil$ red points of coordinates $ R_i(r_i, 0)$ , with $ 0 < r_i < 2$ , for all $ i \equal{} 1,2,\dots,r$ . Take $ n \minus{} r$ blue points among those $ r(r \minus{} 1)$ given by all pairs $ (i, j)$ , $ 1 \leq i < j \leq \left \lceil \sqrt{n} \right \rceil$ , and of coordinates $ B_{i,j}(x_{i,j}, b_{i,j})$ and $ B'_{i,j}(x_{i,j}, \minus{}b_{i,j})$ , with \[ x_{i,j} \equal{} \frac {r_i \plus{} r_j} {2} \ \textrm{ and } \ b_{i,j} \equal{} \sqrt{1 \minus{} \left ( \frac {r_i \minus{} r_j} {2} \right ) ^2 }.\] It is trivial to check that on a unit circle of center $ B_{i,j}$ or $ B'_{i,j}$ lie points $ R_i$ and $ R_j$ , and only them. The choices made warrant that $ n \minus{} r \leq r(r \minus{} 1)$ , since it comes to $ n \leq \left \lceil \sqrt{n} \ \right \rceil ^2$ , and that $ \displaystyle \left ( \frac {r_i \minus{} r_j} {2} \right ) ^2 < 1$ . For the given $ n \equal{} 2009$ , the answer is thus that the largest possible number of blue points is $ 2009 \minus{} \left \lceil \sqrt{2009} \ \right \rceil \equal{} 2009 \minus{} 45 \equal{} 1964$ .

stem_md: Given are natural numbers  $ a,b$  and  $ n$  such that  $ a^2\plus{}2nb^2$  is a complete square. Prove that the number  $ a^2\plus{}nb^2$  can be written as a sum of squares of  $ 2$  natural numbers.
solution_md:
Given are natural numbers $ a,b$ and $ n$ such that $ a^2 \plus{} 2nb^2$ is a complete square. Prove that the number $ a^2 \plus{} nb^2$ can be written as a sum of squares of $ 2$ natural numbers.
$ a^2 \plus{} 2nb^2 \equal{} k^2 \iff (a^2 \plus{} nb^2)^2 \equal{} (ak)^2 \plus{} (nb^2)^2$ . And the result follows..
Why? The question is to prove that the number $ a^2 \plus{} nb^2$ can be written as sum of two non-zero squares . But you only prove the number $ (a^2 \plus{} nb^2)^2$ can be written as sum of two non-zero squares.
We just use the well-known fact: $ n$ can be written as a sum of two squares iff every primedivisor $ p \equiv 3 \bmod 4$ divides it an even number of times. Wlog $ (a,b) \equal{} 1$ and that $ n$ is squarefree. Assume $ p \equiv 3 \bmod 4$ is such that $ p \mid a^2\plus{}nb^2$ . Then $ p^2 \mid (ak)^2\plus{}(nb^2)^2 \iff p \mid ak, p \mid nb^2$ . If $ p \nmid b^2$ then $ p \mid n$ and $ a^2 \equiv k^2 \bmod p$ from the first equation. Hence $ p \mid a,k$ and then $ p^2 \mid n$ . contradiction. Hence $ p \mid b^2 \iff p \mid b$ . Then again from the first: $ p \mid a^2\minus{}k^2$ and hence $ p \mid a,k$ . But $ (a,b) \equal{} 1$ . Contradiction. And we are done. solution_md:
In isosceles right triangle $ ABC$ a circle is inscribed. Let $ CD$ be the hypotenuse height ( $ D\in AB$ ), and let $ P$ be the intersection of inscribed circle and height $ CD$ . In which ratio does the circle divide segment $ AP$ ?
[geogebra]cffcb969f3bf81e648aa52bfc167ff7ec1607a69[/geogebra] We have $ r\equal{}\frac{[\triangle ABC]}{s}\equal{}\frac{x}{2\plus{}\sqrt{2}}$ , where $ x\equal{}AC$ and $ s$ is the semiperimeter of $ \triangle ABC$ . WLOG, we assume that $ x\equal{}2 \sqrt{2}\plus{}2$ , so $ P\equal{}(\minus{}1,\minus{}1)$ , $ A\equal{}(\minus{}\sqrt{2},2 \sqrt{2}\plus{}2\minus{}\sqrt{2})\equal{}(\minus{}\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}\plus{}2)$ So $ PA\equal{}\sqrt{14\plus{}4\sqrt{2}}$ Let $ AP$ intersect the circle at $ Q$ , then $ (AQ)(AP)\equal{}(\sqrt{2}\plus{}2)^2$ So $ \frac{AQ}{AP}\equal{}\frac{(\sqrt{2}\plus{}2)^2}{14\plus{}4\sqrt{2}}\equal{}\frac{3\plus{}2\sqrt{2}}{7\plus{}2\sqrt{2}}\equal{}\frac{13\plus{}8\sqrt{2}}{41}$

stem_md: In the decimal expression of a  $ 2009$ -digit natural number there are only the digits  $ 5$  and  $ 8$ . Prove that we can get a  $ 2008$ -digit number divisible by  $ 11$  if we remove just one digit from the number.
solution_md:
We shall prove using induction that it is possible not only for  $ 2009$ , but for any odd natural number  $ 2n\minus{}1$ . We will also use the fact that a number is divisible by  $ 11$  if the difference between the sum of the digits placed on the odd places and the sum of the digits placed on the even places is divisible by  $ 11$ .
If  $ n\equal{}2$ , then there are  $ 8$  such  $ 3$ -digit numbers:  $ 555$ ,  $ 558$ ,  $ 585$ ,  $ 588$ ,  $ 855$ ,  $ 858$ ,  $ 885$ ,  $ 888$ . It is obvious that we can remove one digit so that remaining number is divisible by  $ 11$ .
Now consider the statement is true wtih  $ 2k\minus{}1$   $ (1)$ . Now we will prove it is also true with  $ 2(k\plus{}1)\minus{}1$ .
**case 1.** In this  $ 2(k\plus{}1)\minus{}1$ -digit number we can find two consequent digits which are equal. Now we remove them and get some  $ 2k\minus{}1$ -digit number - it is obvious that this number gives the same rest as the first one by  $ (\bmod{11})$ . According to  $ (1)$ , now we can take one digit away so the rest number will be divisible by  $ 11$ . Inserting these two consequent digits back to its place we obtain the number, which is divisible by  $ 11$ .
**case 2.** If there are no such two digits, then the  $ 2(k\plus{}1)\minus{}1$  number is either  $ 5858\ldots 585$ , or  $ 8585\ldots 858$ . Now we take away the  $ k\plus{}1$  digit away and obtain the number which is divisible by  $ 11$  (because it will be symmetric).

Now that we have  $ 2009$  - an odd number, the statement is also true for it,  $ q.e.d.$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Junior Balkan Team Selection Test/279829.json

candidates:
It's easy to show that the residue of a number mod 11 is the alternating sum of its digits from right to left. This means that if we have two consecutive digits that are equal, we can completely ignore them and basically take them out without changing its value mod 11. So do that to whatever our 2009 digit number is until we can't do it any more. Then we must be left with a number that has an odd number of digits and is of the form $ 858\ldots 858$  or  $ 585\ldots 585$ 
Take the middle digit out of this number, whichever one it is. The fact its digits alternate means that the consecutive digits step can cancel everything out, so we're left with 0 and the new number is divisible by 11. This generalizes pretty readily.

stem_md: From the set  $ \{1,2,3,\ldots,2009\}$  we choose  $ 1005$  numbers, such that sum of any  $ 2$  numbers isn't neither  $ 2009$  nor  $ 2010$ . Find all ways on we can choose these  $ 1005$  numbers.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Divide the numbers into groups  $ (1,2009), (2,2008),\ldots ,(1005)$ . We see that we can take a maximum of 1 number per group, as the sum is 2010 in every group, but as we take 1005 numbers, there will be exactly 1 number per every group.

We take 1005, so we can't take 1004. Now we have to take 1006 (exactly 1 number per group), so we can't take 1003, so we must take 1007 and so on.

We see that if we take  $ n$ , we can't take  $ 2009\minus{}n$ , so we must take  $ n\plus{}1$ . Now from this we see that we take all the number from 1005 to 2009, exactly 1005 numbers.

Answer: 1 way, all the numbers from 1005 to 2009 inclusive</details>

stem_md:
Is there exist four points on plane, such that distance between any two of them is integer odd number?

May be it is geometry or number theory or combinatoric, I don't know, so it here :blush:
solution_md:
;Answer: No.

Suppose  $A,B,C,D$  are points in the plane that satisfy the problem's condition. Let  $\alpha=\angle BAC$ . Then  $\cos{\alpha} =\frac{AB^2+AC^2-BC^2}{2AB\cdot AC}=\frac{a_1}{2a_2}$  for some odd integers  $a_1,a_2$ . Similarly for all angles between sides and diagonals which intersect at  $A,B,C$  or  $D$ . In particular, for  $\beta=\angle ABD$ ,  $\cos{\beta}=\frac{b_1}{2b_2}$ .

Let  $E=AC\cap BD$  and  $\gamma=\angle AEB$ . It is not hard to see that
\[|\cos{\gamma}|=|\frac{AC-AB\cos{\alpha}-CD\cos{\angle DCA}}{BD}|
=|\frac{AC-\frac{AB^2+AC^2-BC^2}{2AC}-\frac{AC^2+CD^2-AD^2}{2AC}}{BD}|
=| \frac{BC^2+AD^2-AB^2-CD^2}{2AC\cdot BD}|=\frac{2^k c_1}{c_2}\]
for some odd integers  $c_1,c_2$  and integer  $k\ge 2$  (since  $AB^2\equiv BC^2\equiv CD^2\equiv DA^2\equiv 1 ($  mod 8).

It is well know that for  $\alpha +\beta +\gamma=180^\circ$ ,  $\cos^2{\alpha}+\cos^2{\beta}+\cos^2{\gamma}+2\cos{\alpha}\cos{\beta}\cos{\gamma}=1$  (It easily follows from  $\cos{\gamma}=\sin{\alpha}\sin{\beta}-\cos{\alpha}\cos{\beta}$ ). So \[\frac{a_1^2}{4a_2^2}+\frac{b_1^2}{4b_2^2}+\frac{2^{2k}c_1}{c_2^2}+\frac{2^{k-1}a_1 b_1 c_1}{a_2 b_2 c_2}=1\]
Since  $\frac{a_1^2}{4a_2^2}+\frac{b_1^2}{4b_2^2}=\frac{e_1}{2e_2}$  for some odd integers  $e_1,e_2$ , it is clear that the L.H.S. is of the form  $\frac{f_1}{2f_2}$  for some odd integers  $f_1,f_2$ , which is absurd  $(\frac{f_1}{2f_2}\neq 1)$ .

In triangle  $ABC$   $AA_1; BB_1; CC_1$ -altitudes. Let  $I_1$  and  $I_2$  be in-centers of triangles  $AC_1B_1$  and  $CA_1B_1$  respectively. Let in-circle of  $ABC$  touch  $AC$  in  $B_2$ . 
Prove, that quadrilateral  $I_1I_2B_1B_2$  inscribed in a circle.
solution_md: The key is to show that  $B_2$  is equidistant from  $I_1,I_2.$  For instance, a step of   [this proof](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?f=46&t=98421) (see post #2) shows that  $B_2$  lies on the perpendicular bisector of segment  $I_1I_2$    $\Longrightarrow$   $B_2I_1=B_2I_2.$  Since line  $AC \equiv B_1B_2$  is the external bisector of  $\angle I_1B_1I_2,$  it follows that  $B_2$  lies on  $\odot(I_1I_2B_1)$   and it's the midpoint of the arc  $I_1B_1I_2.$

stem_md:
In chess tournament participates  $n$  participants ( $n >1$ ). In tournament each of participants plays with each other exactly  $1$  game. For each game participant have  $1$  point if he wins game,  $0,5$  point if game is drow and  $0$  points if he lose game.
If after ending of tournament participant have at least  $ 75 %
$  of maximum possible points he called  $winner$   $of$   $tournament$ .
Find maximum possible numbers of  $winners$   $of$   $tournament$ .
solution_md: suppose that these  $n$  people are  $n$  vertices of a complete graph where each edge worths  $1$  point. suppose that  $k$  people of them are  $winner$   $of$   $the$   $tournament$ , so the one between them with the least point has at most  $\frac{\dbinom{k}{2}}{k}+n-k$  points. so we have  $\frac{\dbinom{k}{2}}{k}+n-k\ge \frac{3}{4}(n-1)$  and hence the result is followed.

Let  $0<a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots\leq a_n $  ( $n \geq 3; n \in \mathbb{N}$ ) be  $n$  real numbers. Prove the inequality
\[\frac{a_1^2}{a_2}+\frac{a_2^3}{a_3^2}+\cdots+\frac{a_n^{n+1}}{a_1^n} \geq a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n\]
solution_md: It can be also proved using Holder inequality in this way: Let $S=a_1+...+a_n$ $S_1\cdot S_2 \cdots S_n \cdot \left( \frac{a_{1}^{2}}{a_{2}}+\frac{a_{2}^{3}}{a_{3}^{2}}+....+\frac{a_{n}^{n+1}}{a_{1}^{n}} \right) \ge S^{n+1} $ Where $S_1=a_2+a_3+...a_n+a_1$ $S_2=a_1+a_3+a_4+...a_n+a_1=S-a_2+a_1$ ... $S_k=a_1+a_2+...a_{k-1}+a_{k+1}+...+a_n+a_1=S-a_k+a_1$ ... $S_n=a_1+...+a_{n-1}+a_1=S-a_n+a_1$ Since $S_k \le S$ for $k=1,2,...,n$ , we conclude $\frac{a_{1}^{2}}{a_{2}}+\frac{a_{2}^{3}}{a_{3}^{2}}+....+\frac{a_{n}^{n+1}}{a_{1}^{n}} \ge a_1+...a_n$ Done. Edit to fix a typo.

Let us take a point  $B'$  such that  $\angle B'OC=\angle COD$  so  $AO$  is the external bisector of  $\angle B'OD$ .Applying the theorem of bisector and of external bisector we get  $\frac{B'C}{CD}=\frac{OB'}{OD}=\frac{AB'}{AD}$  so  $B'=B$ .

Let  $S_n$  be number of ordered sets of natural numbers  $(a_1;a_2;....;a_n)$  for which  $\frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+....+\frac{1}{a_n}=1$ . Determine 
1) $S_{10} mod(2)$ .
2) $S_7 mod(2)$ .

(1) is first problem in 10 grade, (2)- third in 9 grade.
solution_md:
a)
Note that since  $(a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{10})$  is ordered, then for any satisfying (multi)set  $\{a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{10}\}$  where not all elements are equal and is not equal to the multiset {a,a,a,a,a,a,a,a,b,b} for any distinct natural numbers a,b (which contributes 45 permutations per solution), the number of permutations of the set is divisible by two (since the element 10 from 10! is not divided out by anything), and thus the number of permutations of that set is equivalent to 0 mod 2. So the only sets that affect the modulo are the sets where all numbers are equal or the set is in the pattern {a,a,a,a,a,a,a,a,b,b}. The first case yields the set  $\{10, 10, \cdots, 10\}$ . The second case yields: $\dfrac{8}{a_1} + \dfrac{2}{a_9} = 1$  $8a_9 + 2a_1 = a_1a_9$  $(a_1 - 8)(a_9 - 2) = 16$ Which have four solutions ( $(9,18),(12,6),(16,4),(24,3)$ , which makes the sets  $\{9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,18,18\}, \{12,12,12,12,12,12,12,12,6,6\}, \{16,16,16,16,16,16,16,16,4,4\}, \{24,24,24,24,24,24,24,24,3,3\}$ ), so this case yields 180 solutions, equivalent to 0 mod 2.
So  $S_{10} \mod 2 = 1$ .

b)
Similar to above; however, we have some more cases, the number of permutations of whose is 1 mod 2:
- All elements are equal (1 permutation)
- 6 elements are equal, the other one is different (7 permutations)
- 5 elements are equal, the other two are equal but different from the five (21 permutations)
The other cases can be checked to always yield a prime factor of 2, so the number of permutations of each other case is equivalent to 0 mod 2.
The first case obviously yields  $\{7, 7, \cdots, 7\}$ .
The second case makes: $\dfrac{6}{a_1} + \dfrac{1}{a_7} = 1$  $6a_7 + a_1 = a_1a_7$  $(a_1 - 6)(a_7 - 1) = 6$ Which yields three possible solutions ( $(8,4),(9,3),(12,2)$ , which makes the sets  $\{8,8,8,8,8,8,4\}, \{9,9,9,9,9,9,3\}, \{12,12,12,12,12,12,2\}$ ), so the second case contributes 21 permutations; 1 mod 2.
The third case makes: $\dfrac{5}{a_1} + \dfrac{2}{a_6} = 1$  $5a_6 + 2a_1 = a_1a_6$  $(a_1 - 5)(a_6 - 2) = 10$ Which also yields three possible solutions ( $(6,12),(10,4),(15,3)$ , which makes the sets  $\{6,6,6,6,6,12,12\}, \{10,10,10,10,10,4,4\}, \{15,15,15,15,15,3,3\}$ ), so the third case contributes 63 permutations; 1 mod 2.
So  $S_7 \mod 2 = 1$ .

Eh, hopefully I understood the problem correctly and present the proof clearly.

Let  $H$ - intersection point of altitudes in  $A_1B_1C_1$ ,  $I$  and  $O$ -be in-center and circumcenter of  $ABC$  respectively.

solution_md:
Let in-circle of $ABC$ touch $AB$ , $BC$ , $AC$ in $C_1$ , $A_1$ , $B_1$ respectively. Let $H$ - intersection point of altitudes in $A_1B_1C_1$ , $I$ and $O$ -be in-center and circumcenter of $ABC$ respectively. Prove, that $I, O, H$ lies on one line.
I use different notation.**Problem.** *The incircle $(I)$ of the triangle $\triangle{ABC}$ touche sides $BC$ , $AC$ and $AB$ at $A_1$ , $B_1$ and $C_1$ respectively. let $H_1$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle{A_1B_1C_1}$ . Prove that the circumcenter of $\triangle{ABC}$ lies on $IH_1$ .*
My solutionLet $A_2$ , $B_2$ and $C_2$ be the midpoints of sides $B_1C_1$ , $C_1A_1$ and $A_1B_1$ respectively. $B_1C_1$ is the polar of $A$ with respect to $(I)$ , then $AI \perp B_1C_1$ it follow that $A_2$ lies on $AI$ . Furthermore, $\triangle{IFA_2} \sim \triangle{IAF}$ , then $IA_2.IA=IF^2=r^2$ therefore, an inversion through the circle $(I)$ maps $A_2$ to $A$ , similary, it maps $B_2$ and $C_2$ to $B$ and $C$ respectively, meaning, it maps $\odot(A_2B_2C_2)$ into $(O)$ , then $O$ lies on $IO_e$ where $O_e$ is the nine-point center of $\triangle{A_1B_1C_1}$ , but $IO_e$ is Euler's line of $\triangle{A_1B_1C_1}$ , it follow that $O$ lies on $IH_1$ .

stem_md:
Let  $P(x)$  be polynomial with integer coefficients.
Prove, that if for any natural  $k$  holds equality:  $ \underbrace{P(P(...P(0)...))}_{n -times}=0$  then  $P(0)=0$  or  $P(P(0))=0$
solution_md:
Consider the sequence  $a_n=P(a_{n-1}), a_0=0=a_k$ . We consider the indices module  $k$ , just for fun we define  $b_n=a_n-a_{n+1}$ Using division with residue on the polynomial  $P(x)$  we get  $P(x)=(x-a_n)*Q_n(x)+c_n$ .

Making  $x=a_n$  we get  $c_n=a_{n+1}$  so  $P(x)=(x-a_n)*Q_n(x)+a_{n+1}$ .

Finally making  $x=a_{n-1}$  we get  $a_n=(a_{n-1}-a_n)Q_n(a_{n-1})+a_{n+1}\Leftrightarrow Q(a_{n-1})=\frac{a_n-a_{n+1}}{a_{n-1}-a_n}$  so  $b_{n-1}|b_n$  for all  $n$ , and by the cyclic form of  $b_n$  we get that  $b_n=\pm c$ . No suppose that  $b_n$  is constant, so it is zero because  $a_n$  is cyclic to, then  $a_0=a_1$  and  $P(0)=0$ . So there is some  $m$  such that  $b_m=c$  and  $b_{m-1}=-c$ , so  $b_m+b_{m-1}=0\Leftrightarrow a_m-a_{m+1}+a_{m-1}-a_m=0\Leftrightarrow a_{m+1}=a_{m-1}$ , but then  $a_m=a_{m+2}$  by definition, and intuitively, that means that  $a_m=a_k$  or  $a_{m-1}=a_k$  and then  $0=a_k=a_m=a_{m+2}=P(P(a_m))=P(P(a_k))=P(P(0))$  or  $0=a_k=a_{m-1}=a_{m+1}=P(P(a_{m-1}))=P(P(a_k))=P(P(0))$ .

stem_md: $ABC$  is an obtuse triangle. (angle  $B$  is obtuse) Its circumcircle is  $O$ . A tangent line for  $O$  passing  $C$  meets with  $AB$  at  $B_1$ . Let  $O_1$  be a circumcenter of triangle  $AB_1C$ .  $B_2$  is a point on the segment  $BB_1$ . Let  $C_1$  be a contact point of the tangent line for  $O$  passing  $B_2$ , which is more closer to  $C$ . Let  $O_2$  be a circumcenter of triangle  $AB_2C_1$ . Prove that if  $OO_2$  and  $AO_1$  is perpendicular, then five points  $O,O_2,O_1,C_1,C$  are concyclic.
solution_md:
Why did this take too long :(

Clearly  $OO_2 \perp AC_1$ , so combine this with  $OO_2 \perp AO_1$  to get  $A, O_1, C_1$  colinear.
Now  $\angle O_1C_1O=\angle C_1AO = \angle O_1AO = \angle O_1CO$ , so  $O_1,C_1,C,O$  is cyclic.
Now   $$ \angle B_2AC_1 = 90-\angle ACB_1 = \angle ABC - 90 $$     $$ \angle B_2C_1A = \angle ACC_1 = 180-\angle ABC - \angle CBC_1 $$   so  $\angle AB_2C_1 = 180-(\angle B_2AC_1 + \angle B_2C_1A) = 180-(90-\angle CAC_1) = 90+\angle CAC_1$ .
This gives us  $\angle C_1AO_2 = \angle AB_2C_1 - 90=\angle CAC_1$ , giving  $A, O_2, C$  colinear.

Now  $\angle O_1C_1O_2 = \angle O_1AO_2 = \angle O_1CO_2$ , giving  $O_1, O_2, C, C_1$  cyclic. This concludes the proof.

stem_md:
2008 white stones and 1 black stone are in a row. An 'action' means the following: select one black stone and change the color of neighboring stone(s).
Find all possible initial position of the black stone, to make all stones black by finite actions.
solution_md:
Starting off we shall tweak the problem into the following: Suppose instead off 2009 stones, we will have $n \in 2\mathbb{N}+1$ . Because of symmetry we are going to just look at one side We will say that the stones are also numbered $1$ to $n$ . So we shall look at the stones whose index number is less than $\frac{n+1}{2}$ So let's say that the $i^{th}$ stone is black. So now we devise an algorithm...**The algorithm:** The algorithm looks at the first black stone, and does the action in the text, and from that point onwards, he will try to fill in the white stones, who are the closest to an end, black.If he does this successfully he goes forth to the other end, and if holes in a consecutive array of black stones appear he tries to fill 'em up. By this way will "theoretically" end up with all the stones cover black. From here we see 2 possible cases. The first case is when $i \equiv 0 (mod \; 2)$ , we can easily fill up the first half using some of those moves. We notice that if we have the following configuration (for example): $$ \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{1} \boxed{0} \boxed{0}\boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} $$ We can easily cover the first half (and more) up using a finite number of moves. So we have ended up with a configuration like this (following from the earlier example): $$ \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \boxed{1}\boxed{1} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} \boxed{0} $$ So now the algorithm continues it just pushes forward. But using this algorithm we see that we will always end up moving the white stone that will be generated after the move that follows from that, always down by one, until it end up in the second square, and we refill it using the first square. So now we have $\frac{n+1}{2} + 1$ black stones. And we see that if we apply this logic again we will always end up in the first stone being white, but we can't recover from since the second and the third stone are black, and if shift them we will get two white stones, and one black stone, but if we repeat the process we just end up doing nothing that will either increase or decrease the number of black or white stones, so the algorithm here fails. The same logic is applied for the second case when $i \equiv 1 (mod \; 2)$ , but the algorithm terminates more faster. So we have seen that this doesn't work for our algorithm, whenever we had that $i < \frac{n+1}{2}$ . But let's see what happens when $ i = \frac{n+1}{2}$ . We will prove this works by induction. So the base case is $n=3$ . Obviously this works, with just one applied move. Now let's say that this works for some $n=k$ . We add one stone to each of the ends of the array, and of course they are white. So now we have that: $$ \boxed{0} \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \dots \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \dots \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \boxed{0} $$ We now apply our algorithm to this configuration, and we get the first half successfully filled up, and the second half will look like this (including the center): $$ \boxed{0} \boxed {1} \boxed{0} \boxed{1} \boxed{1} \dots \boxed{1} \boxed{1} $$ This is easily finished with one move. (the center got white, because when the algorithm tired to fill up the first half it got used) We see now that this holds for $k+1$ . By induction we saw that if the central piece is black then we have that our array of rocks can be filled up So in our case for $n=2009$ , we see that the piece which is numbered with the number $1005$ is black.... :D
RemarkIt can be also seen using this logic that if $n \in 2 \mathbb{N}$ , then the pieces with indexes $\frac{n}{2}$ and $\frac{n}{2}+1$ , also do the trick. Here we have 2 solutions because of symmetry . . . :D

A bit lengthy solution.

We shall show that one can make all the stones black if and only if the stone in the middle is black in the initial configuration.  The "if" part is easy by induction.  We prove below the "only if" part.

Let  $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_{2009}$  denote the stones arranged in that order.  For  $1 \le i \le 2009$ , let  $M_i$  denote the move in which we select  $S_i$  (which is black) and change the colour of its neighbours.  Suppose that  $S_k$  is black in the initial configuration and we can make move  $M_{i_1} M_{i_2} \cdots M_{i_N}$  after which all the stones are black.  We assume that  $N$  is minimum possible among such possible moves.  In any move, the number of black stones in the odd positions changes either by zero or by two and hence  $k$  is odd.

Note that if  $1 \le i, j \le 2009$  are such that  $|i - j| > 1$  then  $M_i M_j = M_j M_i$ .  Thus, since the chosen sequence is minimal, it follows that between two consecutive appearances of  $M_i$ 's one of  $M_{i+1}$  or  $M_{i-1}$  should appear.  In fact, we claim that both  $M_{i+1}$  and  $M_{i-1}$  should appear exactly once.  Suppose that  $M_{i+1}$  appears at least twice between two consecutive  $M_i$ 's.  It follows that  $M_i$  does not appear between two such  $M_{i+1}$ 's, and hence at least two  $M_{i+2}$ 's should appear (so that the colour of  $S_{i+2}$  is black again).  By induction it follows that there are two consecutive appearances of  $M_{2009}$  between which  $M_{2008}$  does not appear.  This gives a contradiction to the minimality of  $N$ .  Therefore  $M_{i+1}$  appears at most once between two consecutive  $M_i$ 's.  The other case is similar.  Since  $S_i$  should be black to make move  $M_i$  it follows that  $M_{i-1}$  and  $M_{i+1}$  appear exactly once between two consecutive  $M_i$ 's.  Note that, in particular, we have shown that  $M_1$  and  $M_{2009}$  appear at most once (since  $M_0$  and  $M_{2010}$  do not exist).

For  $1 \le i \le 2009$ , let  $T_i$  denote the number of times  $M_i$  appears in this sequence of moves.  We have shown that  $T_i \le T_{i+1} + 1$  and  $T_i \le T_{i-1} + 1$ .  Suppose now that  $i < k$ .  Then it is easy to show by induction that  $M_{i+1}$  appears before  $M_i$ .  Therefore we have  $T_i \le T_{i+1} \le T_i + 1$ .  Similarly, if  $j > k$  then  $T_j \le T_{j-1} \le T_j + 1$ .  Moreover, we have shown that  $T_1, T_{2009} \le 1$ .

With  $T_0 = T_{2010} = 0$ , for  $i \ne k$ , we have that the colour of  $S_i$  at the end is black if and only if  $T_{i-1} + T_{i+1}$  is odd.  And the colour of  $S_k$  is black if and only if  $T_{k-1} + T_{k+1}$  is even.  This shows that  $T_{2i} \equiv i \pmod{2}$  for all  $i < k/2$ .  Since  $T_1 \le 1$ , it follows that  $T_{2i} = i$  for all  $i < k/2$ .  In particular,  $T_{k-1} = (k-1)/2$ .  Similarly  $T_{k+1} = (2009-k)/2$ .  Since  $T_{k-1} \le T_k \le T_{k+1} + 1$ , it follows that  $k \le 1006$ .  By symmetry, we have  $k = 1005$ .

Here is a reformulation of what people did above. Write down a configuration as a string consisting of  $b$  and  $w$ , like  $bwbbw \ldots wwwb$ . Put auxiliary stones on both sides, to take care of problems at the boundary. Now the problem is, when can I make the string \[ w (\text{string of length } 2009) w\] into \[ \square (\overbrace{bbb \ldots bbb}^{2009}) \square \] by doing the operations  $bbb \leftrightarrow wbw$  and  $bbw \leftrightarrow wbb$ ? 

Now I'll define an invariant. Given a string of  $b$  and  $w$ , we replace  $b$  by the matrix  $(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0  0 & -1 \end{smallmatrix})$  and replace  $w$  by the matrix  $(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix})$ . Then multiply all the matrices together to get a single  $2 \times 2$  matrix. The claim is that this is an invariant of the operation, and this can be easily checked by computing \[ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0  0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}^3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0  0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0  0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \] and  \[ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0  0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}^2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0  0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}^2. \]

So in our problem, if there are  $a$  white stones on the left and  $2008 - a$  white stones on the right, we want to check if we can make this to all black. If we look at this invariant, this tells us something like 
\[ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^{a+1} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0  0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^{2009-a} = (b \text{ or } w) \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0  0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}^{2009} (b \text{ or } w). \]
If you calculate both sides and do some case work, you will get  $a = 1004$ . (By the way,  $(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1  0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix})^n = (\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & n  0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix})$ .)

What I'm really doing is trying to compute the monoid generated by  $b$  and  $w$  with the relations  $bbb = wbw$  and  $bbw = wbb$ . Because I'm lazy, I was also imposing the relation  $b^2 = 1$  and looking at its groupification. The result is the infinite dihedral group  $\mathbb{Z} \rtimes \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ . Because I wanted to solution to be elementary, I embedded this group into  $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ .

stem_md:
There is a  $m \times (m-1)$  board. (i.e. there are  $m+1$  horizontal lines and  $m$  vertical lines)  A stone is put on an intersection of the lowest horizontal line. Now two players move this stone with the following rules.
(i) Each players move the stone to a neighboring intersection along a segment, by turns.
(ii) A segment, which is already passed by the stone, cannot be used more.
(iii) One who cannot move the stone anymore loses.
Prove that there is a winning strategy for the former player.
solution_md:
Say that the first player moves up and reaches point  $A$ .
Crossing out the bottom line, we get an  $m \times m$  square.
Consider a rectangle  $\Box ABCD$ , where the slope of each lines are either  $1$  or  $-1$ .
( $\Box ABCD$  is inscribed in the  $m \times m$  square)
Note that the first player can always keep the stone inside (including borders)  $\Box ABCD$ Since every point except  $B,C,D$  has an even degree, neither player can claim victory there.
Also, since the first player can move to  $B,C,D$  first by parity, moving there can ensure the first player's victory  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: $a,b,c$  are the length of three sides of a triangle. Let  $A= \frac{a^2 +bc}{b+c}+\frac{b^2 +ca}{c+a}+\frac{c^2 +ab}{a+b}$ ,  $B=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(a+b-c)(b+c-a)}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{(b+c-a)(c+a-b)}}$  $+\frac{1}{\sqrt{(c+a-b)(a+b-c)}}$ . Prove that  $AB \ge 9$ .
solution_md:
Lemma 1 :  $ A \ge a+b+c $ proof : Wlog  $ a \ge b \ge c $  . Then  $ \frac{a^2}{b+c} + \frac{b^2}{c+a} + \frac{c^2}{a+b} \ge \frac{a^2}{a+b} + \frac{b^2}{b+c} + \frac{c^2}{c+a} $  or $ A \ge \frac{a^2}{a+b} + \frac{ab}{a+b} + \frac{b^2}{b+c} + \frac{bc}{b+c} + \frac{c^2}{c+a} + \frac{ca}{c+a} = a+b+c $ LEMMA 2:  $ B \ge \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} $ proof : we have  $ (a+b-c)(a+c-b)=a^2-(b-c)^2 \le a^2 \implies B \ge \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} $  .
Finally ,  $ AB \ge (a+b+c)(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}) $ .DONE !

Remark : I think the inequality  $ A \ge a+b+c $  from IZHO-2008 SHORTLIST (was proposed by HoJolee ) .

stem_md: Find all pairs of two positive integers  $(m,n)$  satisfying  $ 3^m - 7^n = 2 $ .
solution_md: Clearly  $m = 2, n = 1$  is a solution.  Suppose that  $n \ge 2$ .  Then  $3^m \equiv 2 \pmod{49}$ .  Note that  $3^m \equiv 3 \pmod{7}$  implies that  $m \equiv 2 \pmod{6}$ , and using this we can try to find the value of  $m$  modulo  $42$  for which  $3^m \equiv 2 \pmod{49}$  holds.  With this one can conclude after some calculations that  $m \equiv 26 \pmod{42}$ .  We now consider the equation modulo  $43$ .  We have that  $7^n + 2 = 3^m \equiv 3^{26} \equiv 15 \pmod{43}$ .  On the other hand  $7^6 \equiv 1 \pmod{43}$  and a quick check for  $n = 1, \ldots, 5$  shows that  $7^n \not\equiv 13 \pmod{43}$  for any natural number  $n$ .  Hence there is no solution with  $n \ge 2$ .

stem_md: Let  $I, O$  be the incenter and the circumcenter of triangle  $ABC$ , and  $D,E,F$  be the circumcenters of triangle  $ BIC, CIA, AIB$ . stem_md:
Let  $ a,b,c$  be positive real numbers. Prove that
\[ \frac{a^3}{c(a^2 + bc)} + \frac{b^3}{a(b^2 + ca)} + \frac{c^3}{b(c^2 +ab )} \ge \frac{3}{2} . \]
solution_md:
Cauchy Schwarz galore! :P Cheers!
Let $ a,b,c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that \[ \frac{a^3}{c(a^2 + bc)} + \frac{b^3}{a(b^2 + ca)} + \frac{c^3}{b(c^2 +ab )} \ge \frac{3}{2}. \]
Titu's Lemma yields $\sum_{cyc}\frac{a^3}{c(a^2+bc)}=\sum_{cyc}\frac{a^4}{ac(a^2+bc)}\geq \frac{(\sum_{cyc}a^2)^2}{\sum_{cyc}ac(a^2+bc)}$ . Thus we wish to prove $$ 2(\sum_{cyc}a^2)^2 \geq 3\sum_{cyc}ac(a^2+bc)\implies 2\sum_{cyc}a^4+4\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq 3\sum_{cyc}a^3c+3\sum_{cyc}abc^2. $$ AM-GM yields $\sum_{cyc}a^4+\sum_{cyc}a^2c^2\geq 2\sum_{cyc}a^3c$ , hence $2\sum_{cyc}a^4+4\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq 4\sum_{cyc}a^3c+2\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2$ . Thus we wish to prove $$ \sum_{cyc}a^3c+2\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq 3\sum_{cyc}abc^2, $$ which is true by Muirhead. $\blacksquare$
Let $ a,b,c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$ \frac{a^3}{c^2 (2b+c+a)} + \frac{b^3}{a^2 (2c+a+b)} + \frac{c^3}{b^2 (2a+b+c)} \ge \frac{3}{4} . $$
Titu's Lemma yields $\sum_{cyc}\frac{a^3}{c^2 (2b+c+a)}=\sum_{cyc}\frac{a^4}{ac^2 (2b+c+a)}\geq \frac{(\sum_{cyc}a^2)^2}{\sum_{cyc}ac^2(2b+c+a)}$ . Thus we wish to prove $$ 4(\sum_{cyc}a^2)^2\geq 3\sum_{cyc}ac^2(2b+c+a)\implies 4\sum_{cyc}a^4+8\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq 6\sum_{cyc}abc^2+3\sum_{cyc}ac^3+3\sum_{cyc}a^2c^2\implies $$ $$ 4\sum_{cyc}a^4+5\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq 6\sum_{cyc}abc^2+3\sum_{cyc}ac^3\implies 8\sum_{cyc}a^4+10\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq 12\sum_{cyc}abc^2+6\sum_{cyc}ac^3. $$ AM-GM yields $\sum_{cyc}a^4+\sum_{cyc}a^2c^2\geq 2\sum_{cyc}a^3c$ , hence we wish to prove $$ 5\sum_{cyc}a^4+7\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq 12\sum_{cyc}abc^2, $$ which is true by Muirhead. $\blacksquare$
Let $ a,b,c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$ \frac{a^3}{c^2 (3b+c)} + \frac{b^3}{a^2 (3c+a)} + \frac{c^3}{b^2 (3a+b )} \ge \frac{3}{4}. $$
Titu's Lemma yields $\sum_{cyc}\frac{a^3}{c^2(3b+c)}=\sum_{cyc}\frac{a^4}{ac^2(3b+c)}\geq \frac{(\sum_{cyc}a^2)^2}{\sum_{cyc}ac^2(3b+c)}$ . Thus we wish to prove $$ 4(\sum_{cyc}a^2)^2\geq 3\sum_{cyc}ac^2(3b+c)\implies 4\sum_{cyc}a^4+8\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq 9\sum_{cyc}abc^2+3\sum_{cyc}ac^3. $$ Muirhead yields $\sum_{cyc}a^4\geq \sum_{cyc}ac^3\geq \sum_{cyc}abc^2$ and $\sum_{cyc}a^2b^2\geq \sum_{cyc}abc^2$ , as desired. $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
There are  $n ( \ge 3) $  students in a class. Some students are friends each other, and friendship is always mutual. There are  $ s ( \ge 1 ) $  couples of two students who are friends, and  $ t ( \ge 1 ) $  triples of three students who are each friends. For two students  $ x, y $  define  $ d(x,y)$  be the number of students who are both friends with  $ x $  and  $ y $ . Prove that there exist three students  $ u, v, w $  who are each friends and satisfying
\[ d(u,v) + d(v,w) + d(w,u) \ge \frac{9t}{s} . \]
solution_md: Ok, so this is pretty simple with basic probabilistic arguments. So label the edges  $1, 2, 3, \cdots, s$  and let edge  $i$  be in exactly  $e_i$  triangles. Now sum over the sum of the edges in all triangles. But each edge is in  $e_i$  triangles, so our sum $S = \sum_{\text{triangles with edges i, j, k}}(e_i+e_j+e_k) = \sum e_i^2 \ge \frac{(\sum e_i)^2}{s} = \frac{9t^2}{s}$ . Since we have  $t$  triangles, the average is  $\frac{9t^2}{st} = \frac{9t}{s}$ , so one triangle has edge sum at least that.

stem_md: Let  $ A = \{ 1, 2, 3, \cdots , 12 \} $ . Find the number of one-to-one function  $ f :A \to A $  satisfying following condition: for all  $ i \in A $ ,  $ f(i)-i $  is not a multiple of   $ 3 $ .
solution_md:
Denote set  $X={1,4,7,10},Y={2,5,8,11},Z={3,6,9,12}$ . Then elements of  $X$  maps to elements in  $Y$  or  $Z$  and etc.
Case 1: Elements in  $X$  map to all  $4$  elements in  $Y$ , then elements in  $Z$  map to all  $4$  elements of  $X$ , and  $Y$  all maps to  $Z$ . This gives  $24^3$ .
Case 2: Elements in  $X$  map to 3 in  $Y$  and  $1$  in  $Z$ . Since  $Y$  does not map to  $Y$  and function is bijective,  $Z$  maps to 1 in  $Y$  and thus  $3$  in  $X$ , and so  $Y$  maps to  $3$  in  $Z$  and  $1$  in  $X$ . There are (4x4x3x2x4)x(4x4x3x2x1)x(4x3x2x1x1) ways. 
Case 3:  $X$  maps to  $2$   $Y$  and  $2$   $Z$ , then similarly  $Z$  maps to  $2$  in each  $X$ , $Y$ ,  $Y$  maps to  $2$  in each  $X$ , $Z$ . This gives (6x4x3x4x3)x(6x4x3x2x1)x(6x2x1x2x1) ways.
Case 4 and 5 will be similar to 1 and 2. 
Hence in total,  $4769280$  ways

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be a triangle and  $ P, Q ( \ne A, B, C ) $  are the points lying on segments  $ BC , CA $ . Let  $ I, J, K $  be the incenters of triangle  $ ABP, APQ, CPQ $ . Prove that  $ PIJK $  is a convex quadrilateral.
solution_md:
Since  $\triangle ABP, \triangle APQ, \triangle CPQ$  do not share any interior point, therefore segment  $PK,KJ,JI,IP$  will not intesect each other at points except for  $P,K,J,I$ . Hence quadrilateral  $PKJI$  is simple, so if we have  $I,K$  lie on the different side of  $PJ$  and  $P,J$  lie on the different side of  $IK$ , then we are done.
Since  $\triangle APQ$  is between  $\triangle ABP$  and  $\triangle CPQ$ ,and  $PJ$  is inside of  $\triangle APQ$ , it follows  $I,K$  lie on the different side of  $PJ$ .
Let  $I_1,I_2$  be the incenters of  $\triangle ABC$  and  $\triangle APC$  respectively, easily we have  $I$  lies on segment  $I_1B, I_2$  lies on segment  $KI_1, J$  lies on segment  $I_2A$ . it follows  $P,I_1$  lie on different side of  $KI$  and  $J,I$  lie on different side of  $KI_1$ , which means  $P,J$  lie on different side of  $KJ$ .
Q.E.D.

stem_md: Does  $ a^2 \plus{} b^2 \plus{} c^2 \leqslant 2(ab \plus{} bc \plus{} ca)$   hold for every  $ a,b,c$   if it is known that  $ a^4 \plus{} b^4 \plus{} c^4 \leqslant 2(a^2 b^2 \plus{} b^2 c^2 \plus{} c^2 a^2 )$ .
solution_md:
I'd like to give a complete solution to this nice problem. I'm sure that the statement of the problem gives $a, b, c\geq0.$ The given condition $ a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}\leqslant 2(a^{2}b^{2}+b^{2}c^{2}+c^{2}a^{2}) $ is equivalent to $ (a+b+c)(a+b-c)(a-b+c)(-a+b+c)\geq 0\ (*) $ . For $a=b+c$ or $b=c+a$ or $c=a+b$ , the inequality $ a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\leqslant 2(ab+bc+ca) $ is satisfied. Therefore, let's suppose that $a\neq b+c$ and $b\neq c+a$ and $c\neq a+b$ . These conditions and $a, b, c\geq0$ allow us to notice that $a+b+c>0.$ From $(*)$ we get $ (a+b-c)(a-b+c)(-a+b+c)> 0.\ (**) $ Denoting $x=a+b-c, y=a-b+c, z=-a+b+c,$ we have the following possibilities: 1. $x, y, z<0$ - in this case we get $xyz<0$ = contradiction with $(**).$ 2. $x,y<0, z>0$ , and the similar cases - in this situation we get $x+y=2a<0$ = contradiction with $a\geq0.$ 3. $x<0, y,z>0$ , and the similar cases - in this situation we get $xyz<0$ = contradiction with $(**).$ 4. Therefore, it is compulsory to have $x,y,z>0$ . $x>0 \Leftrightarrow\ a+b-c>0\ \Rightarrow\ ac+bc>c^2$ Similarly $ab+bc>b^2$ $ab+ac>a^2$ Adding them up we obtain $ 2(ab+bc+ca)> a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}.$ Done. :lol:

<details><summary>Solution - grinding POTD</summary>$$ \color{red} \spadesuit\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{POTD Solution.}}\color{red} \spadesuit $$  Notice that, by telescoping the intial condition, we obtain that  $$ f(N+2)=f(3)+\sum_{k=2}^N f(f(k)) \quad(N \geq 2), $$  from where (since all summands are natural, thus at least  $1$ ) by induction it follows that  $f(N) \ge N \quad \forall N \in \mathbb{N}$ . solution_md:
For function $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ given that $ f(x^2 \plus{} x \plus{} 3) \plus{} 2 \cdot f(x^2 \minus{} 3x \plus{} 5) \equal{} 6x^2 \minus{} 10x \plus{} 17$ . Calculate $ f(2009)$ .
Quite nice ... First, write $ f(x)\equal{}g(x\minus{}2009)\plus{}2x\minus{}3$ . The original equation becomes : $ g(x^2\plus{}x\plus{}3\minus{}2009)\plus{}2(x^2\plus{}x\plus{}3)\minus{}3$ $ \plus{}2(g(x^2\minus{}3x\plus{}5\minus{}2009)\plus{}2(x^2\minus{}3x\plus{}5)\minus{}3)$ $ \equal{}6x^2\minus{}10x\plus{}17$ , so : $ g(P1(x))\plus{}2g(P2(x))\equal{}0$ with $ P1(x)\equal{}x^2\plus{}x\minus{}2006$ and $ P2(x)\equal{}x^2\minus{}3x\minus{}2004$ One root of $ P_1(x)$ is $ r\equal{}\frac{\minus{}1\minus{}\sqrt{8025}}{2}$ and $ P_2(r)\equal{}4\plus{}2\sqrt{8025}\equal{}a$ One root of $ P_2(x)$ is $ s\equal{}\frac{\plus{}3\plus{}\sqrt{8025}}{2}$ and $ P_1(s)\equal{}4\plus{}2\sqrt{8025}\equal{}a$ Putting $ r$ then $ s$ in $ g(P1(x))\plus{}2g(P2(x))\equal{}0$ , we get : $ x\equal{}r$ $ \implies$ $ g(0)\plus{}2g(a)\equal{}0$ $ x\equal{}s$ $ \implies$ $ g(a)\plus{}2g(0)\equal{}0$ So $ g(0)\equal{}0$ and $ f(2009)\equal{}g(2009\minus{}2009)\plus{}2*2009\minus{}3\equal{}4015$ So, if we have at least one solution to the original equation, $ f(2009)\equal{}4015$ But we know that $ g(x)\equal{}0$ is a solution of $ g(P1(x))\plus{}2g(P2(x))\equal{}0$ , so $ f(x)\equal{}2x\minus{}3$ is a solution of the original equation. So $ f(2009)$ exists and $ f(2009)\equal{}4015$ for all the solutions.

stem_md: $ a,b,c$  are sides of triangle  $ ABC$ . For any choosen triple from  $ (a \plus{} 1,b,c),(a,b \plus{} 1,c),(a,b,c \plus{} 1)$  there exist a triangle which sides are choosen triple. Find all possible values of area which triangle  $ ABC$  can take.
solution_md:
We claim that the set of all possible values is  $\{A\in\mathbb{R} : A>\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\}$ .

It is easy to check that taking  $a=b=c=t$  for any  $t>1$  satisfies the given constraints. This yields an equilateral triangle of area  $A=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}t^2$ , which yields all possible values of  $A$  greater than  $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}$  as  $t$  ranges over all possibilities.

Now, we show that all triangles satisfying the given constraints must have area  $A>\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}$ . From the triangle inequality, we can see that
\begin{align*}
b+c>a+1 &\implies b+c-a>1 
a+c>b+1 &\implies a+c-b>1 
a+b>c+1 &\implies a+b-c>1
\end{align*}
and adding these together we also get  $a+b+c>3$ . So, by Heron's formula,  $$ A=\frac14\sqrt{(a+b+c)(b+c-a)(a+c-b)(a+b-c)}>\frac{\sqrt3}{4} $$  and we are done.

solution_md:
Prove for all natural $n$ that $\left. {{{40}^n} \cdot n!} \right|(5n)!$
$v_2(RHS)=\left\lfloor\frac{5n}2\right\rfloor$ $+\left\lfloor\frac{5n}4\right\rfloor$ $+\sum_{k=3}^{+\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{2^k}\right\rfloor$ $=\left\lfloor 2n+\frac{n}2\right\rfloor$ $+\left\lfloor n+\frac{n}4\right\rfloor$ $+\sum_{k=3}^{+\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{2^k}\right\rfloor$ $\ge 3n +\left\lfloor \frac{n}2\right\rfloor$ $+\left\lfloor \frac{n}4\right\rfloor$ $+\sum_{k=3}^{+\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2^k}\right\rfloor$ $=3n + \sum_{k=1}^{+\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2^k}\right\rfloor$ $=3n +v_2(n!)$ $=v_2(LHS)$ $v_5(RHS)=\sum_{k=1}^{+\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{5^k}\right\rfloor$ $=n+\sum_{k=1}^{+\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5^k}\right\rfloor$ $=n+v_5(n!)=v_5(LHS)$ So : $v_2(RHS)\ge v_2(LHS)$ $v_5(RHS)= v_5(LHS)$ and obviously $v_p(RHS)\ge v_p(LHS)$ for any prime $p$ different from $2,5$ Hence the result.

stem_md:
Find all real  $(x,y)$  such that
  $x + {y^2} = {y^3}$  $y + {x^2} = {x^3}$
solution_md:
Subtract the two equations to get $x-y+y^2-x^2=y^3-x^3$  $-1(y-x)+(y-x)(y+x)=(y-x)(y^2+xy+x^2)$  $(y-x)(-1+y+x)=(y-x)(x^2+xy+y^2)$  $(y-x)(x^2+xy+y^2-x-y+1)=0$ So either  $y-x=0$  or  $x^2+xy+y^2-x-y+1=0$ .

Case 1:  $y-x=0$ So  $x=y$ . Substituting to the first equation, we get: $x+x^2=x^3$  $x(x^2-x-1)=0$ With the solutions  $x=0, \dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}, \dfrac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}$ .
So we get the solutions  $(x,y) = (0,0), \left(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2},\dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right), \left(\dfrac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2},\dfrac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$ Case 2:  $x^2+xy+y^2-x-y+1=0$ Multiplying by 2, we get $2x^2+2xy+2y^2-2x-2y+2=0$  $(x+y)^2+(x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=0$ Since  $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$ ,  $(x+y)^2, (x-1)^2, (y-1)^2 \ge 0$ . So  $x+y=0, x-1=0, y-1=0$ . However, this set of equations has no solution.

So the solutions are: $\boxed{(x,y) = (0,0), \left(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2},\dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right), \left(\dfrac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2},\dfrac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)}$

stem_md: Find all natural  $a,b$  such that  $\left. {a(a + b) + 1} \right|(a + b)(b + 1) - 1$ .
solution_md:
Write  $b=aq+r$ , where  $q ,r \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$  and  $r < a$ .  We see that  $b \geq aq \geq q$ , and thus, \begin{align*} 
\big((a+b)(b+1)-1\big)-q\big(a(a+b)+1\big) &= (a+b)(b+1-aq)-(q+1) \geq (a+b)1-(q+1) 

&= (a-1)+(b-q) \geq 0\,.\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;...(*)
\end{align*}  However, because  $r+1 \leq a$ , \begin{align*}\big((a+b)(b+1)-1\big)-q\big(a(a+b)+1\big) &= (a+b)(r+1)-(q+1) \leq (a+b)a-(q+1) 

&< a(a+b)+1\,.
\end{align*}  We conclude that  $(a+b)(b+1)-1 = q\big(a(a+b)+1\big)\,,$  which is true by (*) if  $a=1$  and  $q=b$ .  It is easy to see that  $(a,b)=(1,b)$  is always a solution.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Kyrgyzstan National Olympiad/404094.json

stem_md: Find all natural numbers  $x,y,z$  such that  $a+2^x3^y=z^2$ .
solution_md:
We have  $ 2^x3^y=(z-1)(z+1) $  Note that if both  $ z-1 $  and  $ z+1 $  are divisible by  $ 3 $  or  $ 4 $  we have  $ 3|2 $  or  $ 4|2 $  which is not true so it must be  $ z+1=2 \cdot 3^y $  and  $ z-1=2^{x-1} $  or  $ z+1=2^{x-1} $  and  $ z-1=2 \cdot  3^y $ .
In the first case we obtain that    $ 2^{x-2}=3^y-1 $  if  $ x=3 $  then  $ y=1,z=5 $  Now  $ x \ge\ 4 $  and  $ y $  must be even so  $ 2^{x-2}=(3^a-1)(3^a+1) $  and since  $ 4 $  divides at most one of the products we must have  $ 3^a-1=2, a=1, y=2, x=5,z=17 ( 3^a-1 $  can't be  $ 2 $  )
If  $ z+1=2^{x-1} $  and  $ z-1=2 \cdot 3^y $ , we have  $ 2^{x-2}=3^y+1 $  For  $ y=1,x-2=2, x=4 $  and  $ z=7 $  Let  $ y \ge\ 2. x $  must be even  so  $ (2^a-1)(2^a+1)=3^y $  Since  $ 3 $  divides at most one of the products  $ 2^a-1=1 $  or  $ 2^a-1=3 $ . In the first case we get the previous solution and the second case is not possible.

stem_md:
Let  $a,b,c$  be positive real numbers for which  $ab+bc+ca=\frac{1}{3}$ . Prove the inequality
\[ \frac{a}{a^2-bc+1}+\frac{b}{b^2-ca+1}+\frac{c}{c^2-ab+1}\ge\frac{1}{a+b+c}\]
solution_md:
The following similar one is also nice with the same condition: \[\frac{a}{2(a^2-bc)+1}+\frac{b}{2(b^2-ca)+1}+\frac{c}{2(c^2-ab)+1}\leq \frac{1}{a+b+c}\]
Since $2(a^2-bc)+1=2(a^2-bc)+3(ab+bc+ca)=2a(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca),$ the inequality can be written as \[ \sum \frac{a(a+b+c)}{2a(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca)} \le 1,\] or \[\sum \frac{2a(a+b+c)}{2a(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca)} \le 2.\] Now, notice that \[\frac{2a(a+b+c)}{2a(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca)}=1-\frac{(ab+bc+ca)}{2a(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca)}.\] Therefore, the inequality is equivalent to \[(ab+bc+ca) \sum \frac{1}{2a(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca)} \ge 1.\] Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we get \[\begin{aligned} \sum \frac{1}{2a(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca)} & \ge \frac{\left(\sum bc\right)^2}{\sum b^2c^2\left[2a(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca)\right]} &=\frac{\left(\sum bc\right)^2}{2abc(a+b+c)\sum bc +(ab+bc+ca)\sum b^2c^2} &=\frac{1}{ab+bc+ca}. \end{aligned} \] From this estimation, the conclusion follows. We are done. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $ y_0$  be chosen randomly from  $ \{0, 50\}$ , let  $ y_1$  be chosen randomly from  $ \{40, 60, 80\}$ , let  $ y_2$  be chosen randomly from  $ \{10, 40, 70, 80\}$ , and let  $ y_3$  be chosen randomly from  $ \{10, 30, 40, 70, 90\}$ . (In each choice, the possible outcomes are equally likely to occur.) Let  $ P$  be the unique polynomial of degree less than or equal to  $ 3$  such that  $ P(0) \equal{} y_0$ ,  $ P(1) \equal{} y_1$ ,  $ P(2) \equal{} y_2$ , and  $ P(3) \equal{} y_3$ . What is the expected value of  $ P(4)$ ?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Using finite differences, the polynomial is  $ P(x)=y_0+\binom{x}{1}(y_1-y_0)+\binom{x}{2}(y_2-2y_1+y_0)+\binom{x}{3}(y_3-3y_2+3y_1-y_0)$ . Plugging in  $ x=4$ , we have \begin{align*}
P(4)&=y_0+4(y_1-y_0)+6(y_2-2y_1+y_0)+4(y_3-3y_2+3y_1-y_0)
&=-y_0+4y_1-6y_2+4y_3.
\end{align*}
The expected values of  $ y_0,y_1,y_2,y_3$  respectively are  $ 25,60,50,48$ , so the expected value of  $ P(4)$  is  $ -25+4\cdot60-6\cdot50+4\cdot48=107$ .</details>

candidates:
Math Prize for Girls #19

I believe the answer is 17, but I'm not sure that I have a solid proof. Perhaps another reader can take what I write here and tighten it up?

First, there is some extraneous information in this problem.

Given that S is a set of 100 points, only 5 points are really important, and we can do away with some of those. 

Here's why: we are seeking the smallest possible value of d, the integer approximation of a distance determined by choice of point A which ranges over the 100 points of set S. Just set A to be the choice that gives the absolutely minimum distance between the resulting points B and C.

The other two points that are important are X and Y, the two points that are a distance 30 apart, the largest distance between any two points of set S.

So really only points X, Y, A, B, and C are important.

Another piece of extraneous information is that the distance between every pair of points is different. Since the final answer is rounded to the nearest integer, we could consider the general question about any 100 points with greatest distance 30. If two distances are the same, or two points coincide, we could perturb the configuration slightly to satisfy the original conditions without changing the value of d, the integer approximation to the distance between points B and C.

What about the other 95 points? Can you convince yourself that the value of d would not change if we remove those 95 other points? If you like, we could replace them with 95 points extremely close to X without changing the choice of A which yields the smallest possible value of d.

Point C is also extraneous. Given points X, Y, A, B and C as above, what would happen by moving C to a new location extremely close to X? Then either the new distance BC (now extremely close to BX) becomes smaller, or stays the same. In any event, we could find a new set of 100 points whose value of d is smaller or equal to the original value of d.

Let's rephrase the problem:
We are given points X and Y in the plane that are 30 units apart. Where can we place points A and B so that 
(1) Each distance between two of A, B, X and Y is no more than 30 units.
(2) Distance AB is greater than (or equal to) distance AX and AY.
(3) The largest of distances BA, BX and BY (which we call d) is as small as possible?

The points B, X and Y determine three regions of the plane: P_B is the region of points furthest from B, P_X is the region of points furthest from X and P_Y is the region of points furthest from Y. These three regions meet at the circumcenter O of triangle BXY, and point A must be in region P_B. If we move point A toward point O, then distance d either stays the same or decreases. This observation lets us assume that A is the circumcenter of triangle BXY.

We can now rephrase the problem again: Points B, X and Y are on the circumference of a circle with center A. Distance XY is 30, and no other distance between two of A, B, X and Y is greater than 30. What is the least possible value for the largest of the distances BA, BX and BY?

Since no other distance is greater than distance XY, point B must be on minor arc XY. Name angle XAY as theta. Since distance XY is no less than the radius of the circle, angle theta must be at least 60 degrees.

If theta is between 60 and 120 degrees: we can decrease the maximum of BX and BY by moving B to the center of minor arc XY. Then the maximum of lengths BX, BY and BA is BA, the radius of the circumcircle. Moving point A towards segment XY, i.e. increasing angle XAY, will decrease the length of the radius, and thus d. Thus, increasing theta will decrease d.

If theta is between 120 and 180 degrees: In this case as well, moving B to the center of arc XY will decrease the maximum of BX and BY, so assume that B is at the center of arc XY. The equal lengths BX and BY are both greater than the radius BA, so d will be the length of BX. Decreasing theta will also decrease length BX, thus d.

From the above two arguments, length d will be minimized when segment AB is perpendicular to segment XY, with angle XAY equal to 120 degrees. In this situation, triangles XAB and YAB are both equilateral, with height 15. That is, length d is the side of an equilateral triangle with height 15, or 10sqrt{3} = 17.32, thus the closest integer is 17.

It should not be difficult now to find a set of 100 points that match the original specifications, yielding a value of d equal to 17.

Regards,

Al Gebra

\[ \frac{13}{a - 13} + \frac{23}{b - 23} + \frac{42}{c - 42} \, ?\]

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Label the equations (1), (2), (3).
By (2)-(1), we have  $ (a\minus{}13)x\plus{}(23\minus{}b)y\equal{}0 \iff (a\minus{}13)x\equal{}(b\minus{}23)y$ , and by (3)-(2), we have  $ (b\minus{}23)y\plus{}(42\minus{}c)z\equal{}0 \iff (b\minus{}23)y\equal{}(c\minus{}42)z$ . Thus, we have  $ (a\minus{}13)x\equal{}(b\minus{}23)y\equal{}(c\minus{}42)z\equal{}k$ . Since  $ a\neq 13, x\neq 0$ , we have  $ k\neq 0$ .

Now, adding  $ (a\minus{}13)x$  to (1) tells us that  $ ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz\equal{}k$ . From this, we have  $ ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz\equal{}(a\minus{}13)x \iff \frac{1}{a\minus{}13}\equal{}\frac{x}{ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz}$ , or  $ \frac{13}{a\minus{}13}\equal{}\frac{13x}{ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz}$ . Similarly, we have  $ \frac{23}{b\minus{}23}\equal{}\frac{23y}{ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz}, \frac{42}{c\minus{}42}\equal{}\frac{42z}{ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz}$ . Thus, our desired sum is equal to  $ \frac{13x\plus{}23y\plus{}42z}{ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz}$ .

To compute this, we add (1),(2),(3) to obtain  $ 13x\plus{}23y\plus{}42z\plus{}2(ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz)\equal{}0 \iff 13x\plus{}23y\plus{}42z\equal{}\minus{}2(ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz)$ . Since  $ ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz$  is nonzero, this means that  $ \frac{13x\plus{}23y\plus{}42z}{ax\plus{}by\plus{}cz}\equal{}\boxed{\minus{}2}$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $ x$  be a real number such that the five numbers  $ \cos(2 \pi x)$ ,  $ \cos(4 \pi x)$ ,  $ \cos(8 \pi x)$ ,  $ \cos(16 \pi x)$ , and  $ \cos(32 \pi x)$  are all nonpositive.  What is the smallest possible positive value of  $ x$ ?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>For  $ \cos(2\pi u)$  to be nonpositive, the fractional part of  $ u$  must lie between  $ \frac{1}{4}$  and  $ \frac{3}{4}$ .

We will now consider all numbers mod 1 (or the fractional part of all numbers). Call a number valid if (its fractional part) lies in  $ [\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}]$  We must have  $ x,2x,4x,8x,16x$  be valid. Note that the range  $ [\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}]$ , when doubled, maps to  $ [\frac{1}{2},1]$ . The valid part of this range is  $ [\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}]$ , meaning that only the first half of the range  $ [\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}]$  will go to a valid number when doubled, Similarly, only the second half of the range  $ [\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}]$  will go to a valid number (in  $ [\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}]$ ) when doubled.

Since we want  $ x$  minimized, assume that it lies in  $ [\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}]$ . For  $ 2x$  to be valid,  $ x$  must lie within the first half of this range, namely  $ [\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{8}]$ . Now,  $ 2x$  lies in  $ [\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}]$ , so for  $ 4x$  to be valid,  $ 2x$  must lie within the second half of its range, meaning that  $ x$  lies within in the second half of  $ [\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{8}]$ , which is  $ [\frac{5}{16},\frac{3}{8}]$ . Repeating this process, we have that  $ x$  must lie in  $ [\frac{5}{16},\frac{11}{32}]$  for  $ 8x$  to be valid, and that  $ x$  must lie in  $ [\frac{21}{64},\frac{11}{32}$  for  $ 16x$  to be valid. Thus, the smallest possible value of  $ x$  is  $ \boxed{21}{64}$ .</details>

stem_md: Jenny places 100 pennies on a table, 30 showing heads and 70 showing tails.  She chooses 40 of the pennies at random (all different) and turns them over.  That is, if a chosen penny was showing heads, she turns it to show tails; if a chosen penny was showing tails, she turns it to show heads.  At the end, what is the expected number of pennies showing heads?
solution_md: We expect  $ \frac{7}{10} \cdot 40 \equal{} 28$  pennies originally showing tails to be turned over to heads, and  $ \frac{3}{10} \cdot 40 \equal{} 12$  pennies originally showing heads to be turned over to tails. Therefore, at the end, we would expect  $ 28 \plus{} (30 \minus{} 12) \equal{} 28 \plus{} 18 \equal{} \boxed{46}$  pennies showing heads.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2009 Contests/2009 Math Prize For Girls Problems/312242.json

stem_md: An arithmetic sequence consists of  $ 200$  numbers that are each at least  $ 10$  and at most  $ 100$ .  The sum of the numbers is  $ 10{,}000$ .  Let  $ L$  be the *least* possible value of the  $ 50$ th term and let  $ G$  be the *greatest* possible value of the  $ 50$ th term.  What is the value of  $ G \minus{} L$ ?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let the sequence be  $ a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{200}$ . The average value is 10000/200=50, so we have  $ a_1\plus{}a_{200}\equal{}100$ . This means that  $ 10\le a_1\le 90$ .

We have the formula  $ a_n\equal{}a_1\plus{}(n\minus{}1)d$ . Plugging in  $ n\equal{}200$  gives  $ a_{200}\equal{}100\minus{}a_1\equal{}a_1\plus{}199d \iff d\equal{}\frac{100\minus{}2a_1}{199}$ . Then  $ a_{50}\equal{}a_1\plus{}49\cdot\frac{100\minus{}2a_1}{199}\equal{}\frac{4900}{199}\plus{}a_1(1\minus{}\frac{98}{199})$ . This is monotonically increasing with respect to  $ a_1$ , so  $ G\equal{}\frac{4900}{199}\plus{}90\cdot\frac{101}{199},L\equal{}\frac{4900}{199}\plus{}10\cdot\frac{101}{199}$ , and  $ G\minus{}L\equal{}\frac{80\cdot101}{199}\equal{}\boxed{\frac{8080}{199}}$ .</details>

stem_md: When the integer  $ {\left(\sqrt{3} \plus{} 5\right)}^{103} \minus{} {\left(\sqrt{3} \minus{} 5\right)}^{103}$  is divided by 9, what is the remainder?
solution_md:
Let  $ a_{n\plus{}2} \equal{} 2\sqrt{3} a_{n\plus{}1} \plus{} 22 a_{n}; a_{1}\equal{}10, a_{3}\equal{}340$ .
So  $ a_{n\plus{}4} \equal{} 56a_{n\plus{}2} \minus{} 484a_{n}$ .
Therefore  $ a_{n\plus{}4} \equiv 2(a_{n\plus{}2}\plus{}a_{n}) \pmod{9}$ .
And  $ 2(1\plus{}7) \equiv 7 \pmod{9}$ ,  $ 2(7\plus{}7) \equiv 1 \pmod{9}$ .

Now  $ 103 \equal{} 1 \plus{} 6 \times 17$ .
Thus  $ \boxed{1}$ .

\[ 2009^4 \minus{} 4 \times 2007^4 \plus{} 6 \times 2005^4 \minus{} 4 \times 2003^4 \plus{} 2001^4 \, .\]
solution_md:
Sonnhard is implicitly assuming that the polynomial on the left-hand side of his equation is a constant (which is true).  With that approach, we may as well set  $a = 0$ , which simplifies the calculation to
\[
  4^4  - 4 \cdot 2^4 + 0 - 4 \cdot (-2)^4 + (-4)^4
    = 256 - 64 + 0 - 64 + 256
    = \boxed{384}.
\]

Here is the finite-differences solution I had in mind:
<details><summary>Finite-Differences Solution</summary>Let  $f(x) = {(2x + 1)}^4$ .  Then our problem is to evaluate
\[
  f(1004) - 4 f(1003) + 6 f(1002) - 4 f(1001) + f(1000).
\]
That expression is the fourth finite difference of  $f$  evaluated at  $1000$ .

Note that  $f$  itself is a quartic polynomial with leading coefficient  $16$ .  So the first difference of  $f$  is a cubic with leading coefficient  $64$ .  The second difference is a quadratic with leading coefficient  $192$ .  The third difference is a linear function with leading coefficient  $384$ .  The fourth difference is the constant  $\boxed{384}$ .</details>

Finite differences also proves that Sonnhard's polynomial is a constant, and so then we can substitute  $a = 0$ .

stem_md: Consider a fair coin and a fair 6-sided die.  The die begins with the number 1 face up.  A *step* starts with a toss of the coin: if the coin comes out heads, we roll the die; otherwise (if the coin comes out tails), we do nothing else in this step.  After 5 such steps, what is the probability that the number 1 is face up on the die?
solution_md: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>If the coin flips tails all 5 times, then the dice will always have 1 face up; otherwise, the dice has a probability of  $ \frac{1}{6}$  of having 1 face up. Thus, the desired probability is  $ \frac{1}{32}\plus{}\frac{31}{32}\cdot\frac{1}{6}\equal{}\frac{37}{192}$ .</details>

stem_md: The admission fee for an exhibition is  $ \$ 25 $ per adult and $  \ $12$  per child.  Last Tuesday, the exhibition collected  $ \$ 1950 $ in admission fees from at least one adult and at least one child.  Of all the possible ratios of adults to children at the exhibition last Tuesday, which one is closest to $  1$?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Seems fairly straightforward I think</summary>Let's start with the best case scenario. If we had the same number of adults and children, then the ratio would be exactly. Division of 1950 and 37 yields 52 + 26/37.

Thus, with 52 children and 52 adults, the total cost is at -26 of what we want. Consider the following statements:

1. If we add an adult and subtract two children  $ \implies$  net gain of 1.
2. If we add an adult,  $ \implies$  net gain of 25.

Thus, if we add 2 adults and subtract two children, we will get a net gain of 26 which is what we wanted, and it is safe to assume (or check) there are no smaller cases that seem to work.

Thus, the ratio must be  $ \boxed{\dfrac{54}{50} \equal{} \dfrac{27}{25}}$</details>

Edited for accuracy.

stem_md:
The *Fibonacci numbers* are defined recursively by the equation 
\[ F_n \equal{} F_{n \minus{} 1} \plus{} F_{n \minus{} 2}\] 
for every integer  $ n \ge 2$ , with initial values  $ F_0 \equal{} 0$  and  $ F_1 \equal{} 1$ .  Let  $ G_n \equal{} F_{3n}$  be every third Fibonacci number.  There are constants  $ a$  and  $ b$  such that every integer  $ n \ge 2$  satisfies
\[ G_n \equal{} a G_{n \minus{} 1} \plus{} b G_{n \minus{} 2}.\]
Compute the ordered pair  $ (a, b)$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>weird solution</summary>This is a linear recurrence so we change the equation  $ G_{n}\equal{} a G_{n\minus{}1}\plus{}b G_{n\minus{}2}$  to  $ x^2 \minus{} ax \plus{} b \equal{} 0$  so the general solution to this recurrence is  $ C_1 \left (\frac{a\plus{}\sqrt{a^2\minus{}4b}}{2} \right )^n \plus{} C_2 \left (\frac{a \minus{}\sqrt{a^2\minus{}4b}}{2}\right )^n$ plugging in 0 for n, we get  $ C_1 \equal{} \minus{}C_2$  

plugging in 1 and substituting in  $ C_2$  for  $ \minus{}C_1$ , we get  $ C_1\sqrt{a^2 \minus{} 4b} \equal{} 2$  

also plugging in n = 2, and repeating the substitution, we get  $ C_1 a \sqrt{a^2 \minus{} 4b} \equal{} 8$ . Therefore, we can conclude that  $ \boxed{a \equal{} 4}$ . Now that we know  $ a$ , we can just use a small example to find  $ b$ . $ G_3 \equal{} 4G_2 \plus{} bG_1$  gives us  $ 34 \equal{} 4*8 \plus{} 2b$  so  $ \boxed{b\equal{}1}$ . The answer is  $ \boxed{(4,1)}$</details>

stem_md:
Determine all integers  $n\ge1$  for which there exists  $n$  real numbers  $x_1,\ldots,x_n$  in the closed interval  $[-4,2]$  such that the following three conditions are fulfilled:
- the sum of these real numbers is at least  $n$ .
- the sum of their squares is at most  $4n$ .
- the sum of their fourth powers is at least  $34n$ .
*(Proposed by Gerhard Woeginger, Austria)*
solution_md: How is this a number theoretical problem? It should belong to either the Algebra or the Inequalities forum. Fixed. Sorry about that. Consider $\sum_{i=1}^n \left(x_i+4\right)\left(x_i-2\right)\left(x_i-1\right)^2$ . This sum has to be nonpositive (according to to the condition that all the $x_i$ 's belong to $[-4,2]$ ). Therefore, we have \[34n+18n \leq \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^4 + 18 \sum_{i=1}^nx_i \leq 11\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 + 8n \leq 11(4n)+8n\,.\] However, the above expression is indeed an equality. Therefore, (1) $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = n$ , (2) $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = 4n$ , (3) $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^4 = 34n$ , and (4) $x_i \in \{-4,1,2\}$ for every $i=1,2,\ldots,n$ . If there are $p$ terms equaling $-4$ , $q$ terms equaling $1$ , and $r$ terms equaling $2$ , then (A) $-4p+q+2r=n$ , (B) $16p+q+4r=4n$ , and (C) $256p+q+16r=34n$ . Solving this system of equations, we obtain $p=\frac{n}{10}$ , $q=\frac{2n}{5}$ , and $r=\frac{n}{2}$ . Consequently, $10 \mid n$ is the necessary and sufficient condition.

stem_md:
Decide whether the integers  $1,2,\ldots,100$  can be arranged in the cells  $C(i, j)$  of a  $10\times10$  matrix (where  $1\le i,j\le 10$ ), such that the following conditions are fullfiled:
i) In every row, the entries add up to the same sum  $S$ .
ii) In every column, the entries also add up to this sum  $S$ .
iii) For every  $k = 1, 2, \ldots, 10$  the ten entries  $C(i, j)$  with  $i-j\equiv k\bmod{10}$  add up to  $S$ .
*(Proposed by Gerhard Woeginger, Austria)*
solution_md:
Suppose that such an arrangement of  $1,2,\ldots,100$  is possible. Since the sum of all entries is  $\frac12\cdot100\cdot101$ , we get that  $S=505$  is an odd number. We partition the cells  $C(i,j)$  into four sets:


- Set  $A$  contains the cells with  $i$  and  $j$  both odd;
- set  $B$  contains the cells with odd  $i$  and even  $j$ ;
- set  $C$  contains the cells with even  $i$  and odd  $j$ ;
- and set  $D$  contains the remaining cells with  $i$  and  $j$  both even.[/list]
We denote the sum of all entries in  $A,B,C,D$  by  $S_A,S_B,S_C,S_D$ , respectively.
[list]
- Since  $A$  and  $B$  together contain all cells in the odd rows, we get  $S_A+S_B=5\,S$ .
- Since  $B$  and  $D$  together contain all cells in the even columns, we get  $S_B+S_D=5\,S$ .
- Since  $A$  and  $D$  together contain all cells  $C(i,j)$  with even  $i-j$ , we get  $S_A+S_D=5\,S$ .

Adding up these three equations yields  $2(S_A+S_B+S_D)=15\,S$ . Since in this equation the left hand side is even and the right hand side is odd, we have the desired contradiction.

In boxes labeled  $0$ ,  $1$ ,  $2$ ,  $\dots$ , we place integers according to the following rules: $\bullet$  If  $p$  is a prime number, we place it in box  $1$ . $\bullet$  If  $a$  is placed in box  $m_a$  and  $b$  is placed in box  $m_b$ , then  $ab$  is placed in the box labeled  $am_b+bm_a$ .

Find all positive integers  $n$  that are placed in the box labeled  $n$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We first prove by induction that the number  $p_1p_2\cdots p_k$ , where  $p_1, \cdots, p_k$  are not necessarily pairwise distinct primes, is in box  $\left(\prod p_1\right)\left(\sum \frac{1}{p_1}\right)$ .  For the base case,  $p_1$  is placed in box 1.

Now consider the number  $p_1p_2\cdots p_k \cdots p_{k+1}$ ; it is in box
\begin{eqnarray*} B &=& \left(p_1p_2\cdots p_k\right) \cdot 1 + p_{k+1}\left(p_1p_2\cdots p_k\right)\left(\frac{1}{p_1} + \frac{1}{p_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{p_k}\right) &=& \left(p_1p_2\cdots p_{k+1}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{p_{k+1}} + \left(p_1p_2\cdots p_{k+1}\right)\left(\frac{1}{p_1} + \frac{1}{p_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{p_k}\right) &=& \left(p_1p_2\cdots p_{k+1}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{1}{p_1} + \frac{1}{p_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{p_{k+1}}\right)\end{eqnarray*}  and our induction is complete.

It now remains to find all numbers  $n = q_1q_2\cdots q_m$  (with  $q_1, \cdots, q_m$  being not necessarily pairwise distinct primes) such that

Multiply both sides by  $q_1q_2\cdots q_m$  and consider the resulting equation (which we'll denote (*) )  $\pmod{q_1}$ .  (*) becomes  $q_2q_3\cdots q_m \equiv 0 \pmod{q_1}$ , so at least one other prime, WLOG  $q_2$ , is equal to  $q_1$ .  

Now consider (*)  $\pmod{q_1^2}$ .  Then we have

This process will continue on.  It follows that all of the primes must be equal, so  $n=p^p$  where  $p$  is a prime number.</details>

Let  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$  be positive numbers satisfying  $abc=1$ . Show that

\[\frac{a^3}{a^3+2}+\frac{b^3}{b^3+2}+\frac{c^3}{c^3+2}\ge1\text{ and }\frac1{a^3+2}+\frac1{b^3+2}+\frac1{c^3+2}\le1\]
solution_md: **Inequality (1)** Notice that $\sum_{cyc}\frac{a^3}{a^3+2}=\sum_{cyc}\frac{a^2}{a^2+2bc}\overset{\text{T2'S}}{\ge}\frac{\left(\sum_{cyc}a\right)^2}{\sum_{cyc}a^2+2\sum_{cyc}ab}=\frac{\left(\sum_{cyc}a\right)^2}{\left(\sum_{cyc}a\right)^2}=1$ **Inequality (2)** Multiplying the $LHS$ we obtain $\frac{4\sum_{cyc}a^3+\sum_{cyc}a^3b^3+12}{\prod_{cyc}(a^3+2)}\le1\Longleftrightarrow4\sum_{cyc}a^3+\sum_{cyc}a^3b^3+12\le\prod_{cyc}(a^3+2)=4\sum_{cyc}a^3+2\sum_{cyc}a^3b^3+9$ Thus the inequality boils down to $\sum_{cyc}a^3b^3\ge3$ which is clearly true by $\text{AM-GM}$ and our problem condition $\blacksquare$ .

Let  $n>1$  be an odd integer, and let  $a_1$ ,  $a_2$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $a_n$  be distinct real numbers. Let  $M$  be the maximum of these numbers and  $m$  the minimum. Show that it is possible to choose the signs of the expression  $s=\pm a_1\pm a_2\pm\dots\pm a_n$  so that

\[m<s<M\]
solution_md:
Let these numbers be WLOG  $a_1<a_2<\dots<a_n$ . Then adding  $a_3-a_2>0$ ,  $a_5-a_4>0$  ...  $a_n-a_{n-1}>0$  with  $a_1$  gives and adding  $a_1-a_2<0$ ,  $a_3-a_4<0$ ,..., $a_{n-2}-a_{n-1}<0$  with  $a_n$  gives  $a_1<a_1-a_2+a_3-a_4+\dots+a_{n-2}-a_{n-1}+a_n<a_n$ , so choice +-+-+-...-+- works.

Q.E.D.

stem_md: Consider a triangle  $ABC$  and a point  $M$  on side  $BC$ . Let  $P$  be the intersection of the perpendiculars from  $M$  to  $AB$  and from  $B$  to  $BC$ , and let  $Q$  be the intersection of the perpendiculars from  $M$  to  $AC$  and from  $C$  to  $BC$ . Show that  $PQ$  is perpendicular to  $AM$  if and only if  $M$  is the midpoint of  $BC$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $E$  and  $F$  represent the feet of the perpendiculars from  $M$  to  $\overline{AB}$  and  $\overline{AC}$ , respectively. Let  $D$  denote the intersection of  $\overline{PQ}$  and  $\overline{AM}$ . $\color{red}\textbf{Part 1:}$  If  $\overline{PQ} \perp \overline{AM} \implies M$  is the midpoint of  $\overline{BC}$ .

Note that  $\triangle{MEB} \sim \triangle{MBP}$  and  $\triangle{MFC} \sim \triangle{MCQ}$  by angle-angle. Thus,   $$ \frac{BM}{MP} = \frac{ME}{BM} $$   
and  $$ \frac{CM}{QM} = \frac{FC}{CM}. $$   

We can rewrite these two equations in the following way:  $$ BM^2 = MP\cdot ME $$  and   $$ CM^2 = QM\cdot FC. $$  Note that since  $\angle{QFA} = \angle{QDA} = 90^\circ$ ,  $ADFQ$  is a cyclic quadrilateral and since  $\angle{AEM} + \angle{AFM} = 180^\circ$ ,  $AEMF$  is a cyclic quadrilateral. 
From these, we get that  $\underline{\angle{MEF}} = \angle{MAF} = \angle{DAF} = \underline{\angle{DQF}}$ , thus  $PEFQ$  is also a cyclic quadrilateral.

By power of a point,  $MP\cdot ME = QM\cdot FC$ . This only occurs if  $BM^2 = CM^2$ , thus  $BM = CM$ . $\color{red}\textbf{Part 2:}$  If  $M$  is the midpoint of  $\overline{BC} \implies \overline{PQ} \perp \overline{AM}$ .

Since  $AEMF$  is a cyclic quadrilateral,  $\angle{EAM} = \angle{EFM}$ . From  $\triangle{MEB} \sim \triangle{MBP}$  and  $\triangle{MFC} \sim \triangle{MCQ}$ , we get that  $BM^2 = MP\cdot ME$  and  $CM^2 = QM\cdot FC$ . Since  $BM = CM$ ,  $MP\cdot ME = QM\cdot FC$ . Thus  $PEFQ$  is a cyclic quadrilateral and  $\angle{ADP} = \angle{AEP} = 90^{\circ}$ .

Therefore  $\overline{PQ} \perp \overline{AM} \iff M$  is the midpoint of  $\overline{BC}$ .</details>

stem_md: At a party with  $n$  people, it is known that among any  $4$  people, there are either  $3$  people who all know one another or  $3$  people none of which knows another. Show that the  $n$  people can be separated into two rooms, so that everyone in one room knows one another and no two people in the other room know each other.
solution_md: Let's colour the edges into red and non-edges in blue. We will show that it's possible to partition the graph into one red and one blue clique. The result holds for  $n=4$ . Let's induct on  $n$ . Let  $G=R\cup B\cup \{v\}$  where  $R$  is a red clique,  $B$  is the blue one. Assume that we cannot add  $v$  into  $R$  or  $B$ . There must exist  $u\in B$  and  $w\in R$  such that the edge between  $u,v$  is red,  $v,w$  is blue. Set  $R=\{r_1,\dots,r_m,w\}$  and  $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_k,v\}$  where  $m,k\geq 0$ . WLOG let the colour of the edge between  $v,w$  be red. Consider  $\{u,v,w,r_i\}$ , since  $u,v$  and  $w,r_i$  are red, there is no blue triangle. The red triangle has either  $v$  or  $w$  thus, the edge between  $u$  and  $r_i$  must be red. Similarily, consider  $\{u,v,w,b_i\}$ . Since  $u,b_i$  and  $v,w$  are blue, there cannot be a red triangle. The blue triangle doesn't contain  $u$  hence both  $v,b_i$  and  $w,b_i$  must be blue. We see that  $u,r_i$  are red,  $w,b_i$  are blue and  $v,b_i$  are blue thus, the sets  $R'=\{r_1,\dots,r_m,u\}$  and  $B'=\{b_1,\dots,b_k,w,v\}$  hold the condition as desired. $\blacksquare$

candidates: Take a maximum clique in one room. We must prove no one in the other room knows each other. Suppose  $u$  knows  $v$ . Pick  $x$  in the clique so that  $u$  does not know  $x$ , and pick  $y$  in the clique so that  $v$  does not know  $y$  (if  $u$  or  $v$  knew everyone in the clique, the clique would not be maximal). If  $x=y$ , and no alternative such  $x$  or  $y$  does exist, then  $u$  and  $v$  know everyone in the clique except for  $x$ , so removing  $x$  and adding  $u$  and  $v$  gives us a larger clique. If  $x\neq y$ , we can consider  $\{u,v,x,y\}$ , and these four vertices don't satisfy the requirement.
suppose it is true for 1,2,...,N.prove it is true for n+1. ...

A solution by induction:
For  $n \leq 3$  it's clear. For  $n \geq 4$ , pick a person  $a$  and apply induction on the remaining  $n-1$  people so that they can be divided into two rooms  $S$  and  $T$ , in which everyone knows everyone and nobody knows anybody, respectively. If  $a$  can't be joined to either, it means that  $a$  doesn't know someone from  $S$ , call it  $u$ , and knows someone from  $T$ , call it  $v$ . Suppose without loss of generality that  $u$  and  $v$  know each other. For any  $x$  in  $S$  distinct from  $u$ , the set  $\{u, v, a, x\}$  can't contain three people that don't know each other, as either both  $u, x$  or  $a, v$  must be among those three. Hence there are three people that know each other, and  $u$  and  $a$  can't be at the same time among the three, so  $x$  must know  $v$ . So for every  $x \neq u$  from  $S$ ,  $v$  knows  $x$ , and also  $v$  knows  $u$ , so we can enlarge  $S$  by adding  $v$  to it.
When we make this change, the total amount of people in  $S$  that don't know  $a$  plus the total amount of people in  $T$  that do know  $a$  decreases, so after a number of steps we won't be able to find such  $u$  and  $v$  and it will mean that we can merge  $a$  either into  $S$  or into  $T$ .
